arxiv-2511-20057:
Van de Voorde and Zullo chart how point weights distribute inside finite geometry structures. Their 2025 paper continues work on linear sets with complementary weights. A linear set is a point set built from a vector subspace. Each point carries a weight, the size of its overlap with that subspace. Complementary weights pair points in a balancing way.

The authors give criteria for finding points of any fixed weight. Those tests locate exactly which points carry a given weight. Special constructions yield few points of weight above one. A product-type construction then builds new sets from old ones. It starts from any linear set of complementary type. The builder controls the resulting weight distribution directly. Many distinct weights can be forced into one set. Even-type point sets with many intersection numbers follow. Such sets matter for blocking sets and rank-metric codes. Finite geometry gains finer design tools here.
arxiv-2511-20357:
Srivastava, Ketkar, Shrivastava, and colleagues steer photons between twisted resonators. Their 2025 paper studies photon tunneling in chiral hybrid systems. Two inverted split-ring resonators face each other closely. Each ring can sit at four chiral angles. A shared guide excites both rings coherently.

Spacing between rings was varied systematically. Transmission spectra shifted strongly with distance. Chirality and proximity jointly set the coupling strength. Mode splitting and interference patterns appeared clearly. Dark states emerged at specific configurations. Full-wave simulations matched the bench measurements. A circuit model explains the behavior. It captures coupling sign reversal past two hundred seventy degrees. Bright and dark modes form through phase interference. Devices were fabricated and measured directly. Tunable photonic parts could exploit this control. Biosensing and signal handling are targets. Phase-set isolators look feasible on this basis. Geometry becomes a tuning knob for light.
arxiv-2511-20457:
Kilic and Batselier identify nonlinear systems while honestly reporting uncertainty. Their 2025 paper introduces Bayesian Tensor Network Volterra kernel machines. Volterra series model systems whose output depends in nonlinear ways on past inputs. Their kernel coefficients explode in number as model order grows. Tensor compression plus probability tame that growth.

Volterra kernels are written in a factorized tensor form. Complexity drops from exponential in order to linear scaling. Every tensor part and parameter is treated as a random variable. Predictive uncertainty then comes out at no extra cost. Sparse priors pick the effective rank on their own. Fading memory behavior is learned straight from the data. Tests used the Cascaded Tanks benchmark system. Accuracy stayed competitive with rival methods throughout. Uncertainty estimates improved while computing cost fell. Funding came from the Dutch Research Council. A multi-input multi-output extension is planned next.
arxiv-2511-20557:
Bostan, Dejrah, Dioguardi, and Racioppi rescue a pretty inflation model by changing gravity's rules. Their 2025 paper embeds natural inflation inside Palatini F(R) gravity. Natural inflation's field is a pseudo-Goldstone boson with a wavy potential. Its flatness needs little fine-tuning, which theorists love. Plain versions now clash with microwave background data.

The modified gravity adds a power term to the action. The exponent n between 1.75 and two does the rescuing. In that window predictions match BICEP/Keck and ACT constraints. The tensor ratio and spectral index both land in allowed ranges. Exponents above two fail to deliver the same fix. There agreement returns only as n approaches two from above. Palatini corrections thus revive natural inflation in a specific corner.
arxiv-2511-20657:
Raziyeh Zall and four colleagues survey in 2025 the field of emotionally intelligent software agents, systems meant to notice and show feelings. The field, called affective computing since Rosalind Picard coined the term, matters more as such systems spread through daily life. Earlier reviews each covered one slice of the topic. Zall's team instead maps the pipeline, from reading a user's mood to producing an emotional reply.

The survey follows three stages. First comes understanding emotions from combined text, speech, and facial data. Next comes affective cognition: judging what caused a feeling, then letting that judgement shape decisions, learning, and reasoning. Last, the agent synthesises emotional expression back in words, voice, and face. Along the way the authors catalogue problems: small and noisy datasets, trouble merging data types, and large models that misunderstand context or invent details. They close by pointing to generative technologies as the most promising way forward.
arxiv-2511-20857:
Tianxin Wei and a large team introduce in 2025 Evo-Memory, a benchmark for whether language-model agents actually learn from experience while deployed. Most memory tests are static: the agent recalls old chat to answer a question. Evo-Memory instead feeds tasks as a stream, so the agent must search, adapt, and rewrite its memory after each job. The suite unifies over ten existing memory modules for a fair comparison.

The modules face 10 datasets spanning multi-turn goal-driven tasks and single-turn reasoning and question answering. Two reference methods anchor the scores: ExpRAG, which retrieves past experience for reuse, and ReMem, a loop that interleaves acting, thinking, and memory updates. The benchmark exposes which memory designs improve over a stream and which merely store. Code and data accompany the paper for agent builders.
arxiv-2511-20957:
Haoming Lu, David Kocharian, and Humphrey Shi redefine in 2025 image composition for the way people actually edit online. Classic composition research chases realism: paste an object so it looks physically plausible. On creative platforms, users instead place stickers and filters playfully, hunting likes, not believability. The authors call this expressive composition and build StickerNet to learn it. StickerNet works in two stages: it picks the composition type first, then predicts how the added element should sit, its opacity, mask, location, and scale.

Training data came from real behaviour, not simulation: 1.8 million editing actions harvested from the Picsart platform, each a placement the community had validated. Two subtypes dominate, filter-style and sticker-style placements. In user studies and quantitative tests, StickerNet beat common baselines and closely matched human placement choices. The paper argues the field should model user intent and style, not only physical realism.
arxiv-2511-21157:
Bare-hand interaction in augmented and virtual reality has a feedback problem: hands must stay empty, so nothing can buzz or push against the fingers. Taejun Kim and five colleagues presented QuadStretcher at CHI 2024, a forearm display that stretches the skin instead. Four driven units ring the forearm, and paired tactors pull against each other, so no bulky grounding base is needed. The stretches run along the forearm, echoing how its tendons move during real hand actions.

In a comparative study with 20 participants, QuadStretcher beat the squeeze-based baseline Squeezer at expressing force direction and heightening realism. The advantage showed most in three-degree-of-freedom tasks: stretching a rubber band, casting a fishing line, and swinging a tennis racket. Interviews added design lessons for future forearm-haptic systems. The authors frame skin stretch on the arm as a practical substitute channel when the hand itself must stay bare.
arxiv-2511-21257:
Sullivan Hué, Sébastien Laurent, Ulrich Aiounou, and Emmanuel Flachaire propose a better way to pick variables in crowded economic regressions in 2025. The popular Post-Double-Lasso method guards a target estimate, like an average treatment effect, by letting an algorithm choose control variables twice. The authors show this can still leave substantial omitted variable bias in realistic samples, especially when some variables correlate negatively with the outcome.

Hué and his coauthors build Post-Double-Autometrics on Autometrics, a selection method driven by statistical testing rather than shrinkage penalties. In simulations their method beats Post-Double-Lasso, keeping irrelevant variables near the chosen 5 percent target size while missing fewer true controls. Applied to the standard economic growth dataset, the new method casts fresh doubt on the convergence hypothesis, the claim that poor economies naturally catch up with rich ones.
arxiv-2511-21357:
Sergey Traytak and Georgiy Babushkin sharpen a classic theory of how wandering particles get captured, in 2025. Howard Berg's model describes diffusion-controlled reactions, where a small particle drifts randomly until an absorber traps it, a core picture for chemistry inside cells. Berg assumed a fully reactive spherical absorber. Real targets are pickier: often only one small patch on the surface reacts, and the particle moves inside a closed spherical cavity.

Traytak and Babushkin generalize Berg's theory to exactly that case, an axially symmetric reactive patch inside a spherical cavity. Using the dual series relations method, they obtain the trapping probability and reaction rate semi-analytically, with convergence so fast the authors call the solution practically exact. They also uncover a close link between their method and generalized separation of variables. The results benchmark simulation codes for anisotropic reactivity in cavities and open domains alike.
arxiv-2511-21457:
Victor de Vries studies when two points on a variety give the same reading of its Brauer group, in a 2025 arithmetic geometry paper. The cohomological Brauer group measures subtle obstructions on a variety. Evaluating its elements at rational points is central to the Brauer-Manin obstruction, a tool for proving that expected rational points cannot exist. His setting is an open variety over a local field, completed by a divisor boundary inside a regular model.

De Vries proves that two points yield identical evaluation maps on the tame part of the Brauer group whenever two conditions hold. First, the points must lift to integral points whose reductions in the special fiber agree. Second, their intersection patterns with the boundary divisor must define the same local cohomology class. The theorem turns a global comparison into smaller checks on the boundary and the special fiber.
arxiv-2511-21757:
Andrew Maranhão Ventura D'addario releases Medical Malice, a dataset built to teach healthcare language models what harm looks like in context, in 2025. Standard safety training uses generic definitions of harm. In medicine that misses context-dependent violations such as office fraud and clinical discrimination, the failures most dangerous to patients.

The dataset holds 214,219 hostile prompts tuned to Brazil's Unified Health System, known as SUS. Each prompt ships with the reasoning behind its violation, so models can internalize ethical boundaries instead of memorizing fixed refusals. An unaligned Grok-4 agent, steered by personas, generated high-fidelity threats across seven taxonomies. They range from queue-jumping and procurement manipulation to obstetric violence. D'addario discusses the ethics of publishing such weakness signatures openly: defenders, he argues, need the same knowledge attackers already exploit. The goal is a shift from universal safety rules to context-aware ones fitted to high-stakes medical settings.
arxiv-2512-00157:
Young stars are ringed by disks of gas and dust where planets form. Miguel Vioque and a large team present an astrometric view of companions inside the inner dust cavities of such disks in 2025. These disks, often called transition disks, may be signposts of planet formation.

Few companions have been found inside the cavities, and their role in shaping the gaps remains unclear. Precise position measurements help the team search for and characterize hidden companions. Knowing whether young planets carve the cavities would sharpen astronomers' picture of how planetary systems, including our own, got started. Astrometry, the precise measurement of positions, is what gives the study its title.
arxiv-2512-00557:
What a brain region encodes can be probed by evolving images until the region responds as desired. Haomiao Chen, Keith Jamison, Mert Sabuncu, and Amy Kuceyeski present NeuroVolve in 2025, a method for evolving visual stimuli toward programmable neural objectives. Earlier generative work replicated category selectivity in isolated regions, like faces in the fusiform area.

Isolated results give limited insight into how regions interact during complex, naturalistic vision. NeuroVolve targets combinations of regions, so interactions become part of the experiment. Programmable neural objectives could turn brain mapping into a design discipline, testing theories of how distributed patterns build a visual scene. Programmable objectives mean the same machinery can test many hypotheses about a region. For brain labs, the gain is craft. They can aim at a mix of zones at once, and ask how the zones sway each other as a scene plays out.
arxiv-2512-00657:
Arthur Ramos, Tiago de Veras, Ruy de Queiroz, and Anjolina de Oliveira wrote a 2025 study in logic and type theory. Their subject is Martin-Löf type theory, a formal system used in math and computer science. Earlier work by Lumsdaine and by van den Berg and Garner showed that types there carry a rich layered structure.

The gap they address is that those older proofs stayed abstract. They did not give clear computing steps for the witnesses that hold the structure together. The authors turn to computational paths, which record steps of reasoning as data. Readers get a more concrete account of how the layered group-like structure arises.
arxiv-2512-00857:
Gonzalo Roa, Manuel Suarez-Roman, and Juan Tapiador study a naming mess in cybersecurity in a 2025 paper. Its title plays on an old philosophy puzzle: two names can point to the same thing. Different threat intelligence vendors give the same hacking group different names, each under its own private system.

That inconsistency confuses researchers and makes it hard to merge reports from several vendors. The team maps these naming taxonomies at scale, linking vendor names that refer to the same threat actor. A shared map could help defenders correlate reports, track groups over time, and avoid treating one actor as many.
arxiv-2512-01457:
Rohin Manvi and co-authors give language models a sense of their own odds. Big models reason well but cannot judge their own work. They do not know if they will pass or fail a task. They also cannot gauge how much work a task will take.

Humans use that inner sense to set effort. They choose when to retry, when to stop, and when to ask for help. The team's method adds that sense with no extra cost at run time. Models that know their limits can save compute and flag hard cases for human review.
arxiv-2512-01757:
Recchiuti and co-authors track ion distributions as Alfven waves decay in ionospheric plasma. Parametric decay lets a big wave split into smaller ones. Ion velocity patterns then shift in complex ways. Earth's ionosphere gives a low-beta setting for that process.

Hybrid particle-in-cell simulations follow the ions in detail. The team maps how velocity distributions evolve through the decay. Those maps show heating and beam formation step by step. Insight helps read satellite data on ionospheric turbulence and its effects on signals. Ionospheric plasma is reachable by rockets and radar, so simulation maps can be checked against in-situ data within the same decade.
arxiv-2512-01957:
Quantum computers are noisy, and one fix is probabilistic error cancellation, which applies deliberately unphysical operations after a run to undo the noise on average. Leonhard Moske and five co-authors examine in 2025 what those unphysical operations really look like, using the mathematics of random matrices.

They model a noisy quantum algorithm as a random matrix ensemble and study the channels needed to cancel its errors in general terms. Understanding these channels' properties shows what error cancellation costs and when it can work at all. The analysis gives the technique, widely used on today's hardware, a firmer theoretical footing.
arxiv-2512-02157:
AI control tries to keep untrusted, possibly scheming AI systems safe by watching them with weaker but trusted monitors. Aaron Sandoval and Cody Rushing argue in 2025 that this monitoring fails when the task outruns the monitor's understanding, and propose a factored alternative.

Their approach, factoring the task and the untrusted work into pieces a monitor can actually judge, strengthens oversight of systems that might intentionally misbehave. Existing protocols that rely on a weaker overseer tend to break on complex work. Factoring cognition offers a way to keep human control meaningful as AI systems take on harder jobs.
arxiv-2512-02357:
Fast radio bursts cross the universe and arrive smeared by the ionized gas they passed, an effect measured as diffuse dispersion. Jiaming Zhuge uses Padé approximants in 2025 to compute that smearing as a function of redshift without the slow line-of-sight integration usually required.

Bursts have become tools for studying the universe's ionization and its cosmological parameters, precisely because the smearing records what they traveled through. Padé approximants are ratios of polynomials that mimic a function well and evaluate fast. Speeding the integral matters when thousands of bursts from new telescopes must each be turned into cosmological evidence.
arxiv-2512-02457:
Audio and video generation are usually trained apart, yet sound and picture in real footage shape each other. Jianzong Wu and eight co-authors ask in 2025 a pointed question: does training audio and video denoising together improve the video itself, even if only video quality counts?

Recent joint systems hinted that coupling the modalities improves synchrony, and possibly the picture too. Their experiment isolates that benefit by judging video alone. A positive answer would change how generative models are trained, making audio a teacher for vision rather than a mere companion track.
arxiv-2512-02657:
Naveen George and four co-authors help image generators forget concepts they should no longer produce. Models trained on huge web datasets can clash with privacy and copyright law, including Europe's right to be forgotten. Retraining from scratch to remove one concept costs far too much.

Their Distill, Forget, Repeat framework unlearns concepts one after another in a continual way. Each cycle aims to erase the target while keeping other skills intact. Reliable unlearning could let model owners honor removal requests quickly, without rebuilding models or losing their wider abilities. A tool that can drop one face or one style on call is a tool rights desks can use at last.
arxiv-2512-02857:
Adya Shukla, A. Gopakumar, and Paramasivan Arumugam test a bold claim about a lopsided pulsar pair. Precise timing recently suggested the eccentric millisecond pulsar binary PSR J1618-3921 may belong to a hierarchical triple. A third companion, about six tenths of a solar mass, would orbit over roughly three hundred years.

The authors constrain that proposed triple scenario with further analysis. A third body would tug the inner pair in subtle timing patterns. Confirming or ruling out the companion clarifies how such odd, eccentric systems form, a puzzle in stellar evolution. A third star would leave more marks in time to come. So the case can be tried again as new pulse times roll in, year by year.
arxiv-2512-02957:
Arturo Konderak and Patryk Michalski build Bell inequalities that can certify quantum devices from their data alone. Self testing is a powerful form of certification: observed correlations alone pin down the device completely, with no trust in its maker. Recent work framed how to self test whole families of Clifford generators.

The authors now give a systematic construction of ROCN Bell inequalities for that purpose. A repeatable recipe widens self testing beyond hand crafted cases. Device independent certification strengthens quantum communication and computing, where users must trust hardware they cannot inspect. A shared recipe turns a craft skill into a bench test, and bench tests are what let new labs join the field with trust.
arxiv-2512-03157:
Tiny shifts in atomic light can test for new forces. Benoît Assi and co-authors study those shifts in this 2025 work. Precise measures of isotope shifts, called King plots, may reveal a fifth force or teach about heavy nuclei.

Non-linear patterns in King plots have already shown up in some systems. The authors view the effect through effective field theory, a tool that sorts effects by scale. Their framing helps separate new-force signs from nuclear structure effects. That clarity is key before claiming new physics from tabletop experiments. Heavy nuclei are hard to model, so clean theory helps separate their effects from new forces.
arxiv-2512-03757:
Toeplitz operators, built from matrices with constant diagonals, appear wherever waves travel through repeated structures. Yannick de Bruijn, Bryn Davies, Sacha Dupuy, and Erik Orvehed Hiltunen study the non-Hermitian kind in a 2025 analysis preprint. Such operators need not have real eigenvalues, and their modes can pile up at a boundary, an effect known as the skin effect.

Using a generalised Floquet-Bloch theory, the authors construct eigenvectors for these operators directly. The method covers banded matrices and denser ones whose off-diagonal entries fade only algebraically, and it yields sharp estimates for how fast eigenmode amplitudes decay. Numerical tests confirm the formulas, and show banded shortcuts reconstruct dense ones poorly. The team then models a three-dimensional system of tiny resonators. Their approach exposes the mechanism that tips such a system between the skin effect and trapping around a defect.
arxiv-2512-03957:
Type Ia supernovae are used as cosmic distance markers, yet their explosions are not perfectly round, and that lopsidedness leaves marks in polarised light. Aleksandar Cikota and colleagues exploit those marks in a 2025 astrophysics preprint, studying a silicon absorption line in two dozen of them observed before peak brightness.

Earlier work tied stronger silicon polarisation to faster expansion. The team compares the data with multi-dimensional simulations of two asymmetry families: off-centre ignition patterns and global axis-shaped distortions. Their model grid reproduces the observed trend, with faster events showing stronger asymmetry. Transitional and faint normal events show the highest line polarisation and match the off-centre family. Subluminous events instead fit the global family, with weaker line signals but a notable continuum signal. Sorting these contributions, the authors argue, exposes real diversity in how white dwarfs explode.
arxiv-2512-04057:
M-theory, the framework behind string theories, becomes computable on certain curved backgrounds where holography translates hard questions into easier ones. Shai M. Chester and colleagues work on two such backgrounds in a 2025 theoretical physics preprint. Both geometries contain fixed-point loci where gluon-like fields live, dual to strongly coupled conformal field theories in three and six dimensions.

The team computes the cubic couplings in the bulk between graviton modes and those gluon modes, generically of the extremal kind. From them they extract the graviton-exchange contribution to holographic four-point correlators at strong coupling, and check it against the expected flat-space limit. The answer is organised through a reduced correlator that solves the superconformal Ward identities. They derive that solution for all theories with eight supercharges in dimensions three through six, a result reusable well beyond the two backgrounds studied here.
arxiv-2512-04157:
Dark matter detectors deep underground listen for particles whose speeds near Earth decide what the detectors can hear, yet those speeds are uncertain. Ethan Lilie and a large team quantify that uncertainty in a 2025 astrophysics preprint from the DREAMS project. They simulate more than a thousand Milky Way-mass halos, varying initial conditions along with cosmological and astrophysical parameters.

A normalising-flows emulator trained on the suite lets the authors apportion blame among the unknowns. Halo-to-halo variance dominates the spread, with host halo mass second. Feedback from supernovae and black holes, often worried over, turns out negligible by comparison. Their prediction still contains the standard halo model within its error bars, though individual galaxies can stray from it. Applied to the XENON1T experiment, the astrophysical spread proves comparable to the experimental one, a calibration target for the whole direct detection field.
arxiv-2512-04357:
Volodymyr Derkach extends a classic theory of resolvents for symmetric operators to a wider class of objects called linear relations. Operators of this kind sit at the heart of quantum mechanics and signal theory. A resolvent encodes how an operator answers inputs near a given value. The older Krein-Saakyan theory covered densely defined operators with a proper gauge subspace. His 2025 arXiv paper pushes past those limits.

Derkach links boundary triple theory with the resolvent matrix theory for relations whose gauge sits outside the space itself, the improper case. He extends the known formula that writes the resolvent matrix through boundary operators to this new class. He also gives descriptions of spectral functions in this setting. Such results matter where operators fail to be densely defined, as in systems with constraints or point interactions. The work ties two schools of operator theory into one frame.
arxiv-2512-04957:
Weiye Shi, Zhaowei Zhang, Shaoheng Yan, and co-authors ask whether large language models absorb more than word patterns when they read: do syntax, metaphor, and sound leave a mark? Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a multilingual genre study from Project Gutenberg, the free library of public-domain books. Thousands of sentences form paired tasks in six languages, telling poetry from novels, drama from poetry, and drama from novels.

Each text comes with three explicit feature sets: parse tree structures, metaphor counts, and phonetic measures such as rhythm and rhyme traits. The team checks whether models use such features and whether adding them sharpens genre calls. The study probes a deep question for language technology: are models picking up the craft of literature, or only its surface statistics? Answers shape how much trust to place in automated literary analysis.
arxiv-2512-05057:
Saikat Banerjee and six co-authors report evidence for one of topology's most elusive effects: an axion-like coupling between electricity and magnetism inside a quantum material. Theory predicts that certain materials should answer an electric field with magnetization, but catching the effect cleanly has resisted two decades of experiments on exotic quantum matter. The team hunts for it with a scanning tunneling microscope fitted with an unusual tip.

The tip is a nanowire of samarium hexaboride, a topological Kondo insulator, scanned over an iron telluride sample that orders magnetically. Tiny voltages across the junction produce a measurable magnetization in the tip. Flipping the voltage flips the magnetization. That is the signature the axion-like coupling predicts, and one that a fixed magnetism story cannot easily explain. Millivolt control of spin in a tunnel junction also suggests new tools for probing such materials and for future spin-based electronics.
arxiv-2512-05157:
Jaehun Jeong, Donghwa Ji, and Kabgyun Jeong propose an information-based gauge for quantum learning agents. Quantum reinforcement learning promises agents that exploit superposition and entanglement, and policy gradient methods are a route because the agent need not know the environment's rules in advance. But two qualities decide whether such an agent can learn at all. One is expressivity: what its circuit can represent. The other is trainability: whether its gradients stay usable. Existing measures were built for supervised learning, not for agents acting over time.

The authors define a temporal expressivity suited to learning dynamics. They show that the mutual information between the agent's action choices and a discretized reward signal bounds both the scaled gradient size and their new metric. Under assumptions, the measure yields a one-sided screening test that flags fragile initializations across circuit designs before training — a checkpoint for quantum policy pipelines.
arxiv-2512-05357:
Anna Luchnikov, Jim Wittebol, and Jeroen Zuiddam prove a universality result about Shannon capacity of graphs. Shannon introduced capacity in 1956 to measure the rate of zero-error communication. It depends on how independent sets grow in strong powers of a graph. Much about it, even whether it is computable, remains unknown. Recent duality theory recasts capacity through the asymptotic relations between graphs.

The authors ask how complex the ordering defined by those relations can be. Their main theorem: the order is universal for countable preorders, meaning any countable partial order can be embedded inside it. Universality was known for the non-asymptotic version; the proof uses asymptotic spectrum duality and the spectrum's convex structure, and yields a new proof of the older result as a by-product. Asymptotic graph comparison is thus as structurally rich as it could possibly be.
arxiv-2512-05557:
Xingxi Yin and seven co-authors release a dataset built to teach machines visual storytelling with steady characters. Keeping a character's identity steady across a story's panels, while pose, expression, and scene change on cue, is a long-standing failure of generative models. Existing datasets neither reach the needed fidelity nor separate stable identity from transient attributes. Their collection pairs two thousand uniquely stylized characters with ten thousand illustrated stories, each with split control signals.

A human-in-the-loop pipeline generates the data. Expert-verified character templates anchor identity, and language models plan the stories. A quality gate — multimodal scoring, prompt tuning that runs itself, and local image editing — enforces consistency down to the pixel. A split control scheme keeps identity steady while attributes vary. Models fine-tuned on the dataset match closed-source systems at generating visual narratives. The bottleneck, it seems, was the data's structure all along.
arxiv-2512-05857:
Maximilian Freiheit and Ulrich Haisch use jet pairs at the Large Hadron Collider to bound new interactions among heavy quarks. The search frame is the Standard Model effective field theory, which catalogs possible extra interactions as operators. Ten operators couple four third generation quarks at once. Only the five built purely from bottom quarks show up directly in dijet data, pairs of particle sprays.

Renormalization group effects mix the operators across scales, so all ten leave fingerprints in the data. The analysis includes the leading logarithmic part of that mixing up to two loops. The resulting bounds on the five bottom operators are as strong as, or nominally stronger than, current dedicated limits. The other five, reachable only through the mixing, stay weakly constrained even with the enhanced corrections counted. The result maps where jets already squeeze new physics, and where room remains.
arxiv-2512-06257:
Mauricio Martinez and Christopher Plumberg study how a hot, thin gas spreads when it is stretched in a symmetric way. The model has roots in the study of matter made in particle collisions. They place the gas on a curved stage built from a three dimensional space of steady curve, cut into slices that can be flat, round, or saddle shaped. Each slicing has its own set of symmetries.

Using those symmetries, the authors show the gas pattern can depend only on a few key values, no matter the slicing. That yields one exact answer to the flow equation for all three cuts. Two cuts give back two famous flows known for years. The saddle cut gives a new flow, named the Grozdanov flow. Smooth flow and free flight both appear as limits of the new answer. The work unifies old cases and adds a fresh one.
arxiv-2512-06657:
Qiyan Zhao, Yue Yan, and Da-Han Wang build a detector that finds text in wild photos: shop signs, labels, and street writing at odd angles and curves. Convolutional networks read such scenes locally and can miss the long range links that tie a word together. Transformer models see farther but can forget key detail or latch onto clutter when the sequence runs long.

Their detector leans on Mamba, a state space model that handles long sequences with a selective, linear cost mechanism. A top k selection step keeps the encoder focused on the most relevant information and cuts interference from the rest. A dual scale feed forward network and a pyramid enhancement module help features mix across sizes. On three public benchmarks of curved and cluttered text, the method reached top or near top scores, which suits document scanning and scene reading on the move.
arxiv-2512-07057:
Min Ye, Dave Wecker, and Nicolas Delfosse build a faster decoder for quantum error correction, the software that must untangle errors in a quantum computer before they pile up. Their target is a family called quantum LDPC codes, whose checking pattern is sparse. The standard decoder for six years has paired belief propagation with a cleanup step, but it can be slow and still miss too often at the speeds real machines demand.

Their decoder searches instead: a beam of candidate corrections is kept alive, guided by belief propagation's beliefs about each error. Tuning the beam's width trades speed for accuracy. On a well-studied bicycle code under realistic circuit noise, a wide beam cut the logical error rate many-fold against the standard decoder. A narrow beam matched the standard accuracy while running far faster at the tail end of runtimes.
arxiv-2512-07157:
Tony J Puthenpurakal studies a distinguished element in the algebra of a finite group acting on a polynomial ring. Over a finite field, the product of all nonzero linear forms, the top Dickson class, is a classic invariant. Puthenpurakal shows that a power of this single element kills, in the technical sense of annihilation, a wide range of cohomology modules built from the ring and its invariant subring.

Two families of modules are covered: the group cohomology of the full ring viewed over the invariants. At every positive degree, and the local cohomology of the invariant ring itself across most degrees. In each case the Dickson class lands in the radical of the annihilator, the next best thing to annihilating directly. The payoff is uniform: one fixed power of the element serves as a cohomological annihilator for all the modules at once.
arxiv-2512-07557:
Jitendra Tugnait wrote this 2025 statistics paper on learning networks from moving data. Each node in his network is not a single stream but a bundle of attributes over time. The goal is the conditional independence graph, which shows which bundles truly interact.

Older methods were built for one scalar series per node. Tugnait gives a unified theory for the richer multi-attribute case. His approach uses a penalized likelihood written in the frequency domain. The discrete Fourier transform converts the time data for that purpose. Both convex and non-convex penalty shapes come under the same analysis. He proves when the estimated spectrum settles onto the truth. He also proves when the true graph is recovered in high dimensions. No special incoherence conditions are needed for those guarantees. Tuning choices are guided by the Bayesian information criterion. Tests on synthetic and real data show the method at work.
arxiv-2512-07957:
Oleksandr Tomalak wrote this 2025 particle physics paper on a reaction that anchors neutrino science. Inverse beta decay is how reactor antineutrinos reveal themselves in detectors. Its rate sets the scale for everything those experiments claim to measure.

Tomalak works out the radiative corrections to that reaction in full. The tool is heavy-baryon chiral perturbation theory, built for low-energy strong forces. Quantum electrodynamics and chromodynamics join electroweak effects for the first time. The result is an updated cross section with high precision claimed. A full error budget comes with the central value. The positron energy spectrum, with those effects folded in, is also given. Reactor flux scaling rests squarely on numbers like these. Oscillation values are read off against that scaling, aiming below one percent in error. Searches for new physics at power plants lean on the same foundation. Such care quietly underpins a whole experimental program.
arxiv-2512-08057:
Md Mostafizer Rahman, Ariful Islam Shiplu, and colleagues, computer science researchers, posted a survey and evaluation study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is large language models in education and research. They compare two leading systems, ChatGPT and DeepSeek, across accuracy, computing efficiency, and the experience of real users.

The team benchmarks both models on text generation, programming, and specialized problem solving. ChatGPT proved stronger at general language understanding and writing, while DeepSeek did better on programming tasks, thanks to its efficiency focused design. Both models gave medically sound diagnostic outputs and solved hard mathematics problems. A survey of students, educators, and researchers adds the practical side, weighing real benefits against limits. Together, the results give institutions a grounded picture of what these tools can and cannot do.
arxiv-2512-08157:
Lei Xie, Hengtao He, Yifeng Xiong, Fan Liu, and Shi Jin, wireless engineering researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is adaptive matched filtering for sensing with communication signals in cluttered settings. When sensing and data share one waveform, the signal to clutter ratio swings with the random payload, making design for each instant impractical.

The authors shift the goal from the instant value to the average over all payloads. Using random matrix theory, they derive an approximation for that average that stays accurate even at moderate sizes. For a fixed modulation basis, one finding favors phase shift keying over other constellations, and another favors OFDM waveforms. They then design pilot schemes that either chase the best instant performance or optimize the average at lower complexity. Simulations confirm both the theory and the gains.
arxiv-2512-08257:
Preksha Girish, Rachana Mysore, Mahanthesha U, and colleagues, researchers in India, posted a framework paper on arXiv in December 2025. They model the risk of two deadly events: sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and acute ischemic stroke. Both involve tangled links across the cortex, brainstem, and autonomic system, which single signal monitors miss.

Their deep learning framework fuses many signals at once, including brain waves, heart signals, breathing, blood oxygen, muscle activity, and brain scans. It blends curved manifold embeddings, group based features, and energy flow modeling, joined by cross modal attention. Stroke spread is modeled as slow diffusion over structural brain graphs. On a combined dataset, the method improved predictive accuracy over baselines. It also produced readable risk markers, such as manifold curvature and attention entropy, that clinicians could inspect. The authors offer the system as a principled base for early warning in these disorders.
arxiv-2512-08457:
Saketh Virupakshi, Xinzhu Zheng, Karol Frydrych, and colleagues, materials scientists, posted a simulation study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is Hadfield steel, a manganese steel famous for hardening as it deforms, used in crushers and rail crossings. Its strength comes from two deformation modes, slip and twinning, tangled together with geometry effects like notches, and separating their roles is hard in experiments alone.

Detailed finite element simulations use a crystal plasticity model that carries both slip and twinning, including how new twin orientations appear unevenly and how the modes harden each other. Matching tests on single crystal specimens anchor the model, which reproduced each orientation stress strain curve and the lopsided way a notch deforms. By switching mechanisms off one at a time, the team isolated what twinning alone does to the response, giving a mechanistic picture of this steel.
arxiv-2512-08657:
Renato Cordeiro Ferreira and coauthors report lessons from building Ocean Guard, a machine learning system that spots odd behavior at sea. Such systems need many parts to work together, which makes reuse across projects hard. The report focuses on software design choices that helped the team build several services from one shared codebase.

The team used the Ports and Adapters pattern, also called hexagonal design, to keep core logic apart from outside tools and data sources. That split let them reuse much of the system while changing the parts that connect to the maritime setting. The authors share the problems they met and what worked in practice. Their aim is to help other engineers, data scientists, and machine learning teams build systems that are easier to adapt and extend.
arxiv-2512-08757:
Ujjwal Pratap, Steffen Hofmann, and Christian Hans study how to run microgrids well when renewable supply and demand are both uncertain. Microgrids with a high share of wind and solar must stay near optimal across a wide range of weather and load scenarios. The authors frame the task as a minimum regret robust control problem.

Their solution uses the layered control structure that microgrids already have. An enhanced primary layer combines droop control with automatic limits on power and energy. The authors prove that, under set conditions, constant power setpoints from that layer can achieve optimal operation. Those setpoints are then paired with an energy manager that solves a robust scheduling problem inside a predictive control loop. A case study shows the design works in practice. The approach aims for dependable operation without constant complex rescheduling.
arxiv-2512-08857:
Abdurrazaq and coauthors propose a low cost fix to density formula theory that improves predictions for germanium, a key semiconductor. Accuracy in such work depends on the chosen exchange correlation formula. A common formula overestimates lattice size and badly underestimates band gaps, while hybrid formulas do better overall but cost far more.

Even hybrids fail for germanium, since they cannot match both main band gaps at once. The authors trace the problem to a wrong energy gap that causes unreal mixing between states. Their fix applies a semi empirical shift only to a selected set of states. For germanium, that restores the correct ordering and character of band edges. It also yields accurate lattice, elastic, and thermal properties at a fraction of hybrid cost. The result offers a practical alternative for this challenging case.
arxiv-2512-08957:
Dhruv Nigam and coauthors present LUMOS, a transformer system for predicting user behavior on large consumer platforms without task specific models. Standard methods rely on separate models per task and heavy manual feature design. That process is slow, costly, and hard to scale across a growing set of prediction needs.

LUMOS learns many tasks jointly from raw user activity data alone. A new cross attention process conditions predictions on known future events, such as holidays or sales, so questions about upcoming engagement can be answered directly. Activities, event context, and static user traits are tokenized together through specialized embedding paths. Tests use a production data set with activity from hundreds of millions of users. The system beats standard task specific models on classification and regression measures across five tasks. Online testing shows a measurable lift in daily active users, confirming real business value.
arxiv-2512-09457:
Hao Chen, Xu Pan, and Conghui Xie work in projective geometry and coding theory on blocking sets and minimal codes, two linked structures. A blocking set meets every line in a projective space, and a minimal code is an error-correcting code where no codeword's support contains another's. They generalize the notions, adding fold and level parameters.

Their first result is a lower bound on the size of these blocking sets, proved without a restriction the 1983 bound of Beutelspacher required. It is stronger than that result. A matching bound follows for the lengths of such codes. They prove that codes minimal at one level above are minimal at that level, and they generalize the Ashikhmin-Barg condition, a test for minimality. The authors construct many infinite families of codes, some satisfying and some violating the condition. They add binary examples that are minimal but not minimal at the next level.
arxiv-2512-09657:
Carlos Patiño and colleagues use first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations to predict how vanadium doping changes the magnetism of Ti2C. Ti2C is a member of the MXene family of two-dimensional materials. MXenes combine conductivity with surface chemistry, and adding spin centers by doping could make them useful for spintronics, magnetic sensing, and data storage.

Pristine Ti2C, they find, has ferromagnetic coupling within each layer and antiferromagnetic coupling between layers, giving an antiferromagnetic ground state overall. Substituting vanadium alters those couplings, but every doped configuration studied, one with a single vanadium and three with two, keeps a predominantly antiferromagnetic order. Doping strengthens the magnetic response, in one arrangement showing increased low-field susceptibility and partial spin alignment across layers. Since samples will mix types, the collective behavior shows signatures of the vanadium. The authors offer the results as guidance for engineering MXene magnetism.
arxiv-2512-09757:
Kristof Varadi, Mark Marosi, and Peter Antal look inside transformer models that generate chemical structures. These models produce valid and varied molecules, yet little was known about how they learn the rules of molecular notation. The authors carry out a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on small drug like molecules. They trace how the models handle structure at several levels, from basic syntax to broader rules of chemical validity.

Using sparse autoencoders, the team pulls out dictionaries of features tied to chemically meaningful patterns inside the network. They then test what they found on practical prediction tasks. The tests show that insight into the inner workings can carry over into better performance in real settings. The work offers a clearer picture of what these generative chemistry models actually compute.
arxiv-2512-09857: Svetlana Gorokhova studies compactness properties of operators whose outputs land in a Fréchet space, a general kind of topological vector space common in analysis. The operators start either from a Hilbert space or from a Banach lattice. The compactness she examines is not the classical kind. Instead it is tested along special sequences: orthonormal sequences in the Hilbert space case, and disjoint bounded sequences in the lattice case. Such results clarify how operators between different kinds of spaces behave.
arxiv-2512-09957:
Bethel Hall, Owen Ungaro, and William Eiers introduce CloudFix, a tool that repairs broken cloud access control policies automatically. Such policies decide who may touch sensitive data across thousands of users. Administrators write and edit them by hand, which is slow and error prone, and mistakes can open security holes. CloudFix combines both worlds.

Given a policy plus a list of requests that should be allowed or denied, the system first localizes the faulty statements using formal methods. A language model then proposes candidate fixes. Every candidate is checked by an SMT solver before acceptance, so repairs are verified, not merely plausible. The team built a test set of a few hundred real AWS policies gathered from forum posts, with request sets added. CloudFix repaired policies more accurately than a baseline across request sizes.
arxiv-2512-10157:
A team led by Xuance Jiang proposes a layered material that should host helical superconductivity, an exotic state where Cooper pairs carry momentum. Their platform stacks two forms of tungsten disulfide. One layer is a flat superconductor with inversion symmetry. The other is a topological insulator with mirror symmetry. The pairing yields Rashba superconductivity. Under an in plane magnetic field, the theory predicts finite momentum pairing, signaled by a spike in the pairing susceptibility of a model fitted to first principles band structure.

The helical phase would also induce superconductivity in the edge states, with a character that varies in space. Tuning the field then drives the edge into a one dimensional gapless phase, recognizable by narrow segments of zero energy excitations. That tunable transition is valuable: it is a clean test fingerprint for an otherwise elusive phase. Applications include nonreciprocal transport and Majorana devices.
arxiv-2512-10257:
Huichao Men and colleagues build a benchmark and a better method for a voice assistant's first decision: should this query be answered at all? Smart home assistants hear chit chat, stray sounds, ambiguous references, and commands meant for no device. Accepting everything produces nonsense actions; rejecting real commands infuriates users. The team created the first Chinese, open dataset for this task in home settings. It holds nearly twelve thousand manually labeled text and speech pairs spanning twelve dialogue types. Context and multi turn information are included for evaluation of zero shot and fine tuned models..

Their three tier method adds a household history module and a retrieval base memorizing past false rejections. On their benchmark the system clearly beat general language models, with the largest gains exactly where assistants fail most: family specific expressions and complex multi turn exchanges.
arxiv-2512-10457:
Shiv Ratn, Shivang Rampriyan, and Bahni Ray work on forward osmosis, a low-energy way to pull water through a membrane that could help with separation and treatment tasks. Predicting its water flux is tricky: physics-based models lean on shaky measured parameters. While pure machine learning models can stray from the physics and rarely say how unsure they are.

Their hybrid approach trains a Gaussian process model not on the flux itself. But on the gap between a detailed physics model's prediction and the measured flux. They then split the total uncertainty into model doubt and input doubt, and carry the input part through with a formal method. Trained on barely more than a hundred data points, the model matched test measurements almost exactly, making it a trustworthy stand-in for process tuning and digital twins.
arxiv-2512-10757:
Harrison Davies and co-authors give the Moon a new origin story. The leading account, one colossal impact on the young Earth, demands either an impactor uncannily similar to Earth in composition or an extreme, high-energy collision to mix materials thoroughly. Their multiple impact hypothesis relaxes both demands: several ordinary impacts, each more probable than the canonical monster, steadily build Earth and its Moon.

Using the SWIFT hydrodynamics code, the team simulated chains of impacts and followed a moon growing around an Earth-like planet. Chains of three or more impacts produced systems comparable to the real Earth-Moon pair, and with closer compositional matches than the single giant impact gives. Accepted by the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the seven-page paper presents multiple impacts as a serious rival to the textbook story.
arxiv-2512-10857:
Chirag Modi and co-authors learn what clean data looked like when only corrupted data survives. Transport-based generative models are powerful but hungry for pristine training sets. While science and engineering often offer only measurements passed through a noisy, ill-conditioned channel, from a blurred instrument to a lossy sensor. Rebuilding the original distribution means solving an inverse problem at the level of whole datasets.

Their method, the self-consistent stochastic interpolant, iterates a transport map between corrupted and clean samples. It needs only the corrupted dataset plus black-box access to the corruption process itself, never its inner workings. Under stated conditions the iteration converges to a map that genuinely inverts the channel, yielding a generator for the clean data. The authors prove convergence guarantees, report wins on image processing and scientific reconstruction tasks, and note the method is cheaper than variational alternatives, with public code.
arxiv-2512-10957:
Yukai Shi and co-authors introduce SceneMaker, a system for building three dimensional scenes that contain objects never seen in training. Earlier methods struggle when objects hide each other badly, producing weak shapes or wrong positions. SceneMaker splits the job into parts instead of handling everything in one tangled step.

One model first uncovers hidden parts of objects, trained on broad image data and a collected set of occlusion examples. A separate unified model then estimates poses, using both global and local attention to place objects accurately. The team also built an open-set scene dataset to improve general use. Tests on indoor and open scenes show clear gains over prior methods.
arxiv-2512-11357:
Jungwon Lee studies continued fractions whose digits are restricted to small values, a topic centred on Zaremba's famous conjecture. The conjecture claims every denominator admits a fraction whose continued fraction digits stay below a fixed bound. Lee approaches the problem statistically, estimating how large certain fractal sets of bounded digit numbers become when slightly thickened.

Those size estimates translate into a statement about Zaremba's conjecture holding in an averaging sense, rather than for every single case. The paper also extends the discussion to complex continued fractions built over imaginary quadratic fields, where numbers live in a grid like complex plane. Such averaging results complement the all or nothing conjecture by showing the desired fractions are abundant in a measurable sense. The work sits at the meeting point of number theory and fractal geometry.
arxiv-2512-11457:
Andreas Papageorgiou and colleagues design quantum circuits that multiply and convolve functions by processing them while they are encoded in a quantum state. Their slogan is processing through encoding: several complex functions are loaded onto auxiliary qubits, and the pointwise product of two functions emerges naturally among the amplitudes of the resulting state.

Convolution follows from the classical convolution theorem. Encoding the Fourier coefficients of both functions lets their pointwise product form first, and the inverse quantum Fourier transform then yields the convolution. The team simulated the techniques and folded them into an extended version of the quantum audio package, aimed at sound processing. Initial experimental validations are reported. The authors see promise for quantum enhanced audio manipulation and synthesis, and for signal processing more widely, once hardware matures.
arxiv-2601-06757:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Zheyuan Liu and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers MTMCS-Bench. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed as assistants that interact through text and images. Making it crucial to evaluate contextual safety when risk depends on both the visual scene and the evolving dialogue.

Existing contextual safety benchmarks are mostly single-turn and often miss how malicious intent can emerge gradually or. The same scene can support both benign and exploitative goals. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07057:
Research by Valeriy Bardakov and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with idempotents and powers of ideals in quandle rings. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. This article addresses two central problems in the theory of quandle rings. First, motivated by Conjecture 3.10 in Internat.

2350011: for a semi-latin quandle X X. Every nonzero idempotent in the integral quandle ring ℤ [ X ] Z[X] necessarily corresponds to an element of X X. The authors investigate idempotents in quandle rings of semi-latin quandles. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07457:
Elettra Piacentino and eight colleagues examine how atomic oxygen changes benzene ice, in a 2026 astrochemistry preprint. Benzene is a simple ring-shaped aromatic molecule. Small aromatics and their altered forms appear at many stages of star and planet formation. Oxygen-bearing versions, likely including phenol, were found in the coma of comet 67P.

That comet finding raises a basic question: how do such molecules form in cold space? The authors study functionalization, the adding of new chemical groups, when atomic oxygen meets benzene ice. Ice chemistry in cold clouds and disks is a leading route to complex molecules. Readers get a focused look at one reaction path that may link simple rings to the chemistry found around comets.
arxiv-2601-07557:
Enes Kutay İşgörür, Osman Cevheroğlu, and Arkadaş Özakın build a simple quantum system that shows two kinds of behavior. Their model couples one discrete state to an endless ladder of evenly spaced states. The coupling strength follows a Lorentzian profile, a bell-shaped curve. Such models help explain how atoms and molecules exchange energy with their surroundings. The work appears as a 2026 preprint.

With weak or strong coupling, the system can swing between Rabi oscillations and decay with revivals. Rabi oscillations are steady back-and-forth exchanges of energy. Decay-revival dynamics fade and then partly return. One model that interpolates between both regimes gives physicists a clean test case. It can clarify when a bound state survives inside a near-continuum of states.
arxiv-2601-08157: Kewang Chen wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on one-dimensional isentropic gas dynamics, in the form of a Cauchy problem with broad pressure laws. Chen proves that weak entropy solutions exist for all time. One hard spot is the vacuum, where the gas thins to none and the strict wave-like trait of the system fades. To pass that spot, Chen sets out a fix he calls Synchronized Dual Translation. The pressure law in view has an exponent that tends to a value greater than one.
arxiv-2601-08557: Sushant Gautam and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a tool that spots false claims in video answers. Models that watch video and reply in words are called Video-VLMs. They state false claims, called hallucinations, often and with high trust. Past gauges of doubt do not line up well with when a reply is right. The tool, called VideoHEDGE, grows a gauge built for still images into one for video. It groups claims by sense and tests if small twists change the reply.
arxiv-2601-09857:
Dylan Borchert, Semhar Michael, and Christopher Saunders estimate a normal distribution whose edges are unknown. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats parameter estimation for the truncated normal with unknown bounds. Truncated distributions model data that only appears inside a window.

Estimators for known truncation regions are well studied. Work on unknown bounds exists mainly for known parent distributions. The harder joint case is the paper's ground. Fits like these arise in wage data, sensor ranges, and trial windows. In all of them, the cutoffs themselves must be learned from the sample at hand.
arxiv-2601-10257:
Nan Li, Bo Kang, and Tijl De Bie pull apart two ways tongue can shift a model's moral calls. A model may judge a hard case in one tongue and a next tongue. The calls may not match. Two forces could be at play. One is the tongue of the case. One is the tongue of the thought.

Past tests match the two by fate. An English case gets English thought. The team built a test that splits them. A case in one tongue can pair with thought in a next. That split shows which force drives the shift. The work aids fair tests of models in many tongues.
arxiv-2601-10657:
Minghao Yan and a large team of co-authors present PACEvolve, a scaffold for evolution driven by language models. Large language models now act as operators in evolutionary search, proposing varied candidates and keeping the best. Yet the scaffolds that manage this process are mostly ad hoc. Current systems lack a steady way to run the search itself.

PACEvolve aims at long runs that stay consistent and track progress over time. A good scaffold decides what to keep, what to vary, and when to stop. Without one, search quality swings with each prompt trick. The work speaks to teams that use language models to design code, molecules, or plans over many rounds of trial.
arxiv-2601-10757:
Kenichi Takemura studies circulant matrices built from primitive roots over finite fields. A circulant matrix repeats the same pattern in each row, shifted by one. Primitive roots are special generators in finite field arithmetic. Takemura links the two by reducing exponential sums to Jacobi sums, classic objects in number theory.

The results tie character theory to matrix structure in explicit form. They show how circulant layouts encode arithmetic facts in a highly symmetric shape. They also expose rank duality, a pairing between the ranks of related matrices. Such links help both algebraists and engineers, since circulant matrices show up in coding, signal work, and fast transforms.
arxiv-2601-11357:
Steffen Knoblauch and six coauthors rate how buildings hold up in heat. Their 2026 preprint joins drone views with street-level images. Climate change is raising heat exposure for city dwellers. The risk bites hardest in dense centers of the Global South.

Cheap build materials make the heat risk worse there. Surfaces with high thermal mass soak heat and shed it slowly. Yet ways to rate such traits at scale are scarce. The team uses a vision transformer with global context. It reads both the aerial and the street imagery at once. Coupled views can flag the walls, roofs, and shades that count. Scalable ratings help cities target aid where heat hits most.
arxiv-2601-11457:
Joshua Roy Palathinkal and four coauthors compare indoor neutral-host networks. Their 2026 preprint uses real-world deployments for the test. Indoor coverage is often weak in dense built areas. Thick walls cause heavy penetration loss for signals.

Outdoor macro cells also face an uplink power cap. Phones can only send so hard back to the tower. That gap makes uplink speeds lag far behind downlink. Neutral-host networks share spectrum and infrastructure among carriers. The team compares such setups as built in the real world. Operators must split spectrum across low and mid bands. The study shows how sharing plays out in practice.
arxiv-2601-11557:
Seyed Moein Abtahi, Majid Fekri, Tara Khani, and Akramul Azim rethink vector search. Their 2026 preprint runs from HNSW to information-theoretic binarization. Semantic search and RAG systems lean on approximate nearest neighbors. Most keep vectors in memory at full float precision.

That stack is HNSW plus float32 plus cosine similarity. Its operational cost keeps climbing with data scale. Latency, throughput, and accuracy trade off against each other. Past cost cuts include storage disaggregation and lossy quantization. Each cut sacrifices performance or accuracy in the end. Binarization guided by information theory is the proposed path. One-bit vectors could slash memory while holding accuracy.
arxiv-2601-11657:
Jack Beerman, Shobhan Roy, H. Udaykumar, and Stephen Baek argue size is not the fix. Their 2026 preprint uses deformable convolutions for physics-aware learning. Such learning predicts complex physical systems at high speed. Standard CNN designs struggle with highly nonlinear flows.

Scaling model size is the usual answer in broad AI. For physics modeling, that path yields diminishing returns. Bigger nets cost more yet add little accuracy here. Deformable convolutions bend their sampling grids to the data. That bend can track curved shocks and swirling flows. The team tests if shape-shifting filters beat raw scale. The claim speaks to fast surrogates for fluid physics.
arxiv-2601-11757:
Walter Moreira and Joe Stubbs report a bid to put a famed maths data base into a strict proof tool. The data base is the OEIS, a web list of whole number sequences and linked theorems. It is cited in more than 12,000 works and is a core source in pure maths.

Their project, named Sequencelib in the work, states OEIS maths in Lean. Lean checks each proof step by machine. A checked form would let users trust and reuse those results in new proofs. The work sets out the plan and the form of the new library.
arxiv-2601-11957: Bingxuan Li, Jeonghwan Kim, Cheng Qian, and their co-authors present a self-evolving aide for time management. The aide, named PEARL in the work, learns by reinforcement learning. It aims to grow its skill at plans and schedules as it works. Time plans shift with new tasks and delays, so a fixed rule set soon fails. An aide that learns from results could adapt its advice to each user. The work is a joint effort from the University of Illinois and Eightfold.
arxiv-2601-12057:
V. Smaldore studies a family of graphs tied to polar spaces and to Ramanujan graphs. Ramanujan graphs are strong expanders. They keep the second eigenvalue of their link matrix as small as can be. A recent work built small codes from a near-Ramanujan family.

Smaldore calls such graphs Ramanujan, since known strict builds rest on the Ramanujan conjecture in number theory. His polar graphs give a new build route. Good expanders help networks, codes, and derandomized algorithms. The work links graph maths to finite geometry.  The graphs are strongly regular, a strict form class.
arxiv-2601-12157:
Paolo Bordignon studies congruences for meromorphic modular forms via p-adic cohomology. The congruences link Fourier coefficients of the forms to Frobenius eigenvalues of elliptic curves tied to their poles. Such links are deep and hard to prove by plain means.

He builds a p-adic frame for them. The frame reads the congruences through rigid cohomology of modular curves. It also uses the crystalline structure of the linked curves. The work joins two strong tools to one problem in number theory.  The frame may serve more forms than the cases shown.
arxiv-2601-12257:
Fadlullah Raji and John Murray Bruce rebuild hidden scenes from soft shadows, a form of imaging round corners. Normal imaging needs a line of sight. That line may be unsafe, blocked, or not there at all in key cases.

Non-line-of-sight imaging rebuilds a scene from indirect data. Their method, called Soft Shadow Diffusion in the work, is led by physics and learns in 3D. Shadow data are faint, so a physics guide helps a lot. The work targets search, defence, and medical uses.  Soft shadows are a faint but rich data source.
arxiv-2601-12357:
Hailong Jin and Huiying Li work on semantic correspondence, the task of matching points that mean the same thing in two images. Recent gains in this task have come from large pre trained models. Those models have a catch, though. They need high resolution input images to do their best work.

High resolution images cost a lot of compute, and that cost adds up fast. Jin and Li put forward a method called SimpleMatch as a fix. The name frames it as a simple and strong baseline for the task. A baseline like this gives the field a clear bar to beat. It also hints that good matching may not need the heaviest tools on hand.
arxiv-2601-12457:
Semchankau A. S. and Shkredov I. D. take a first step toward a structure theory for set addition with two operations. Sets in a ring can be combined by addition and by multiplication at once. Most past theory treats one operation at a time. The pair ask what can be said when both act together on sets inside a finite field.

They prove a series of inverse results for such sets. Inverse results work backward: if a set of sums stays small, the set itself must have a rigid form. Their bounds tie the size of power sum sets to the size of the base set and the field. Results like these are core tools in additive combinatorics. They help explain when arithmetic structure must appear.
arxiv-2601-12657:
Yin Wu and four co authors use multi agent reinforcement learning to harden microgrids against extreme weather. Power cuts from severe weather events grow more frequent each year. Microgrids can island from the main grid and keep local power flowing. Good energy management systems already coordinate distributed energy resources to boost resilience.

The hard part is the uncertainty of load demand during extreme weather. Demand can swing in ways that calm day models miss. Multi agent learning lets each resource act as an agent with a shared goal. Agents learn policies that adapt as conditions shift. The work was published in an expert systems journal under an open license. It targets grids that must ride out storms without going dark.
arxiv-2601-12957:
Hanne Kekkonen and Andreas Tataris select regularization strength automatically in Bayesian inversion. Inverse problems infer hidden causes from noisy data, and priors keep solutions sane. Random tree Besov priors are both expressive and computationally feasible, a rare pairing. One key challenge is picking the regularization parameter that balances fit and prior.

The team develop a data driven algorithm for that choice under these priors. Automatic selection removes a hand tuned knob that can bias results. Besov priors suit functions with edges and local spikes, like images. Tree structure adds adaptivity across scales. The work serves imaging and other inverse problems in science.
arxiv-2601-13157:
Hang Zou, Bohao Wang, and co-authors ask if vision language models can read radio waves as pictures. Such models join sight and text in one brain. Radio work, by old habit, builds a fresh net for each task, such as naming the mode of a signal.

The team turns wave forms into images and feeds them to such a model. They find that the model can learn to name modes from the pics, with no past radio skill. They also stress a clear read of why the model picks a mode. For radio teams, the path hints at one broad tool in place of many narrow ones.
arxiv-2601-13257:
Giulia Manco, for the ATLAS team, sums up marks of jet rich crashes at the Large Hadron Collider. Jets are tight sprays of bits made when quarks and gluons fly out of a crash. Some crashes make many jets at once. Others make a vector boson, such as a W or Z, plus jets.

Such events give a sharp test ground for quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. That force is hard to sum at high energy, so lab marks count. The sum covers how ATLAS counts such events and what the counts say. For force theory staff, the marks are a check that no model can skip.
arxiv-2601-14157:
Bruno Sienkiewicz, Łukasz Neumann, and Mateusz Modrzejewski build a dataset for explaining music AI in 2026. Concept-based interpretability methods like TCAV need clean concept examples. They require well-separated positive and negative examples for each concept. Existing music datasets lack this structure, with sparse, noisy, or ill-defined tags.

Their ConceptCaps holds twenty-one thousand music-caption-tags triplets. Explicit labels come from a two hundred attribute taxonomy. Clean concept data lets researchers test what a music model has learned. Explanations of model taste could build trust in recommendation tools. The set is built for tests, not for play lists. Its clean tags let teams probe one trait at a time.
arxiv-2601-14257:
Om Sharan Salafia leads a team of nine authors on this 2026 study of a record gamma-ray burst. The burst is GRB 221009A, the brightest one seen to date. Its afterglow was tracked in fine detail at TeV energies by the LHAASO observatory. The burst is also the most energetic one known.

One odd trait is a line in its spectrum at MeV energies. The team offers a self-consistent account of that line. Their title says the account also points to a dense circum-stellar medium, gas packed close around the star that burst. Readers get a case where one odd signal helps map the space near the source.
arxiv-2601-14357:
Alice P. Curtin and eight co-authors report on one astronomy meeting in this 2026 paper. The meeting is FRB 2025, a conference on fast radio bursts. The FRB field has grown fast, and its conferences have grown with it. Such meetings matter for meeting peers and starting joint work. Many stay out of reach, though.

Travel funds, flexible schedules, and sheer distance shut many researchers out. The team describes one attempt to run an inclusive and accessible hybrid conference. Hybrid means people could join in person or online. Readers get a case study of what the team tried, framed for others who plan science meetings.
arxiv-2601-14457:
Martin Burger, Ariane Fazeny, Gilles Mordant, and Jan-Frederik Pietschmann study transport distances on networks in this 2026 math paper. The networks are metric graphs that represent gas networks. Their tool is the p-Wasserstein distance, a measure of the cost of moving mass from one distribution to another. They start from the dynamic formulation of that distance.

The authors review extensions of the distance to networks. Some versions allow mass to be stored on the vertices, and some do not. They then examine the static Wasserstein distance on a three-dimensional network domain. That domain converges to a metric graph, a 3D to 1D limit. Readers get a careful bridge between pipe-flow models and graph models.
arxiv-2601-14957:
Harry Mead, Bruno Lacerda, Jakob Foerster, and Nick Hawes work on training agents in worlds that design themselves. Their 2026 arXiv paper sits in unsupervised environment design. The goal is curricula that make reinforcement learning agents generalize and cope with new tasks.

Building a good curriculum is still hard. A few settings in a world's design space can sharply raise the skill a policy needs. Methods in this field lean on a regret estimate to pick the next task. The authors work on making that regret estimate closer to the truth.
arxiv-2601-15157:
Laura Monk proves that a typical curved surface is hard to split in two. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with hyperbolic surfaces, shapes with constant negative curvature. The key gauge is the spectral gap, the first nonzero eigenvalue of the Laplace operator.

A large gap means the surface is well connected. Such a surface has a small diameter and mixes fast. Monk shows that typical hyperbolic surfaces have an optimal spectral gap. In other words, the generic surface is about as hard to cut apart as the theory of such surfaces allows.
arxiv-2601-15757:
Yimin Zhu and a large team make hyperspectral image classification easier to read in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hyperspectral images record many wavelength bands per pixel. Deep models classify them well, but their feature mixing is opaque. Users cannot see how a decision was reached. The team presents a white-box framework called ES-mHC. It is aware of the electromagnetic spectrum by design.

The framework models interactions among spectrum groupings directly. It uses structured, directional matrices for those interactions. The residual stream carries information between groupings in a traceable way. Interpretability is the headline gain. Analysts in remote sensing need to defend their maps. A model that shows its spectral reasoning earns more trust than a black box.
arxiv-2601-15857:
Giovanni Ceccio, Jiri Vacik, Yuto Kondo, and co-authors study hybrid thin films in a 2026 arXiv paper. The films mix cobalt with C60 fullerene molecules. Such organic-metal hybrids draw interest for electronics and magnetism. The study tracks how the film surface changes. Various external stimuli supply energy to the system. The team watches the morphological and structural evolution that follows.

How a film's surface reshapes under stimuli decides its uses. A film that reorganizes may switch properties on demand. One that degrades sets limits on handling and operation. Detailed surface studies guide both hopes. The work sits in materials science, where thin hybrid layers are building blocks for sensors and devices. Knowing their response to energy input is basic design knowledge.
arxiv-2601-15957:
Courtney Carreira and a large team catalog galaxy shapes from JWST images in a 2026 arXiv paper. The catalog belongs to JADES Data Release 5. It covers sources in the GOODS-N and GOODS-S fields seen by NIRCam. For each source, the team reports morphological parameters and their uncertainties. Morphology describes a galaxy's shape and structure. Those numbers feed studies of how galaxies formed and changed.

The team models each galaxy's brightness profile with a single Sérsic component. Bayesian inference yields the structural parameters. Uncertainties come with them, which honest catalogs require. A single-component fit is a simplification, but it scales to huge samples. Data releases like this are infrastructure. Hundreds of later papers will build on these measured shapes.
arxiv-2601-16057:
James Agostino and a large team weigh the gas near the hearts of two merging star systems. Their 2026 preprint uses sharp CO views of the GOALS set. The two rich mergers hold much mass in their first tens of parsecs. If all that mass were a black hole, it would look too big. That clash with known black hole to host links drives the study.

The team weighs the cool gas from the CO light. Gas mass can then be split from black hole mass in the core. A clean split tests if the black holes are in truth too big. It also shows how much fuel sits near the core. The work aids the study of mergers and their core growth.
arxiv-2601-16157:
Sanjeev Verma shows why summed acts oft level off in spread systems. His 2026 preprint deals with sums that grow then reach a cap. Past work oft ties the cap to case facts. Those facts span clash counts, wave match or set fade laws. Each case then needs its own tale of the cap.

Verma shows the cap can come from plain local ease alone. Local ease means each spot drifts back at a set rate. No case tale is then needed for the cap. A plain root for the cap eases work in many fields. It warns teams not to add need less case parts.
arxiv-2601-16357:
Allyson Bieryla and coauthors report a giant world on a long, bent path round its star. Their 2026 preprint sets out TOI-6692 b. The world is of Jupiter size and takes a span of days to loop its star. Its path is bent, with a curve mark near the mid range. It was first seen as one pass in TESS views.
