Citizen groups, the Visual Survey Group and Planet Hunters, flagged that lone pass. More work then pinned the long loop and bent path. A lone pass world is hard to pin, so proof took care. Such long loop giants test tales of how worlds move. The work adds a rare case to that set.
arxiv-2601-16557:
Pierre Colmez and Wiesława Nizioł survey p-adic Hodge theory for analytic forms. Their 2026 preprint sums a field born with Tate in 1967. Tate set a claim of a Hodge like split for p-adic sums. Those sums live on firm analytic forms in the p-adic world. Fontaine then honed that claim in key ways through his work.

The survey traces how the claim grew to a full theory. It maps main proofs, tools and open ends in one place. Such maps let new teams enter a deep field with speed. They also show which claims still lack full proof. The work is a guide note, not a new proof.
arxiv-2601-17257:
Javier Porras-Valenzuela, Samar Hadou, and Alejandro Ribeiro rethink how transformers are trained. They treat training as constrained optimization. Each layer must lower the goal value as data flows through. That rule makes the network act like a descent method. Standard training, by contrast, just cuts mean loss with no layer rule.

Their scheme uses a primal-dual method to enforce the layer rules. The payoff is models whose inner steps drop the loss in a steady way. Such models are easier to read and to trust. Each layer has a clear job tied to the goal. The work links deep learning to classic optimization in a tight, useful way.
arxiv-2601-17457:
David Delepine and A. Yebra extend a classic neutrino result. The Dirac-Majorana confusion theorem says the two neutrino types look alike at high energy. Their split shrinks with the square of mass over energy. That makes them near-impossible to tell apart in many tests. The authors add new physics vector interactions to the frame. They also add CP-violating phases.

With those terms, the old suppression may shift. The generalized theorem maps where tells can survive. Neutrino type is a deep open question in physics. Any window that splits the two types draws wide interest. This work tells experimenters where to look. It also warns where the old blind spot still holds.
arxiv-2601-17557:
Aref Farhadipour and five co-authors describe a system for the WildSpoof 2026 challenge. The task joins two checks at once. One check verifies who is speaking. The other checks if the audio is real or spoofed. Their system is called spoofing-aware speaker verification. It runs as a cascade, one stage after the next.

A key part uses wavelet prompt tuning on a speech model. A multi-model ensemble adds more votes. Joint checks matter as voice fakes grow sharp. A system that trusts a good fake fails both tasks. The challenge setting tests real-world fraud risk. Call centers and banks face that risk daily. The design shows one path to meet it.
arxiv-2601-18057: Christian Koke studies Laplacians on graphs whose clusters grow ever more tightly linked. His 2026 preprint follows graphs on a shared node set where edge weights inside set clusters tend to infinity. As the links inside a cluster grow, the graph Laplacians converge, in the resolvent sense, to an effective graph Laplacian. The note gives a clean limit picture for graphs with tight groups.
arxiv-2601-18157:
Aniket Rege and co-authors build agents that can understand very long videos. Their 2026 preprint starts from a shift in daily tech. Always-on assistants, worn in devices like smart glasses, are becoming real. They face a nonstop, day-long stream of first-person video. Understanding that stream is a step past reading short, isolated clips. The meaning of a moment may depend on hours of prior context.

An agentic design lets the system plan what to re-check and recall. Memory and search over the stream become core skills. Such understanding serves memory aids, work logs, and safety tools. The work targets a form of video that barely existed a few years ago.
arxiv-2601-18357:
Vishnu Varma and Bernhard Müller study how computer models of exploding stars change when the detail of the grid is changed. Their work looks at a star that does not spin and has about thirteen times the mass of the Sun. The models also test how strong the starting magnetic field should be.

The team tracks three things across the runs. First comes the moment when the stalled shock wave starts to move out again. Next comes the shape and the strength of the blast that follows. Last comes what is left behind at the core once the star has blown apart. Work like this helps show which parts of a model can be trusted. It also shows which parts shift when the grid gets finer or coarser.
arxiv-2601-18457:
Fake Lin and seven colleagues tackle a clash at the heart of smart shops that use language models to pick goods. Old shop tools learn from what users clicked and bought in the past. That past gives rich signs of taste. Language models, in turn, learn word by word. The two ways of learning do not line up in a neat way.

Their plan aligns the two at the level of single words and word parts. Shop signs are fed in so the model can use them as it picks each next word. A tight fit should give picks that feel both apt and in line with what like users chose. The work aims at shop tools that learn taste from text and from clicks at once. Such tools could serve each user a list that fits them more.
arxiv-2601-18557:
Tony Feng, Zhiwei Yun, and Wei Zhang study a kind of stack that charts bundles on a curve in a deep field of maths. The stacks are built from a trick that mixes a curve with a twist of its own past. They have grown key in the study of how counts and waves meet. The pair of authors and their mate set out new classes that live on those stacks, built from the stack's own form.

They then prove a claim that ties the size of those classes to the slopes of deep wave scores at a key point. The claim is a kin of a famed rule that ties shape counts to size counts. Such ties let staff work out hard counts by a shift to a twin field. The work is a deep brick in a long build.
arxiv-2601-18957:
Karlo Lelas and Dario Jukić solve classic mechanics problems by a fresh route: splitting total energy into factors. They use complex numbers to factor the energy of systems whose potential energy stays positive. From that one start, they reach exact answers for several well known problems.

The list covers the simple harmonic oscillator and a projectile thrown straight up. It also covers motion under a repulsive inverse cube force and a damped oscillator with linear drag. A single energy trick that solves all four gives students and teachers a new lens on old textbook ground.
arxiv-2601-19557:
Riccardo Giubilato and five colleagues release a dataset recorded on a volcanic island. The island is Vulcano, part of the Aeolian Islands near Sicily, Italy. Its rough, natural terrain looks more like another planet than a city street. That makes it a good test ground for robots that must find their way in wild places.

The dataset supports SLAM, the task of mapping a place while tracking your own position in it. It also supports place recognition, spotting that you have been somewhere before. Recordings combine camera images with LiDAR scans, so methods can use both sight and laser depth. Teams can test their algorithms on the same hard sequences and compare scores. Such shared data helps planetary robotics move forward.
arxiv-2601-19857:
Matheus R. de Jesus, Eduardo O. C. Hoefel, and Renato M. Angelo connect graph structure to quantum symmetry. Graph states are a central tool for describing entanglement among many particles. They are built by applying controlled-Z interactions along the edges of a graph. In their standard form they encode symmetric exchange properties.

The authors prove a precise correspondence between a graph's topology and the exchange symmetry of its state. They show exactly when a graph state is fully symmetric under swapping particles. Symmetry decides how states behave in quantum protocols and error correction. A clean graph criterion makes symmetric states easier to design and recognise. The work sharpens the dictionary between combinatorics and quantum information.
arxiv-2601-19957:
Ira Wolfson introduces a deterministic algorithm for a core quantity in Bayesian statistics. The Bayesian evidence measures how well a model explains data, averaged over its parameters. In high dimensions, computing it by sampling becomes far too slow. Sampling also runs step by step, so parallel hardware helps little.

SunBURST replaces global exploration with mode-centric integration. It locates the modes, the peaks of the posterior, and integrates around them with a Laplace approximation. The algorithm is built to run natively on graphics processors, which supply the parallelism sampling lacks. Deterministic output means the same answer every run, easing verification. Faster evidence would sharpen model comparison in fields from astronomy to medicine. The gain is speed with no loss of trust. Each run gives the same score. That is rare for this kind of task. The peaks are found first, then summed. No dice are rolled at any step.
arxiv-2601-20057:
Toby Meadows works on the foundations of mathematics, asking what countable set theory can and cannot do. The theory he studies assumes every set is countable, a stark restriction of standard set theory. One desirable feature of a foundation is eliminating imaginaries: giving concrete representatives for objects defined only up to equivalence. Many theories can do this for arbitrary definable equivalence relations.

Meadows shows this countable theory cannot. Some definable equivalence relations have no representatives the theory can provide. That failure marks a real limit on the theory as a foundation. Foundations research maps which conveniences each axiom system buys. The result tells logicians a popular simplification costs more than it seemed.
arxiv-2601-20257:
Jinren Ding and five colleagues improve decision transformers for automated bidding in online advertising. These models plan bids by learning from sequences of states, actions, and returns. The authors name two limits: the model weakly links state, action, and return-to-go sequences, and it learns from good and bad behavior alike without distinction.

Their design adds a cross-learning module and a constraint-aware loss, reflected in the name C2. Better bidding models matter because ad auctions spend large budgets in real time. A model that reads its own past returns more clearly could bid with less waste.
arxiv-2601-20657:
Valerij G. Kiselev and Jing-Rebecca Li ask what the FEXI method actually measures in neurons. FEXI, filtered exchange imaging, estimates how water exchanges between tissue compartments in brain gray matter, a key quantity for reading diffusion MRI. Reported exchange times are broadly dispersed, spread over about two orders of magnitude.

The authors solve the Bloch-Torrey equation numerically inside digital neurons taken from the NeuroMorpho.org archive. Realistic cell shapes show what the measurement truly responds to. Resolving the spread matters because exchange time is used as a marker of cell structure and health.
arxiv-2601-20957:
Arihant Tiwari, Rachana, M. Vivek, and Suvendu Rakshit hunt for oddballs among a special class of galaxies. Their 2026 paper analyzes narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies from SDSS DR17. The sample holds more than twenty-two thousand such galaxies. Their redshifts run from a tenth to nearly one. The team seeks sources that are spectroscopically anomalous. Odd spectra can flag rare physics or data problems.

The anomalies were detected by the SQuAD algorithm. It combines principal component analysis with hierarchical k-means clustering. That pairing compresses each spectrum and groups the results. Sources far from every group stand out as anomalous. Studying them can reveal extreme black hole behavior. It can also clean catalogs used by many other studies. The paper gives the community a vetted list of strange cases.
arxiv-2601-21257:
Shangbin Feng and more than twenty co-authors build a shared home for research on language models that work together. Instead of one big model, several models can team up, split tasks, and cover each other's gaps. Past work on this idea is scattered across groups with no common way to compare results.

Their platform, MoCo, gathers tasks, tools, and measures in one place. Researchers can test how models combine and check claims against the same yardstick. That shared base should make results easier to trust and repeat. It also shows where teamwork helps and where a single strong model still wins.
arxiv-2601-21357:
Joshua Hang Sai Ip, Georgios Makrygiorgos, and Ali Mesbah improve a workhorse method for tuning costly black-box functions. Bayesian optimization picks each new test point by expected improvement over the best so far. That rule is popular but greedy, and it can stall at points that are not truly optimal.

The authors add gradient size into the choice rule. Points where the slope is still large carry information the classic rule ignores. Their version should keep searching where the function is still changing fast. That helps when each test is expensive, as in lab experiments or engineering design, where wasted trials cost real money.
arxiv-2601-21457:
Tomer Adar, Yahel Hotam, and Amit Levi study how to count the edges in a graph the team cannot see directly. The graph can only be probed through limited questions. Some questions test whether a set of nodes has no edges inside it, while others ask a node's degree or its neighbors.

Mixing both kinds of questions turns out to beat either kind alone. The authors prove the mixed model gives strictly faster edge estimation. Better counting with fewer probes matters for huge networks that can only be sampled, such as web graphs and social platforms.
arxiv-2601-21957:
Cheng Cui and co-authors present an upgraded model for reading documents in the wild. PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 is a vision-language model with just under a billion parameters, tuned for many document tasks at once. The team reports it sets a new best accuracy on the OmniDocBench benchmark for document parsing.

Real documents arrive scanned, skewed, warped, photographed off screens, and badly lit. To test robustness against those physical distortions, the authors propose a new benchmark built around five such real-world conditions. Their 2026 preprint argues the enhanced model holds up under that abuse. Reliable parsing of imperfect documents is the unglamorous core of digitizing archives, invoices, and forms at scale.
arxiv-2601-22057:
Archer Wang, Emile Anand, Yilun Du, and Marin Soljacic teach diffusion models to take data apart and put it back together in new ways. Splitting complex data into factorized parts can reveal reusable components. Recombining those parts then creates new samples that never existed.

In images, the factors might capture background, lighting, and object traits. In robotics, they might capture separate elements of a scene or motion. The team's 2026 preprint studies diffusion models that learn such factorized latent spaces without supervision at the level of individual factors, guided by a discriminator. Unsupervised decomposition matters because labeled factors are rare, while the ability to recombine is the heart of creative generation.
arxiv-2601-22257:
Eva Silverstein, Daniel Kunin, and Vasudev Shyam found spare spin in how a transformer model pays heed to words. In their 2026 preprint they note that the heed step holds twist room that never changes the output. They add a simple fix that picks a set path in that room.

The fix uses small shifts, picked per batch and not learned, for two parts of the step. The team state two gains that tests then backed up. Their work aims to make training both leaner and easier to read. It gives model builders a cheap new dial to try.
arxiv-2601-22357:
Julien Delavande, Regis Pierrard, and Sasha Luccioni put a price, in energy, on saying thanks to a chatbot. Their 2026 preprint uses real chat traces and fine measures of power draw. Short, polite notes feel free to the user, yet each one still makes a large model run.

The team track how input length, reply length, and model size drive the cost. Even tiny asks add up when they occur at vast scale. Their work gives users and firms a clear sense of that hidden bill. It may shape kinder, leaner chat habits. It also aids green design.
arxiv-2601-22457:
The ATLAS team at CERN report on a long-running program of virtual visits to their giant particle detector. Since 2010, the program has offered live, guided tours of the detector and its control room to audiences around the world. Their 2026 preprint sums up what those visits have done for science outreach.

Remote classes and public groups can question working physicists in real time, from any continent. The team weigh how such access breaks down walls between frontier science and the public. Virtual visits cost little and travel anywhere with a network link. The report offers a model other big labs can copy.
arxiv-2601-22557:
Ke Du, William Mansky, Paolo Giarrusso, and Gregory Malecha give recursive mutexes a firm spec in separation logic. A mutex is a lock that guards shared state; a recursive one can be re-taken by its holder. Their 2026 preprint notes that plain mutex specs are well known in this logic.

They build the same two spec styles for the recursive kind: guarding an invariant, and atomically flipping lock state. Sound specs let proofs of lock-heavy code go through. Such code runs through servers and apps in C++ and Java. The work closes a known gap. The result is small, exact, and meant to last.
arxiv-2601-23157:
Paulius Rauba and three co-authors apply the least-privilege principle to language model services. In security, least privilege means granting only the minimum access a request needs. Deployed models rarely follow it: one endpoint serves every user and every request at full power.

That gap persists not because limits would be useless, but because they are hard to build. The authors argue deployments would gain much from cutting needless capability exposure. Least-privilege design could shrink the damage from misuse and prompt attacks. A single open endpoint is the anti-pattern named here, exposing full capability to every request regardless of need.
arxiv-2603-01557:
Aditya Shukla, Yining Yuan, Ben Tamo, and colleagues test whether AI summaries of home health data can be trusted. Their 2026 work uses dementia monitoring records with body measures and room sensors over time. Fluent summaries may sound right yet miss long spells of abnormal readings that matter for care.

The team scores summaries by events, not by word overlap or style. Daily events come from fixed abnormal thresholds that must persist to count as real. Scores track missed abnormal spells, missed durations, covered measures, and invented events. Plain scoring hides a stark split: some models score well on style but recall almost no abnormal events. A vision-based pipeline that reads plotted charts aligns best with true events, which argues for event-aware checks in care tools.
arxiv-2603-01657:
Abderaouf Bahi, Amel Ourici, Ibtissem Gasmi, and colleagues forecast renewable power at new sites with no labeled data there. Their frame, FreeGNN, adapts a graph model to unseen sites with no source data and no target labels. A teacher-student setup guides learning, while a memory store replays past cases to block forgetting. Graph-based rules keep spatial links intact, and a drift-aware weight adjusts how fast the model adapts. Tests span three real data sets for solar, wind, and broad energy contests. Ablation checks confirm that each added part earns its place.
arxiv-2603-01857:
Eugenia Gabriela Loera Villeda, Ivo Steinbrecher, and Alexander Popp mesh contact problems in two independent parts. Contact zones and solid interiors need different element types and resolutions, so one shared mesh serves both poorly.

The contact surface uses a smooth boundary layer mesh built from the CAD model boundary curves. NURBS curves give exact shape and smooth joins between elements on that layer. The bulk instead uses a simple structured Cartesian grid, cheap to build and refine. A mortar-type constraint couples the two non-matching meshes so forces pass correctly across the seam. Several layer-building strategies are detailed, and numeric examples validate the full workflow for contact mechanics.
arxiv-2603-02157:
Kathleen Chang, Zhiyang He, Theodore Yoder, and colleagues speed up quantum error correction in this 2026 paper. Quantum codes spread data across many qubits to guard against noise. Surgery is a flexible way to compute on such codes, but it is slow. Each step can take a number of check rounds that grows with code size.

Their new gadgets perform many logical measures at once in fixed time. Space cost stays near fixed as well, a rare pairing. The trick is sharing cost across many steps: many surgeries finish in time once thought needed for one. The gadgets keep much of surgery's flexibility while matching faster gate methods. They suit near-term tests and open new design paths for fast quantum logic.
arxiv-2603-02257:
M AlMasri studies a classic approximation method in the complex plane in this 2026 mathematics paper. The Rayleigh-Ritz method guesses a wave form, then tunes it to approach the true energy. AlMasri works in the Segal-Bargmann space, a setting where waves are functions of complex numbers. Trial waves are bell-shaped curves stretched by two parameters.

A strict bound on one parameter proves necessary for the guesses to stay valid. For the basic oscillator, the method recovers the exact ground state. For a stiffer oscillator with a quartic term, adaptive bell shapes yield tidy energy formulas. Simpler power guesses give firm upper bounds but cannot adjust their width. Shifted guesses prove vital for lopsided potentials that break symmetry.
arxiv-2603-02357:
Xiaochun Liu and Richard Luger forecast extreme financial losses with a quantile method in this 2026 paper. Banks must estimate Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall, two gauges of worst-case losses. Both live in the far left tail of return distributions. Their method models the conditional scale of returns, defined by the gap between two quantiles.

Restricted quantile regression estimates that scale without assuming a distribution shape. Value-at-Risk comes from the left-tail quantile of rescaled returns. Expected Shortfall averages the quantiles below that level. The approach captures skewness, heavy tails, and leverage effects robustly. arxiv-2603-02857:

Quantum links must be run next to the plain messages that control them, a pairing with no past model. The design splits control logic from node and channel parts, so users can rewire pieces fast. A plug-in slot swaps between three ways to store quantum states. Tests show the tool runs faster than leading rivals while keeping its models flexible. A viewer shows both the real links and the links made by shared quantum states.
arxiv-2603-03257:
Sahar Diskin and five colleagues present a proof in percolation theory, the branch of mathematics that studies how random connections spread through a network. Their 2026 paper works with percolation above its critical point, called the supercritical regime. The setting is broad: every infinite transitive graph, where each point looks like every other.

The team proves that the chance the starting point sits in a finite cluster of a given large size falls off exponentially fast. The rate of that fall is governed by the graph's isoperimetric function, which measures how clusters can grow. Results of this kind are known as sharpness results. They pin down exactly how behavior changes once the critical threshold is crossed.
arxiv-2603-03357:
Taiwo O Sangodapo studies products of picture fuzzy subgroups, an abstract algebra topic built for reasoning under uncertainty. Ordinary sets force yes-or-no membership; fuzzy sets allow degrees. The 2026 paper defines how to combine two picture fuzzy subgroups through a direct product, the standard way of pairing structures in algebra. It then establishes several characterizations of that product using cut sets, which slice a fuzzy object at chosen thresholds into ordinary sets. Such characterizations let researchers verify product properties with simpler tools. The work sits in pure fuzzy algebra, extending a theory already applied to voting analysis and medical diagnosis.
arxiv-2603-03757:
Kento Sakai extends a classic map of surface geometry to graphs with several curves at once. Teichmüller space, the space of shapes a surface can wear, is famously hard to navigate directly. arxiv-2603-03857:

baudelaire-flowers-of-evil-1857:
Charles Baudelaire published The Flowers of Evil in 1857, his condemned masterpiece of spleen and ideal in verse. Many call the book the birth certificate of modern poetry in the judgment of poets since its trial. Baudelaire was fined and six poems banned for offenses against public morals in the Paris of 1857.

The poems move between Spleen, the city's rot and ennui, and Ideal, the reach for beauty beyond it. Lesbos, carrion, wine, and the voyage fill sections that map a soul at war with time and flesh. Baudelaire's form is classical and strict while his matter is modern, urban, and deliberately shocking to bourgeois taste. The banned poems and the trial made the book a banner for art's freedom ever since in France. Every modern poet, from Rimbaud to Eliot, works in a world this book remade.
boucher-antiquites-tome-2-1857:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes was a French customs man and a keen digger. His Antiquities celtiques et antediluviennes, Book Two, came out in French in 1857. The work deals with Celtic and pre-flood finds from the Somme gravel beds. Book One stands just past in the set.

Stone tools found with the bones of lost beasts fill his proof. Boucher held that men lived far past the age the books then gave them. Most sages of his day scoffed, then came round to his side. The set is a root work in the tale of man's deep past.
bronte-the-professor-1857:
Charlotte Brontë wrote The Professor first, and it saw print only in 1857, after her death. The posthumous novel is the seedbed of both Villette and Jane Eyre in her work. Publishers had turned it down nine times while she lived and sought a better fate.

William Crimsworth, a mill owner's son, quits trade and teaches at a Brussels boys' school. He loves Frances Henri, a lace mender and pupil-teacher of Swiss and English blood in Brussels. Jealous heads and a spying director test their modest courtship of work and study there. The pair wed, teach, and prosper in a close, unsentimental close of quiet industry. The plain style shows Brontë before the fire of Jane Eyre lit her prose.
brown-estimate-manners-principles-1757:
Brown's Estimate of the Manners and Principles of the Times, published in 1757, was the most talked-of book of its year in England. Britain had just suffered shocks in the war with France, and readers were ready for a harsh diagnosis. Brown, already known as a controversial clergyman-writer, gave them one.

He charged that England had sunk into luxury, selfishness, and fading religion, and that its ruling class had grown soft. Against that decay he set discipline, public spirit, and a return to serious principle. The book sold by the thousand and provoked answers, sequels, and parodies. It stands as the classic jeremiad of its century, an insider's scolding that tells historians exactly what anxious Britons feared about themselves in the 1750s.
buckle-civilization-england-vol-1-1857:
Henry Thomas Buckle published History of Civilization in England, Volume 1, in 1857. Buckle aimed to make history a science governed by laws. Climate, food, soil, and scenery, he argues, shape the character of nations. Statistics, he claims, show regular patterns even in crime and marriage.

The volume surveys France, Spain, Germany, and Scotland before turning to England. Buckle praises intellect and doubts the power of rulers and churches to drive progress. The book was a sensation and drew fierce attacks. Its positivist program now looks overbold. Yet it changed how Victorians thought history could be written. Volume 2 never matched the first's impact.
