Readers find a dated agency item about those investigations, kept as a brief record rather than a full account of the cases themselves.
cia-0000075857: Monitoring the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075857, dated February 1, 1991, subtitled Looking for a Needle in a Haystack. The paper frames treaty monitoring as a hard search problem. Its vivid subtitle is the record's most memorable feature, preserved in a short declassified item on weapons treaty oversight.
cia-0000096657: Current Developments in Chinese Communist Agriculture, with Chinese misspelled in the heading, is declassified CIA document 0000096657, dated July 4, 1968. The title promises a farm-sector update from China. Readers find a short declassified agriculture paper whose spelling flaw is preserved in the catalog, a companion in subject to the earlier rice crop report.
cia-0000108157: National Intelligence Estimate Probable Developments in Indonesia is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108157, dated May 3, 1958. The title marks a formal estimate on where Indonesia was likely heading. Probable developments is the estimate phrase in the heading itself. The brief record is a country outlook item, filed in the spring of 1958 as released in the files.
cia-0000109057: Cuban Subversive Activities in Latin America: 1959-1968 is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000109057, dated January 5, 1968. The heading sets its own span, nine years of Cuban activity across Latin America. Subversive is the title's own word for the activity it tracks. The brief record is a decade survey item, filed at the start of 1968 as released.
cia-0000126957: A November 1965 CIA report gives the short-term political prospects in Panama. The canal made every turn in Panamanian politics Washington's business, and the country's affairs ran through the Canal Zone. The paper forecasts the political weather ahead for that small, watched state. Canal politics gave every Panamanian election an American echo, and short-term forecasts like this one served officials who managed the zone and its treaty questions.
cia-0000132757: Plans by the Cuban government to draw President Eisenhower further in fill a CIA item dated May 5, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the name Eisenho, short for the president. Havana was pulling the American leader into its public campaign that spring. Each clash gave Castro fresh material for speeches at home. The short item reports the plans as analysts heard them.
cia-0000135857: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 6 January 1954, long since declassified, on cable traffic for PBSUCCESS being compromised. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136157: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 5 April 1954, covers team themes for KUGOWN, the talking points handed to the propaganda teams in the field. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136257: The record dated 6 May 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about a possible need for bomb support to swing the army, bombing meant to break its loyalty. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136857: Headquarters does not concur with a LINCOLN recommendation in this 1954 cable, because of the Caracas conference. If the source called LIONIZER goes out on a limb and the conference flops, he will be completely discredited hemisphere-wide as a trustworthy source and become only a joke. Instead, headquarters suggests he denounce current Guatemalan-Moscow status, plead for positive action by delegates, and send letters to former Latin American contacts. The cable protects a propaganda voice by keeping his predictions safe.
cia-0000136957: The Secretary of State's morning statement is relayed in this May 1954 cable. It went to the Guatemala City station, with orders to exploit it. He said most Guatemalans want the communists cleaned out. But they face intense communist terrorism, he said. He noted reports of an army ultimatum to Arbenz. He named no sources for those reports. He neither confirmed nor denied a foreign ministers' conference. The station should invite attention to the statement. It would validate the station's own guidance.
cia-0000137457: Filed in Spanish in 1961, document 0000137457 is one of the papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force trained by the CIA for the Bay of Pigs landing that April. The record gives no subject line beyond the brigade file it sits in, so its contents should not be guessed at. It survives as a declassified page of that operation's archive, released through the CIA Reading Room, in the language most of the brigade's own paperwork used.
cia-03000957: September 23, 1955 produced this daily intelligence bulletin. The analysts' roundup of world events for Washington leaders. The Cold War's steady output. Its pages add to the record of the past. This file preserves that declassified paper. Kept for readers.
cia-03179157: October 23, 1956: the bulletin briefed Washington on global events. The daily intelligence summary reached leaders. The Cold War's autumn reading. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers.
cia-06218657: PYRAMID STATEMENT OF WORK W/ADDENDUM, a CIA document. The amended statement. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06626857: TIMERMAN MOTION EXPECTED TO BE TURNED DOWN BY LOWER COURT - 1978/09/12, a CIA document. The court motion. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
cia-06954157: PORTUGUESE GUINEA HANDBOOK, a CIA reference. The Guinea-Bissau guide. This file preserves that declassified handbook. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
davis-magic-staff-1857:
Andrew Jackson Davis tells his own strange life in The Magic Staff, his life tale of 1857. Davis rose from a poor youth with scant school to the chief seer of his land. Sickly and keen, he fell in trance states as a boy. In them he claimed to learn the lore that made his famed books of creed and worlds.

Ward tales, trek tales, and the birth of his gifts fill the prose. He writes with zeal and a touch of pride. The book is the chief source on the man back of the faith's first texts. It grips as tale as well.
der-chymischen-wahrsagers-vertheidigung-: Der chymischen Wahrsagers Vertheidigung, 1757. The defended fortune-teller. This book preserves that work. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Writers of history may cite it later.
dumas-companions-of-jehu-1857:
Alexandre Dumas published The Companions of Jehu in 1857, a romance of the French Directory years. The tale follows the royalist Companions of Jehu, highwaymen who robbed state gold for their cause. Secret societies, duels, and Napoleon's rise frame this late and vigorous Dumas historical romance in France.

Roland de Montrevel, a dashing aide to Bonaparte, hunts the Companions across the wild Bresse country. Their chief, Morgan, proves to be Roland's own friend and his sister's secret husband in hiding. Stagecoach raids fund a royalist rising while Bonaparte crushes foes in Italy and Egypt abroad then. The guillotine and the battlefield thin both camps as the Consulate dawns on France victorious. Dumas keeps sympathy divided, a mark of his mature and fairer historical art.
dumas-the-wolf-leader-1857:
Alexandre Dumas gives the wolf tale his grand sweep in The Wolf-Leader, in English from 1904, first told in 1857. Thibault, a poor shoe hand, makes a pact with a great black wolf in the woods. Each wish he spends costs a hair of his head and a step of his soul. Wealth and rank come, and so does the hunt that must end his wild run at last.

Dumas spins the lore of the loup-garou with his famed zest. The tale is part folk yarn, part doom tract. It shows a master at play with dark stuff. Its pace still grips.
europmc-pmc10131557:
Solier and a large team identify a copper-based signaling pathway that drives inflammation and can be targeted by drugs, in a 2023 study. Inflammation defends the body against harm, but in excess it fuels diseases from sepsis to cancer. The team searched for fresh control points in this ancient system.

They found that copper inside certain immune cells helps switch on inflammatory programs. Blocking that copper signal calmed inflammation in their tests. The work names a new drug target in a pathway doctors have long wanted to control more precisely.
europmc-pmc10132957:
Ebrahimi and Samanta review how protein-based drugs are engineered through structural and chemical design, in a 2023 paper. Protein drugs have changed the treatment of cancer, diabetes, and immune disease. The authors note that proteins were set to make up half of the top-selling drugs of the year.

The review explains how scientists reshape proteins to bind better, last longer, and cause fewer side effects. It covers design guided by three-dimensional structure and by chemical tweaks. The paper shows how careful engineering turns natural proteins into precise medicines. It closes with open challenges in the field.
europmc-pmc10287557:
Okuzumi and a large team report that seeds of alpha-synuclein protein in blood serum can serve as markers for a family of brain diseases, in a 2023 study. These diseases, called synucleinopathies, include Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. In each, alpha-synuclein folds wrongly and spreads through the brain in a seed-like way.

The team amplified those seeds from blood samples and read their shapes. Different diseases left distinct seed signatures that matched the clinical diagnosis. A blood test of this kind could ease diagnosis of diseases now confirmed mainly after death.
europmc-pmc10329457:
Finkel and co-authors asked in 2020 how microbes around plant roots shape root growth. Plants live amid a dense web of microbes that trade chemical signals. The team grew Arabidopsis, a small test plant, with a set of 185 bacterial strains. They then took the set apart to find which microbes changed the roots.

Finkel found that one genus, Variovorax, did the key work. It fully undid the strong block on root growth caused by many other strains. Variovorax did this by breaking down auxin, a plant hormone that guides growth. All of its known genomes carry the same gene set for that task. The result hints at ways to grow tougher crops.
europmc-pmc10412457:
Tsuboyama and co-authors measured in 2023 how stably a vast set of proteins fold. A protein must fold into a fixed shape to do its job. How much energy that fold holds shapes health, disease, and protein design. Past work could test just a few proteins at a time.

Their new method can test up to 900,000 protein parts in one week. In all, the team made 1.8 million measures and kept about 776,000 clean ones. The set covers each single change in 331 natural proteins and 148 designed ones. Tsuboyama used it to weigh how place and paired changes shift a fold. The data also showed where designed proteins miss the mark.
europmc-pmc10454957:
Onyeaka and co-authors reviewed in 2021 how Covid lockdowns changed daily life across the world. The World Health Organization named Covid-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Most nations then shut schools, shops, and travel to slow the virus. The team searched past studies for the full spread of effects.

Food access grew shaky as prices swung and supply lines broke. World output shrank, and tourism, hotels, and sport ground to a halt. School moved online, with gaps in who could join. Onyeaka also reports more strain on mental health and more abuse at home. One gain was cleaner air in many cities. The review urges planners to weigh all these costs next time.
europmc-pmc10618257:
Lee and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how fat-based carriers stir the immune system, and what that means for mRNA drugs. The carriers, lipid nanoparticles, ferry mRNA into cells for vaccines and cures. The body reads them as foreign, so they wake the innate immune arm. That wake-up then shapes the learned, adaptive response.

Some of that stir helps a vaccine work, Lee notes. Too much can cause side effects and blunt repeat doses. The review maps which parts of the carrier trigger which alarm. It also tracks the harm reports tied to that response. Ways to tune the stir up or down close the piece. Such tuning may raise both safety and strength of mRNA care.
europmc-pmc10790257:
Xu and co-authors offer a tool that keeps location in view when reading gene activity in tissue in this 2024 paper. Spatial transcriptomics is a method that measures which genes are active at many spots across a tissue slice. The location data helps show how cells are arranged and how they may signal each other. Older tools often lost that spatial detail or scaled poorly on sharp, high-detail datasets.

Their tool, SEDR, learns a compact summary of gene activity with a deep autoencoder, a network that squeezes data down and rebuilds it. A second network then weaves in the spot locations. SEDR grouped tissue regions more accurately than rival tools on standard test sets. It can also fill in missing gene readings and smooth out noise, the authors report.
europmc-pmc11059157:
Lee, Shin, and Chae review how cells choose what to pack into tiny export sacs in this 2024 paper. Exosomes are small sacs cells release to send proteins, fats, and gene messages to other cells. Their cargo decides where they act and what they do on arrival. How cells sort chosen cargo into the sacs is still not fully known.

The review gathers current insight on the sorting machinery for each cargo type. Membrane proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and signal molecules each follow distinct loading rules. The resulting sac contents shape cell growth, immune action, and disease spread. Cancer gets particular emphasis, since tumours use these sacs to aid growth. The authors argue that mastering cargo choice is essential for using sacs as disease markers and drug carriers.
europmc-pmc11128457:
Shi and colleagues review the Notch signal path in cancer and the drugs aimed at it in this 2024 paper. Notch signalling is an ancient cell-to-cell system that decides cell fates and builds organs. Its receptors and partners sit in cell membranes and must touch to fire the signal. In cancer the path can act as a driver or as a brake, depending on the tumour.

Faulty Notch signalling fuels cell shape change, vessel growth, invasion, and spread, the review says. It also keeps cancer cells in a stem-like state that resists chemotherapy. The path helps rewire how tumours burn fuel and shapes the tissue around them. That double role makes dosing tricky. The authors gather the mechanistic detail first, then survey targeted therapies. They argue that this full picture is crucial for designing smarter Notch drugs.
europmc-pmc11491057:
Wu, Zhang, Li, Wu, and Jiang explain the cold and hot tumour distinction and how to heat cold tumours in this 2024 paper. Immune checkpoint blockade frees T cells to attack cancer and has transformed treatment. Yet only a minority of patients respond. Responders usually show an inflamed, immune-active tumour, dubbed hot.

Non-responders often show a cold phenotype, an immune desert with few T cells inside. A third, excluded phenotype keeps T cells at the tumour's edge, between cold and hot. The review details the intrinsic tumour factors, immune traits, microenvironment features, and external factors that set each type. Distinguishing them is critical for predicting response, the authors argue. Targeted strategies to convert cold tumours toward hot are then surveyed. These include combinations that draw T cells in and strip away suppression.
europmc-pmc11718157:
GBD 2021 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators estimate the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts to 2050, in this 2024 study. This resistance, where drugs stop working against bacteria, is a major global health challenge. A prior study quantified the burden for 2019. No study had yet paired historical trends with future forecasts for all places.

The team estimated deaths and years of healthy life lost, both caused by resistance and linked to it. Coverage spans 22 pathogens, 84 pathogen-drug pairings, and 11 infectious syndromes across 204 countries and territories. Inputs covered 520 million single records or isolates: death records, hospital discharges, lab germ data, literature studies, drug sales, and antibiotic use surveys among them. Age-specific and all-age figures were produced for each year.
europmc-pmc1363357:
Díaz-Uriarte and Alvarez de Andrés applied random forest methods to gene chip data in 2006. Gene selection seeks the smallest set that still predicts sample class. Older methods rank genes one by one with arbitrary cutoffs. Many handle only two classes at a time.

Random forest returns its own variable importance measures. It tolerates many noisy variables and few samples. Multi-class problems fit the method naturally. The authors propose a selection method built on those importance scores. Backward elimination trims genes while tracking prediction error. Díaz-Uriarte ties selection directly to the classifier itself.
europmc-pmc1393757:
Coller, Sang, and Roberts gave a new description of resting cells in 2006. Quiescence is a reversible halt in cell growth and division. It was assumed to be one uniform state. Human fibroblasts were driven to rest by three separate signals.

Gene profiling compared mitogen withdrawal, contact, and adhesion loss. Each signal switched its own unique gene set. Beneath the variety sat a shared quiescence program. Its genes enforce the halt and keep it reversible. One trick is suppressing terminal differentiation programs. Coller shows resting states differ by trigger yet share a core.
europmc-pmc1524957:
Silencing a gene fast helps test what it does. Bart and co-authors built such a system for rice in 2006, using protoplasts, plant cells stripped of their walls. Rice protoplasts were hard to prepare well. Their method uses young seedlings grown in the dark.

Reporter genes peaked about 20 hours after DNA delivery. Small plasmids entered 60 to 70 percent of cells. Short interfering RNAs, tiny RNA pieces that mute a target gene, cut reporter output by up to 83 percent within hours. Bart also made protoplasts from green leaf tissue. The system lets labs screen many rice genes quickly.
europmc-pmc1762357:
DNA barcoding trusts public databases, and that trust is shaky for fungi. Nilsson and co-authors audited fungal sequences in 2006 in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database. Species identification by sequence assumes entries are complete and correctly labeled.

Sampling of fungi was far from complete. About 20 percent of entries may be misidentified at species level. Most entries also lacked descriptive, up-to-date annotations. Nilsson warns the greatest challenges to barcoding are taxonomic, not technical. Fixing names and notes in the repositories matters as much as better sequencing.  The authors press database curators to clean up entries and fill the sampling gaps.
europmc-pmc1802757:
Phan, Filler and colleagues identified in 2007 how the yeast Candida albicans invades human cells. This fungus is the most common cause of candidiasis that spreads through the blood and of thrush in the mouth. Its thread-like hyphae enter host cells by triggering endocytosis, the process where a cell swallows material at its surface.

A fungal surface protein named Als3 proved required for that entry into vein-lining cells and two oral cell lines. Als3 binds cadherins, the proteins that glue host cells to each other, namely N-cadherin on vein cells and E-cadherin on oral cells. Beads coated with part of Als3 were swallowed by hamster cells carrying human cadherins, while control beads were not. Computer modeling showed Als3 grips cadherins much as cadherins grip each other.
europmc-pmc1817657:
Pham, Schneider and co-authors reported in 2007 that fruit flies can gain a specific, lasting protection after a first mild infection. Flies rely only on innate immunity, which textbooks said cannot adapt or remember. Yet a sublethal dose of Streptococcus pneumoniae later shielded flies against a dose that would normally kill them.

The protection was coarse but specific to that bacterium and lasted for the life of the fly. A natural fly fungus, Beauveria bassiana, could prime a similar shield. The effect required phagocytes, the cells that swallow microbes, plus the Toll signaling pathway. Switching Toll on alone was not enough to create the protection. The finding breaks the dogma that insect immunity cannot adapt.
europmc-pmc1968657:
Liebmann, Mitchell and co-authors measured in 1993 how paclitaxel, then known by the brand name Taxol, kills human tumor cells in the dish. Paclitaxel was a new anticancer drug, and its dose and timing rules were still being worked out. The team used colony-forming assays on eight human tumor cell lines.

Survival fell sharply after a day of exposure in a narrow low-dose window, with half-kill doses between 2.5 and 7.5 nanomolar across lines. Beyond about 50 nanomolar, extra drug added no killing at one day. At a very high dose, survival oddly rose again. Stretching exposure to 72 hours raised killing fivefold to 200-fold depending on the line, and fast-growing cells were more sensitive than resting ones. The solvent Cremophor EL blunted the drug. The data favor long, modest clinical exposures.
europmc-pmc2125357: A medical paper on the agglutination of bacteria in vivo. The clumping germs. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2125457: A medical paper on the treatment of leprosy with cyanocuprol. The leprosy drug. This article preserves that therapeutics. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2126357: Leptospira survivors among guinea pigs earned a shield against reinfection, which the fourth yellow fever paper quantified. The immune animals faced fresh challenge. The seasoned rodents, tested. The article preserves that tropical medicine research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2140357: A biology paper on the heliotropism of Onchidium, a problem in the analysis of animal conduct. The sun-seeking slug. This article preserves that animal behavior. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2222957:
McKenna and co-workers mapped gut bacteria in rhesus macaques in 2008 using high-throughput DNA sequencing. The gut hosts a vast bacterial community shaped by the immune system, and gut diseases may reflect disrupted host-bacteria relations. The team read 141,000 gene sequences from 100 uncultured gut samples. They compared communities in health, in lentiviral infection, and in chronic gut inflammation called enterocolitis.

Macaque gut communities differed in both abundance and bacterial types from those seen in mice and humans. Communities also varied between gut sites, between animals, over time, and between males and females. Samples from diseased animals differed significantly from healthy ones. Diseased animals had colitis and were receiving antibiotics. The work supplies reference data and methods for using macaques to study human gut disease.
europmc-pmc2265557:
Finlan and co-workers tested in 2008 whether a gene's position inside the nucleus directly changes its activity. Gene-poor chromosome regions sit near the nuclear edge, and inactive genes often gather there. Correlation alone cannot prove causation. The team tethered specific human chromosomes to one protein of the inner nuclear membrane, dragging them to the periphery in living cells, then measured gene expression nearby and farther away.

Tethering reversibly suppressed some endogenous genes near the attachment sites, and even some distant ones. Many other genes showed no detectable reduction, so the periphery is compatible with active transcription. The dampening depended on histone deacetylases, enzymes that tighten gene packaging. Position can therefore modulate selected genes, a tool animals may use during development and differentiation to fine-tune expression.
europmc-pmc2360657:
Zeisberger and colleagues tested a way to starve tumors by removing their helper cells in 2006. Many tumors recruit macrophages, immune cells that here help the tumor grow new blood vessels. The team packed a drug called clodronate into fat bubbles named liposomes, which macrophages swallow.

In two mouse tumor models, the treatment wiped out most of these helper cells. Tumor growth fell by 75% to over 92%, depending on the schedule, and blood vessel density dropped sharply. Adding an antibody that blocks VEGF, a vessel growth signal, gave the strongest effect. Plain clodronate without the bubbles did almost nothing. Vessel counts and helper cell counts fell 85% to over 94% in one model, and the effect lasted nine days after treatment ended.
europmc-pmc2375057:
Fontana and co-authors stopped a resistant childhood cancer in mice by blocking one small RNA in 2008. The cancer is neuroblastoma, a tumor of nerve tissue in young children. In aggressive cases a gene called MYCN runs too high, and it switches on a cluster of small RNAs named miR-17-5p-92.

Those small RNAs hold down two brakes on cancer: p21, which halts cell division, and BIM, which triggers cell death. The blocking drug, an antagomir aimed at miR-17-5p, freed both brakes. In dishes and in mice it abolished growth of tumors that were therapy-resistant and MYCN-driven. In patient tumors, most cases showed raised miR-17-5p and lowered p21, worst in MYCN cases with poor outlooks. The authors claimed the first in-animal proof that an antagomir can stop tumor growth.
europmc-pmc2376357:
Zachariae and co-authors studied how doctors' manner lands with cancer patients in 2003. They asked whether a doctor who listens closely and shows empathy leaves patients calmer and more confident. Questionnaires were given to 454 patients at an oncology clinic, before and after their consultation.

Patients who rated their doctor as more attentive and warm reported greater satisfaction afterwards. They also felt more able to handle their illness, a quality called self-efficacy, and showed less emotional distress. Where ratings were low, doctors also proved poor at guessing how satisfied their patients were. The authors said the pattern confirms and widens earlier findings. They framed communication not as bedside decoration but as a core clinical skill in cancer care, one that shapes how patients cope.
europmc-pmc2410157:
Jin and Varner reviewed integrins as cancer drug targets in 2004. Integrins are grip proteins that anchor cells to the matrix around them and help them crawl. Their signals also control cell growth, survival, and new blood vessel formation, all processes tumors exploit.

The authors singled out several integrins that drive tumor vessel growth and cancer spread to new sites. Blocking them in lab studies stopped cell migration and invasion, and pushed some cells into apoptosis, programmed death. Blocker drugs also starved tumors by halting their blood supply in animal tests. At the time of writing, antibody blockers of two integrins, named alpha5beta1 and alphavbeta3, were in patient trials. Peptide blockers hitting alphavbeta3 and alphavbeta5 were also being tested as vessel-blocking cancer therapies.
europmc-pmc2453157:
Calafat and colleagues measured a sunscreen chemical across the US population in this national survey report. The chemical, benzophenone-3, absorbs ultraviolet light and is used in sunscreens, cosmetics, and some food packaging. The team analysed urine from 2,517 people aged six and older in the 2003 to 2004 national health survey.

The chemical turned up in 96.8% of samples, showing exposure was nearly universal. The typical level was 22.9 micrograms per litre, while the top 5% of people reached 1,040 micrograms per litre. Women and girls carried significantly higher levels than males at every age. Non-Hispanic white participants also carried higher levels than non-Hispanic black participants. Women were 3.5 times as likely as men to sit in the top exposure band, and white participants 6.8 times as likely as black participants. The authors tied the gaps to personal care product use.
europmc-pmc2515157:
Dowd and colleagues tested a faster way to census gut bacteria in cattle in this 2008 paper. Knowing which microbes live in the intestine matters for animal health and food safety, but older census methods were slow and costly. Their method, called bTEFAP, reads tagged pieces of a bacterial gene in bulk using a sequencing technique named pyrosequencing.

The team profiled dung from 20 lactating dairy cows on commercial farms. Common bacteria included Clostridium, Bacteroides, Ruminococcus, and Prevotella, among many others. Four cows carried Salmonella and six carried Campylobacter, two germs that can sicken people through food. The authors show the method can survey herd gut communities cheaply enough for routine use.
europmc-pmc2518857:
Ragon and colleagues traced the family history of Listeria monocytogenes in this 2008 study. The bacterium causes listeriosis, a serious food-borne illness, and also serves as a model for how germs invade cells. The team read parts of seven housekeeping genes, meaning genes every cell needs, in 360 isolates gathered to represent the species.

They found 126 sequence types. Of these, 58 fell into seven tight clonal groups. Those groups covered almost 75 percent of clinical cases. Each group carried a dominant surface type, and gene swapping between strains proved extremely rare, so the family lines stay stable over time. One exception was the invasion protein InlA, which evolved by local recombination and shows signs of selection favouring a shortened form.
europmc-pmc2599757:
Hugo, Brandebourg, Woo, Loftus, Alexander, and Ben-Jonathan tested in 2008 whether bisphenol A, a hormone-disrupting chemical in plastics, alters a protective hormone released by human fat. The hormone, adiponectin, improves insulin sensitivity. It also calms inflammation. Blocking it could raise metabolic risk. The team exposed breast, abdominal, and visceral fat samples and mature fat cells to low doses of the chemical and to estradiol, the natural estrogen.

At doses of 0.1 and 1 nanomolar, squarely in the range found in human blood, bisphenol A suppressed adiponectin release from every depot tested. It matched or beat equal doses of estradiol despite wide variation between patients. The tissues expressed estrogen receptors alpha and beta and the related receptor ERR gamma at similar levels. The authors say the mechanism and receptors involved remain to be pinned down.
europmc-pmc2635757:
Taherzadeh and Karimi reviewed in 2008 how plant waste can be prepared so it yields more ethanol fuel and biogas. Plant waste from farms, forests, and factories is rich in tough fibers. Germs and enzymes struggle to break those fibers down, so yields stay low without a first treatment step.

The review first explains what blocks breakdown: tight crystal packing in the fibers, little exposed surface, and shielding by lignin, the stiff plant glue. It then walks through the treatment options one by one. They include grinding, steam explosion, hot water, ammonia treatment, acids, and living microbes that soften the fibers. For each method, the authors note how much it improved later ethanol or gas output in past studies.
europmc-pmc2654157:
Guo and colleagues asked in 2009 where a muscle-limiting protein called myostatin must be blocked to make animals leaner. Mice born without myostatin grow huge muscles, carry little fat, and resist obesity. But myostatin acts in both muscle and fat tissue, so the source of the benefit was unclear.

The team built two mouse lines: one blocked myostatin signals only in fat, the other only in muscle. Blocking fat alone changed nothing, on normal or fatty diets. Blocking muscle alone copied the full effect: more lean mass, less fat, and better blood sugar control. The full knockout mice also used more glucose and responded better to insulin, even though their muscles burned slightly less fat. Fat loss, the authors conclude, is a side effect of changes inside muscle.
europmc-pmc2662657:
MacIntyre and a large team tested in 2009 whether face masks stop flu-like illness from spreading inside homes. When a pandemic strikes, drugs and vaccines may run short, so simple measures matter. The team ran a randomized trial in Australian households where a child had fallen ill with a respiratory infection.

Adults in some homes were asked to wear surgical masks or high-grade respirator masks around the sick child; others carried on as usual. In practice, few people wore the masks steadily, which weakened the trial's overall result. Among those who did wear them as directed, though, protection was clear and strong. The authors conclude masks can work in the home, but only if people actually keep them on, a real-world hurdle for pandemic plans.
europmc-pmc2706257:
Köhrmann and colleagues measured in 2009 all known matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that cut through the material around cells, in human breast cancer. Tumors use such enzymes to invade nearby tissue and spread. Normal tissue keeps their activity tightly checked, and that balance seems lost in cancer.

They tested 25 tissue samples, five normal and twenty cancers of two grades, plus four breast cancer cell lines. Fourteen of these enzymes were higher in cancer than in normal tissue, and four rose further in higher-grade tumors. One cell line, MDA-MB-468, made the most of most enzymes. The list gives targets for later work on how breast tumors grow and spread.
europmc-pmc2711257:
Tandon and Garcia-Tsao reviewed in 2009 what predicts death in liver cancer with cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is severe scarring of the liver. The cancer form they studied is hepatocellular carcinoma. Most older studies mixed patients with and without cirrhosis, and mixed mild and advanced liver failure. That mix could blur which signs truly matter at each stage.

Across 72 studies with close to twenty-four thousand patients, the firmest predictors were tumor size and spread into the portal vein. A tumor marker in blood and Child-Pugh class, a score of liver function, also predicted death. Both tumor traits and liver traits mattered. Too few studies split mild from advanced cirrhosis to prove that predictors differ by stage.
europmc-pmc2718857:
Schnakers and co-authors tested in 2009 how often doctors mislabel patients with disorders of consciousness as vegetative when they are in fact minimally conscious. A vegetative state shows arousal without awareness, while a minimally conscious state shows uneven but real goal-directed acts. The split matters greatly for care and for end-of-life choices.

In one hundred three patients, they compared team consensus from daily observation with a standardized scale, the JFK Coma Recovery Scale-Revised. Of forty-four patients called vegetative by consensus, eighteen proved minimally conscious on the scale, a rate near forty percent. Most patients left as uncertain by consensus were also minimally conscious on testing, which argues for routine standardized exams.
europmc-pmc2720457:
Treadway and co-authors introduced in 2009 the Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task, a lab game that measures how hard people will work for a reward. Loss of pleasure and drive, called anhedonia, is a core trait in major depression, but it was judged mostly by self-report. An objective task could test drive directly and fairly.

Sixty-one students chose between easy tasks for small pay and hard tasks for larger, uncertain pay, and also rated their own mood and anhedonia. Across several analyses, higher anhedonia meant less willingness to work hard for rewards. The link held for effort choice in particular, which supports the task as a valid measure of reward motivation.
europmc-pmc2732457:
Ko and co-authors ran a worldwide study in 2002 of community-acquired Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia, blood infection caught outside hospitals, covering four hundred fifty-five episodes. This bacterium is a classic cause of severe pneumonia, often tied to alcoholism in textbooks. Reports from Asia also described a new syndrome of liver abscess with spread to the eye or brain coverings.

Bacteremic pneumonia proved rare in the United States, Argentina, Europe, and Australia, with only four cases and none in alcoholics. In South Africa and Taiwan it was common, and the alcohol link held there. Twenty-five cases of the liver abscess syndrome occurred, almost exclusively in Taiwan, which marks a sharp geographic split in disease patterns.
europmc-pmc2763257:
Flora reviewed in 2009 the structural, chemical, and biological aspects of antioxidants used against exposure to heavy metals and metalloids. Oxidative stress drives much of the harm from such exposure, and some treatments, such as chelation therapy, work partly by easing that stress. Natural and synthetic antioxidants, from vitamins and N-acetylcysteine to alpha-lipoic acid, melatonin, and plant flavonoids, have eased metal-induced changes in studies.

Human evidence, however, stays limited, and under some conditions supplements can act as pro-oxidants and worsen damage. The evidence is therefore too thin to recommend antioxidant supplements for exposed people. Flora calls for prospective controlled trials of single agents and of combinations with chelating drugs, testing both safety and benefit. Such trials would show which approach truly helps people who face metal exposure at work or at home.
europmc-pmc2780357:
Dörr, Lewis, and Vulić showed in 2009 that the bacterial SOS response actively creates persister cells that survive the antibiotic ciprofloxacin in Escherichia coli. Persisters are a small subpopulation that endures lethal drug doses without inherited resistance. They were widely viewed as pre-existing dormant cells formed by chance. The authors tested whether DNA damage signaling, the SOS network, helps make them instead.

Most persisters to ciprofloxacin formed only after the drug was applied. Their formation depended on the SOS gene network, the system cells switch on when DNA breaks. Fluoroquinolones kill by breaking DNA, so the survival program answers the very damage the drug causes. This inducible mechanism challenges the purely stochastic picture of persistence. It may shape how antibiotic therapy plays out in patients, since switched-on persisters can seed relapse after treatment ends.
europmc-pmc2803857:
Camacho and colleagues introduced BLAST+ in 2009, a rebuilt version of the BLAST software that searches DNA and protein databases for similar sequences. BLAST is a daily workhorse in biology, but the old code ran slowly on very long queries and had grown hard to maintain after years of patches.

The rewrite splits long queries into chunks, which can cut run times sharply. For huge database entries like whole chromosomes, it fetches only the parts a short query needs, saving time and memory. New tools let users save favorite settings in strategy files and share them through the NCBI website. A modular library also lets the search read sequences from varied data sources.
europmc-pmc2816657:
Chen, Imanaka, Chen, and Griffin showed in 2010 that low oxygen switches on the Notch signaling pathway in breast cancer cells, loosening the cells' grip on each other. Such loosening, part of a shift called EMT, helps cancers spread. Notch was known to feed that shift, but what raises Notch activity as tumors outgrow their blood supply was unclear.

Under low oxygen, two oxygen-sensor proteins piled up and teamed with a Notch helper to boost Notch target genes. Two repressors, Snail and Slug, rose while the glue protein E-cadherin fell, and cells migrated and invaded more. Blocking Notch erased those changes, tying oxygen shortage directly to a spread-ready state through this pathway.
europmc-pmc2846857:
Sena, van der Worp, Bath, Howells, and Macleod pooled animal stroke research in 2010 to measure how much unpublished work distorts the picture. Journals favor positive results, so negative experiments often sit in file drawers while summaries built on published work overstate benefit. Using systematic review data gathered on interventions tested in animal models of acute stroke, they measured the gap.

Adjusting for the missing studies cut the apparent benefit sharply: publication bias alone accounted for roughly a thirty percent overstatement of efficacy across the stroke treatments reviewed. The authors warn that candidate drugs chosen from such inflated summaries enter human trials looking stronger than they are, and they press for fuller reporting of animal experiments.
europmc-pmc2852857:
Xia, Deng, Guo, and Li reviewed in 2010 the health effects of polyphenols from grapes, the plant chemicals behind the famous French paradox of rich food and low heart disease. The review covers how these compounds are extracted and identified, how well the body absorbs them, and where high doses might turn harmful.

Four families carry most of the activity: anthocyanins coloring red skins, flavanols concentrated in seeds and stems, flavonols, and resveratrol. Across studies they acted as antioxidants and showed heart-protective, anticancer, anti-inflammatory, anti-aging, and antimicrobial effects. Yet the authors flag open questions: some large polyphenols are barely absorbed, and very high concentrations have shown negative effects in some settings.
europmc-pmc2854757:
Meeker and Stapleton examined house dust in 2010 for two organophosphate flame retardants and checked whether levels tracked men's hormone and semen measures. The chemicals, TDCPP and TPP, are mixed into furniture foam and plastics as older brominated retardants are phased out. Dust from the homes of fifty men at a fertility clinic was analyzed alongside their blood and semen samples.

Both chemicals turned up in nearly every home, at widely varying levels. Men in dustier homes for TDCPP showed slightly lower free thyroxine, a thyroid hormone, and notably higher prolactin. Higher TPP tracked higher prolactin as well and about a fifth lower sperm concentration. The authors call for more work on exposure sources and health effects.
europmc-pmc2916857:
Cuntz, Forstner, Borst, and Häusser proposed in 2010 a single rule that grows realistic neuron shapes in a computer. A neuron's branching tree balances two costs Cajal named a century ago: the material spent building branches and the time signals take to travel them. Their formalism treats the tree as an optimized graph stretched over the field it must cover.

One balancing factor, weighing material cost against conduction speed, plus the density of that coverage field, reproduced the branching of every neuron type they tested. Changing the factor shifted a synthetic tree's electrical compartmentalization in step with real cells. Their open-source TREES toolbox implements the growth rule, letting modelers generate or repair neuronal morphologies and read developmental or functional meaning from where real trees deviate.
europmc-pmc2958657:
Lemons and co-authors profiled the metabolism of resting fibroblast cells in 2010, challenging the idea that cells which stop dividing also shut down their chemistry. Non-dividing cells were expected to need far less fuel and building material.

Using metabolite measurements, they found resting fibroblasts still push glucose through the main carbon pathways. The cells leaned on a side route, the pentose phosphate pathway, for survival even without dividing. The finding recasts quiescence as an active state with its own fuel logic, relevant to tissues that sit quiet for years yet must stay ready to repair damage.
europmc-pmc2965757:
Padmanabhan led a huge genome scan for blood pressure extremes in 2010, contrasting people with clear hypertension against those with low pressure. Known gene variants then explained only a sliver of blood pressure variation, so more remained hidden.

Follow-up in tens of thousands of cases and controls pinned a variant near the UMOD gene on chromosome sixteen. One version lowered hypertension risk, urinary uromodulin output, and heart and vessel event risk, alongside better kidney function. Because uromodulin is made only in one kidney segment, the finding points at kidney salt handling as a lever on pressure.
europmc-pmc3000457:
Gold led a very large team presenting an aptamer-based technology that measures thousands of proteins from a drop of blood in a 2010 article. Reading the full protein set of a sample, proteomics, stayed slow and narrow compared with gene reading.

Their assay uses folded DNA strands, chemically tweaked for variety, that each grab one protein and then report its amount as DNA on a chip. The current version reads over eight hundred proteins from a tiny serum sample with fine precision across a huge range. Applied to chronic kidney disease, it rediscovered known markers and flagged dozens of new candidates.
europmc-pmc3029257:
Colvin and colleagues examined in 2011 what one slimy sugar coating does for biofilms of a common lung infecting bacterium. Biofilms are dense cell communities glued together by self made material, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa makes three such sugars. Two were well studied, but the third, called Pel, was poorly understood. The team used tiny optical tweezers and gene deletions to test its role.

In one lab strain, removing Pel collapsed the biofilm, showing it acts as a main scaffold holding cells together. In a second strain, another sugar did that job instead, so the need for Pel depends on the strain. Pel also shielded biofilm cells from a class of antibiotics, a protection free floating cells did not get. Its production rose when cells grew as biofilms.
europmc-pmc3037057:
Efird explained in 2011 how blocked randomization keeps clinical trial groups balanced without making assignments predictable. In trials, patients are assigned to treatment or comparison groups by chance. Pure chance can, by luck, stack one group with more patients, weakening the study. Assigning patients in small blocks keeps the counts close throughout enrollment.

Fixed block sizes carry a hidden flaw: when staff are not blinded, the last assignment in each block can be guessed in advance. That opens the door to selection bias, where sicker or healthier patients get steered. Efird shows how picking block sizes at random removes the guesswork while keeping balance. The paper gives trial designers a clear overview of when blocking helps. It also shows the simple change that keeps the process honest.
europmc-pmc3041657:
Chen and Boutros released in 2011 a software package that draws polished Venn and Euler diagrams inside the R statistics system. Such diagrams show how sets overlap, a need that comes up constantly when biologists merge results from several experiments. Older tools offered little control over colors, labels, and layout, and rarely produced print ready files.

The package lets users adjust nearly every feature, from fonts and label placement to rotation and transparency. It handles Venn diagrams of up to four sets and Euler diagrams, which drop empty overlaps for clarity, of up to three. Output is saved as high resolution image files ready for journals. Sensible defaults mean simple diagrams need almost no setup. The authors built it to slot into the analysis pipelines biologists already use in R.
europmc-pmc3114757:
Simon Baron-Cohen and colleagues reviewed why autism is diagnosed far more often in males, in a 2011 paper in PLoS Biology. Rates run several times higher in boys, and the gap is widest for Asperger syndrome. The authors argue this pattern may hold clues to the causes of the condition itself.

Their favoured account treats autism as an extreme form of a typical male style of thinking, strong on rule-based analysis and weaker on social reading. They weigh support from studies of hormone exposure before birth, following children from pregnancy to age ten. Rival accounts based on sex chromosomes or on missed cases in girls are also considered. The authors conclude the accounts can overlap, since autism has many causes.
europmc-pmc3158057:
Joelle Amselem and a large consortium sequenced two notorious crop-killing fungi in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. The two close relatives rot a vast range of crops and linger stubbornly in fields, making them models for broad-host tissue-killing pathogens. One strain of the first and two of the second were read and compared with other fungi.

Their genomes are close in size and share most of their genes, with matching layouts over long stretches. One carries far more jumping DNA than the other. Their tissue-killing toolkits look similar, including wall-digesting enzymes and acid production, while the second species holds a wider stock of toxin-making clusters, perhaps suiting different niches. Differences in mating loci explain their opposite breeding systems and hint at how one evolved from the other.
europmc-pmc3191157:
Marlieke de Kraker, Peter Davey, and Hajo Grundmann calculated the human and cash cost of drug-resistant bloodstream infections in Europe in a 2011 paper in PLoS Medicine. Resistance threatens modern medicine, yet its exact toll had never been counted. The team combined prospective outcome studies from hospitals in thirteen countries with Europe-wide case counts for the two commonest bloodstream germs.

For resistant staph and resistant gut bacteria alike, they estimated extra deaths, extra hospital days, and the spending those days consume, country by country. Trend lines projected the burden forward several years. Resistant infections added a clear extra toll in deaths and bed days beyond matched susceptible infections. The numbers are meant to let resistance compete fairly against other health priorities for funding and attention.
europmc-pmc3198457:
Mark Poritz and a large team introduced the FilmArray diagnostic system in this 2011 paper. The system was built to identify many disease-causing organisms from a single patient sample in about an hour, with little hands-on work. All the chemistry happens inside a sealed disposable pouch, which lowers the risk of contamination between tests.

Inside the pouch, the sample is purified, copied, and put through a nested multiplex PCR step, followed by melting-curve analysis that names the organism. The team validated the approach with a panel covering twenty-one common viral and bacterial causes of respiratory infection. Tests on cultured organisms and on nasal samples from children matched the sensitivity and specificity of existing platforms.
europmc-pmc3237357:
Maryse Bouchard and colleagues measured prenatal and childhood exposure to organophosphate pesticides against IQ at age seven, in this 2011 study in Environmental Health Perspectives. The families came from a farming community in California's Salinas Valley, mostly Latino farmworker households. Exposure was tracked through pesticide breakdown products in urine, collected during pregnancy and repeatedly through childhood.

Children whose mothers had the highest exposure during pregnancy scored about seven IQ points lower on average. The comparison is with children whose mothers had the lowest exposure. Scores were weaker across working memory, processing speed, verbal comprehension, and perceptual reasoning. The children's own later exposures showed no consistent link to their scores. Maternal levels, though higher than average, fell within the range seen in the general United States population, which the authors flag as a wider concern.
europmc-pmc3276357:
Céline Colnot asked where the stem cells that heal broken bones actually come from, in this 2009 study in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. Repair needs adult skeletal progenitors to lay down cartilage and bone at the injury, and the bone marrow and the periosteum, the membrane wrapping bone, were both candidate sources. Colnot tracked the fate of cells from each compartment in living animals.

Injuries to the periosteum healed through a cartilage intermediate, while marrow injuries healed by direct bone formation, showing the two tissues respond differently. Lineage tracing found progenitors recruited locally from both periosteum and marrow, including its inner lining. Both sources produced bone-forming cells, but the periosteum supplied most cartilage-forming cells. Signals from inside the cells and from their surroundings steered the choices, and the two pools differ in their inborn potentials.
europmc-pmc3335257:
Patterson, Wall, Fitzgerald, Ross, and Stanton reviewed the health effects of eating large amounts of omega-6 fats, in a 2012 article. Omega-6 and omega-3 fats are raw material for potent signaling molecules that steer inflammation. Those built from omega-6 fats generally promote inflammation, while omega-3 based ones calm it.

Western diets have shifted over recent decades until omega-6 intake outweighs omega-3 by roughly fifteen to one, tilting the body's signaling toward the inflammatory side. Over the same period, chronic inflammatory conditions have climbed, including fatty liver disease, heart disease, obesity, bowel inflammation, arthritis, and Alzheimer disease. The authors argue that rebalancing the diet toward omega-3 fats could trim the incidence of these conditions, and they survey the evidence linking the fat ratio to each disease.
europmc-pmc3343257:
Joundi, Jenkinson, Brittain, Aziz, and Brown showed that brain rhythms are not just echoes of movement but help cause it, in a 2012 study. When people hold still, motor areas of the brain pulse in a rhythm called beta, which fades as movement begins. A faster rhythm, gamma, rises during action. Whether these rhythms drive behavior or merely reflect it was unproven.

The team passed gentle alternating currents through the scalp at beta and gamma rates while volunteers squeezed a sensor on cue. Beta rate stimulation slowed the initial build up of force and trimmed its peak rate of rise. Gamma rate stimulation did the opposite in the matching task, and the effects depended on whether the cue demanded action or restraint. The authors conclude that cortical rhythms actively shape motor performance, a finding with possible uses in treating movement disorders.
europmc-pmc3375257:
Baker, Nargund, Sun, and Haynes studied in 2012 how cells react when their mitochondria, the cell's power plants, start to fail. One known response switches on helper genes through a pathway involving the exporter HAF-1 and the factor ATFS-1. The team worked with the roundworm C. elegans to test a second pathway.

They found the kinase GCN-2, which slows general protein building, acts alongside the first pathway rather than inside it. Harmful oxygen byproducts from faulty mitochondria switched GCN-2 on. Worms missing both pathways fared far worse under mitochondrial stress, while those missing GCN-2 leaned harder on ATFS-1. The paired system guards both growth and lifespan.
europmc-pmc3417557:
Fraunholz and Sinha reviewed in 2012 the hidden indoor life of Staphylococcus aureus, a germ famous for surface infections that also invades human cells. Once inside, the pathogen's fate varies widely with strain and cell type. The review serves as a guide to recent work on those intracellular lifestyles.

The germ can multiply inside the cell's eating sac or break out and grow freely in the cell's interior. It dodges the cell's self-cleaning system, triggers several kinds of cell death, and can even switch on anti-death programs in the immune cells meant to kill it. Surviving quietly indoors helps explain stubborn, returning infections. The authors map the tricks that make such persistence possible.
europmc-pmc3430657:
Thomsen and colleagues showed in 2012 that a half liter of seawater carries enough stray DNA to reveal the local fish fauna. Marine fish are usually surveyed with nets and other selective, invasive methods that miss rare species and misname others. The team filtered water from a Danish coastal ecosystem and sequenced the environmental DNA in it.

Fifteen fish species turned up, including important food fish and species conventional surveys rarely or never record, plus a rare visiting pilchard and four bird species. National records confirmed every detection. Against nine conventional survey methods, the water test matched or beat each one at covering diversity. The DNA fades within days, so a positive signal means recent presence, a handy truth for monitoring.
europmc-pmc3437557:
Buljan and colleagues investigated in 2012 how tissue-specific splicing reshapes the protein networks inside human cells. Genes can include or skip sections called exons, and the sections used only in certain tissues are key to those tissues' identity. The team compared the structure, partners, and evolution of always-used, tissue-specific, and other optional exons.

Tissue-specific segments often contain floppy, disordered regions studded with chemical-tag sites and conserved docking motifs. Genes carrying them sit at busy crossroads of interaction networks and swap partners from tissue to tissue. They also cluster in signaling, development, and disease roles. Slipping a flexible docking segment in or out, the authors propose, rewires whole pathways per tissue.
europmc-pmc3438057:
Boratyn and colleagues introduced DELTA-BLAST in 2012, a smarter version of the workhorse BLAST tool for finding related proteins. Standard iterated searching builds a scoring profile from scratch each round, wasting what databases already know. Their method searches a library of ready-made profiles from a conserved domain collection first.

On a standard test set, one round of the new tool detected distant relatives far better than the leading context-sensitive rival. The edge shrank over repeated rounds but never vanished. Remote relatives matter because shared ancestry hints at shared function, even when sequences have drifted far apart. The program is offered through the national BLAST web service for protein searches.

europmc-pmc8842557: This research paper covers m6A modification: recent advances (new steps forward), anticancer aimed drug discovery and beyond. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8868457: A fresh look at progress in alternative plans to combat antimicrobial resistance (germs beating drugs): focus on antibiotics (bacteria-killing drugs) arrived with this 2022 research paper. Antibiotic (bacteria-killing drug) resistance, and, in a broader perspective, antimicrobial resistance (germs beating drugs), continues to evolve and spread beyond. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9259657: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on loss-of-function, gain-of-function and dominant-negative mutations have profoundly other effects on protein structure. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9268357: Doctors and scientists took on broad betacoronavirus neutralization by a stem helix-specific human antibody (defense protein) in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9868457: A fresh look at diabetic (of diabetes) retinopathy: looking forward to 2030 arrived with this 2022 research paper. Diabetic (of diabetes) retinopathy is the major ocular complication of diabetes , and is a problem. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
fowler-self-instructor-phrenology-1857:
O. S. Fowler and L. N. Fowler ran the great phrenology trade in the States. Their Illustrated Self-Instructor came out in 1857. The book taught any buyer to read heads at home, his own and those of kin. Cuts show each bump and trait in clear form.

Steps tell how to feel the skull and score each trait on a chart. Advice then links the scores to jobs, mates, and the care of self. The book put a white bust with marked zones in parlors all over the land. It is a prime text of the field at its peak.
frus-1861-d157:
A round of letters on 21 October 1861 included one from William H. Seward to William Dayton. The letter is document 157 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Paris and to Berlin in the same late October round. The letters kept each post aware that it formed part of one front. Dayton's copy shows the Secretary's hand at work across the map in a single week. The round of late October letters spans the map of the Union's foreign front. One week, one hand, a whole front: the round shows the office at its peak load.
frus-1861-d257:
Washington's orders went out to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands in a dispatch dated 4 October 1861. Congress received it as Document 257 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the autumn of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d57:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 June 1861. It is document 57 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

As June closed, both American armies moved toward their first great clash. Adams could only report London's talk and wait, like Seward, for news. His letter shows an envoy holding his post steady while events at home rushed toward battle. From London, even the clash of armies came first as rumor, then as dread fact. Rumor in London ran fast, and Adams learned to sift it with a cold eye.
frus-1862-d157:
Secretary of State William H. Seward directed a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London on 4 October 1862, printed as Document 157 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams, the American minister to Britain, acted on these orders in his talks with British officials.

Orders from Washington had to cover events the Secretary could not foresee, since replies took weeks. Seward therefore mixed firm lines with room for his envoy's judgment. A letter from this week belongs to the stretch when Britain, after Antietam. Chose to wait rather than step into the war, a choice Adams worked to make permanent.
frus-1862-d257:
Dated 8 March 1862, Document 257 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

The day after Seward wrote, the ironclad Virginia attacked Union ships at Hampton Roads, and the Monitor fought it to a draw. Naval news like that echoed loudly in France, a great sea power with its own ironclad plans. Seward's letters to Paris in March belonged to a season when each battle reset foreign guesses about the war. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d357:
On 10 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent Henri Mercier another letter, printed as Document 357 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier was the French minister in Washington throughout this period.

Two letters in four days show the French channel carrying steady traffic in the winter of 1862. Much of that traffic was case work: ships, trade, and the rights of French citizens caught by the war. Such business rarely made headlines, but it filled the envoys' days and kept the larger relationship in repair. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English.
frus-1862-d457:
John Lothrop Motley wrote from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 February 1862. His report is Document 457 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

February 1862 brought a run of Union victories, and Motley's reports could carry that improving story into Austrian ears. Still, Vienna moved slowly and spoke carefully, and its press often echoed Confederate hopes. A minister's dispatch in such a place was part news, part weather report on opinion. Seward gathered these readings from every capital before deciding where the dangers lay. Motley's February letter is one gauge in that wider instrument panel.
frus-1862-d557:
A Mr. Goodrich received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1862. It is Document 557 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed among the Belgian papers of that summer.

The letter sits in the file between Seward's orders to Minister Sanford in Brussels, part of the same run of Belgian business. Instructions of this kind carried Washington's directions to the officers who served the mission and its work. July 1862 was a month of strain, with the Virginia campaign gone wrong, and every post abroad needed steady direction. The document is a reminder that a legation was a small team. The State Department's paper reached beyond the minister whose name heads the file.
frus-1862-d57:
A dispatch dated 2 May 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 57 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d657:
On 9 December 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Robert H. Pruyn, who was set to lead the American legation in Japan. The letter is document 657 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Townsend Harris, the first minister to Japan, was on his way out of the post.

Before an envoy sailed, the State Department loaded him with written orders. Seward's letters to Pruyn that winter formed the base of the new man's charge. This letter is one of them. It shows how much care Washington took with a post that guarded trade and the flag in a land still new to American ships.
frus-1863p1-d157:
On 16 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 157 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of Adams's pair took the next head of the London news in line. That April, the news ran from the shipyards to Parliament, and the legation sorted it all for home. This letter is the mate to document 156. With it, the pair shows the post's mid-April pace: steady, split by topic, and aimed at a reader who used every page.
frus-1863p1-d257:
An instruction dated 7 August 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 257 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Union victories in July 1863 let Washington speak with more confidence. Orders sent after Gettysburg and Vicksburg carry a firmer note than those of the spring. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d357:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 10 January 1863. It appears as document 357 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d457:
A letter of 11 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 457 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1863p1-d557:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State took up his pen on 8 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d57: A Mr. St. John wrote this letter to a Mr. Smith on 28 October 1862. It is document 57 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the last of the Confederate group printed there. The evidence names the two men and the date, but not their posts or the letter's subject. This note stays within those bounds.
frus-1863p1-d657:
Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 6 November 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late autumn of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d157: Kirk wrote on November 21, 1943 to Nahas, Egypt's prime minister and foreign minister, and the letter is Document 157 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired with his note to the royal cabinet chief the same day, it shows the American minister working both doors of the host government on the conference's eve. The record gives the names and the date. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d257:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 23 November 1943, met at half past two in the afternoon. They take up China's role in the defeat of Japan under paper C.C.S. 405. General Stilwell opens with word from Chiang Kai-shek that no Chinese proposals should be laid before the chiefs until he has talked again with Roosevelt and Marshall.

Sir Alan Brooke and Admiral Leahy judge the first four proposals in the paper workable, and the rest unrealistic for now. Formosa is singled out: it could not be attacked from the Chinese mainland without landing craft. General Marshall urges care and sympathy anyway, noting that Chiang, long reluctant to build ground forces, now shows real interest in them for the first time. Admiral King agrees the Generalissimo should not be discouraged if that can be avoided.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d357:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 28 November 1943 record a morning session at half past eleven. The American chiefs weighed British wishes against Overlord. The first plenary session with Stalin was only hours away. President Roosevelt opens the discussion himself.

Roosevelt understands the British think Allied forces in Italy can reach the Pisa-Rimini line. General Marshall lays out the costs of the rival path. Advancing to Ancona and taking Rhodes in February would push Overlord back to about 15 June, perhaps July. Rhodes would suck in considerable means. The British want Rhodes in place of the Andaman operation, and Turkey's entry above all, claiming Bulgaria and Romania would then fall. Marshall doubts the Straits could open for six to eight months even so, and argues for backing Eisenhower without unduly delaying Overlord.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d457:
Closing day at Cairo also brought a further session of the Combined Chiefs of Staff on December 6, 1943, with minutes printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs, top American and British officers, had spent the conference turning the Tehran agreements into a workable common strategy. Their meetings ran alongside those of Roosevelt and Churchill.

The session record follows the standard form: who was present, what was raised, and what was decided. Its interest lies in timing as much as content, since a final session shows which questions were still open when the conference broke up. Paired with the day's agreed minutes, it completes the official picture.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d557:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on March 4, 1944, continuing a run of messages across the first days of March. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, in the follow-up correspondence to the conferences.

Churchill's March letters pressed the business of a coalition approaching its greatest operation: the cross-Channel invasion fixed at Tehran for the late spring. Around that fixed point circled arguments about Italy, the Balkans, and relations with France and Russia. For readers, the message is one more turn of the handle by a prime minister who believed that writing itself was a form of command.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d57: General George Marshall, Chief of Staff of the Army, wrote to Admiral William Leahy, the President's Chief of Staff, on October 25, 1943. The letter is Document 57 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Staff chiefs writing to each other carried the military side of summit planning while the diplomats met in Moscow. The record names the two soldiers and the date. Its subject rests in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1944-quebec-d157:
Roosevelt settled the French Indochina question for the moment with a short memorandum to Hull on August 28, 1944. The British ambassador's proposals, and the French Committee's aide-mémoire behind them, would wait. The president planned to meet Churchill at Quebec, and he intended the matter to be deferred until after that meeting.

One reason for caution appears in his final line. French participation in planning political warfare in the Far East, Roosevelt noted, involved one of the principal partners: China. Indochina lay in the China theater, and Chiang Kai-shek's views could not be bypassed. Hull was also told orally that the president would raise the French proposals with Churchill directly.
frus-1944-quebec-d257:
On September 13, 1944, the United States Chiefs recommended the Combined Chiefs send General Wilson their own draft message rather than the British one. The approved text, dispatched as Fan 415, gave Wilson two decisions for his future planning in Italy. Both responded directly to his requests for guidance in Naf 774.

First, there would be no withdrawals of major units from the Fifth Army until the outcome of Alexander's present offensive was known. Second, for the capture of the Istrian Peninsula, Wilson could count on the amphibious lift then in the Mediterranean. He was to prepare the operation as soon as possible and submit his plan to the Combined Chiefs by October 10 at the latest.
frus-1944-quebec-d57:
September 6, 1944 found Churchill writing to Roosevelt once more. He was on the last stage of his Atlantic crossing. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill reached North America that week. He then traveled on to Quebec. The conference there would open on September 12. His letters ahead of arrival staked out Britain's needs. Britain wanted a voice in the Pacific war. It wanted fair terms for continued American aid. It also wanted agreement on Germany. For readers, the message shows him arriving in writing first. He reached Quebec in person days later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d157:
A memorandum dated 21 June 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was C. H. Carson of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The reader was the Assistant Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Ladd). It is document 157 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d257:
On 17 December 1947, the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 257 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The ink on the National Security Act was barely dry, and both the CIA and the Council were finding their feet.
