A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d357:
The Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum) addressed a letter to Mathias F. Correa on 18 December 1948. Readers meet it as document 357 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d57:
Admiral Chester Nimitz, now chief of naval operations, wrote to Secretary Forrestal on 15 December 1945. Nimitz had taken over the Navy's top uniformed post the month before. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Nimitz brought the prestige of the Pacific victory to every paper he signed. His views on intelligence, formed in a theater where code-breaking had won battles, carried weight beyond their words. Readers should note the change of hand: King had guarded the Navy's claims through the autumn; Nimitz now held them as the settlement neared. The Navy's thread in the volume thus passes from one great wartime admiral to another without losing its force.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d157:
Poland's western frontier kept growing on Soviet maps, Harriman warned on 19 December 1944. His secret cable from Moscow, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, tracks how Moscow's offer to Poland had widened in a few months. He writes that he is somewhat concerned by the expanding concept.

At first the Soviets spoke of East Prussia, less Königsberg, and a frontier perhaps as far as the Oder, with Stettin and Breslau thrown in. Then the Oder line hardened into the settled intention. Talking with de Gaulle, Stalin pushed further: the Oder to the lower Neisse, then south along the Neisse to the Czech border near Görlitz. A Pravda article had confirmed the new line in print.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d257:
General Deane sent the Joint Chiefs Stalin's shopping list on 17 October 1944. His cable from the American military mission in Moscow, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, records the night's meeting with Stalin, Molotov, and General Antonov. The list prices Soviet entry into the Pacific war.

Stalin first handed over the supplies America must furnish for a two months' stock in the Far East. Fuel leads: 120,000 tons of high-octane gasoline, 70,000 of motor gasoline, and collapsible storage tanks. Foodstuffs run to some 180,000 tons. Then come 30,000 trucks, 500 amphibious jeeps, 400 C-47 and 100 C-54 aircraft, and naval craft from frigates to sub-chasers. Railroad needs close the list: 500 locomotives, thousands of cars, and some 800 kilometers of rail.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d357:
Exact words matter in this American paper of February 6, 1945, which prints the proposed voting formula for the Security Council. The formula had gone to Stalin and Churchill on December 5, 1944. Each member of the council would have one vote. Routine decisions would need seven affirmative votes.

All other decisions would also need seven votes, including the concurring votes of the permanent members. A study of the formula's effects follows the text. This was the heart of the Yalta bargain on the United Nations: great powers kept a veto on action, but not on debate. The paper preserves the wording that made the San Francisco conference possible.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d457:
Stalin's dinner on February 10, 1945, ranged from reparations to Jewish problems, and Bohlen's minutes record the talk. Churchill opened with a toast to the King of England, the President of the United States, and Mr. Kalinin of the Supreme Soviet. He asked Roosevelt, the only head of state present, to reply.

Roosevelt answered with a memory from the summer of 1933, his first year as President. His wife had gone to open a school in the country. On its wall hung a map with a great blank space, a place the teacher said it was forbidden to name. The anecdote — about the unrecognized Soviet Union — set the evening's warm tone.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d57:
Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on 15 January 1945. The cable lists who would travel with him to the conference the Americans code-named Argonaut. It was sent by Navy channels and is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta.

Along with Charles Bohlen, Stettinius names H. Freeman Matthews and Alger Hiss, who would handle Dumbarton Oaks matters. Four secretaries and a military aide chosen by General Marshall complete the party. He also asks Harriman to bring stenographer Nelson Newton to help Bohlen write the minutes. Harriman instead brought Edward Page Jr., as the editors' note explains.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d157:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded another extract of his June 16, 1945 talk with President Truman. The extract is document 157 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, drawn from the same White House meeting that produced document 70. This passage turns to China and the Yalta Far East agreement.

Ambassador Hurley had passed on questions from Chiang Kai-shek about how points in the Yalta agreement would be carried out. Grew told the President he saw no way to answer until the matter had been discussed with Stalin, so replies must wait for the Big Three meeting. Nor could China's Dr. Soong well take the questions up with Stalin alone. The President definitely concurred. The passage shows the Yalta Far East bargain hanging over relations with China.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d257:
A briefing paper documented the shut-out of American reporters in Eastern Europe, dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 257 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It supports the agenda item on freedom of communication and information in Europe.

American correspondents have found it practically impossible even to enter the lands freed by the Soviet armies, the paper says. Soviet military authorities and the Soviet-run control commissions have followed a steady policy of exclusion, and applications since December have been refused or ignored. In Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia the picture is only a little better, with strict censorship. Meanwhile Soviet newsmen enjoy the same freedom in the West that American and British reporters do. The paper lays out the record Washington meant to lay before Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d357:
France's exclusion from the reparations talks fills an extract of Grew's memorandum of a June 25, 1945 conversation with Ambassador Bonnet. The French ambassador came to ask a favor. His government wanted the American ambassador in Moscow told to keep the French ambassador there informed of the three-power Reparations Commission's work.

Bonnet stressed France's deep interest in reparations, and its feeling that a French member should have sat on the Commission. France, he said, had suffered greatly in the war. Grew replied that he would give the request prompt consideration. The extract catches France pressing at the door of a club of three.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d457:
Numbers for the Soviet buildup in Bulgaria follow in Kirk's cable of June 30, 1945, again reporting General Oxley. A Russian division, Oxley was informed, had completed crossing the Danube at Ruse about three days earlier. It moved south toward Trnovo and Shumen. His tentative estimate placed ten Soviet divisions across the country.

Two divisions stood near Varna and Burgas, two near Sliven and Kotel, and others toward the Turkish frontier, at Plovdiv, and north of the Balkan mountains. General opinion put Soviet troops in Bulgaria at 200,000 men. Oxley cautioned that many sources were of doubtful truth, but called the picture probably fair, and the best obtainable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d557:
Belgrade charge Harold Shantz wired Washington again on July 14, 1945. His secret report is document 557 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It records a talk that day with Ivan Subasic, Yugoslavia's deputy premier.

Subasic said he would not join the steering group of the new popular front congress. Tito had told him the front would control all political life, and government men must belong to it. Subasic meant to stay in office, since outside it he could sway nothing. Shantz closes with a bleak verdict of his own. There is no hope of free democracy in Yugoslavia, he writes, and new laws will be window dressing for a one-party regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d57:
Field Marshal H. Maitland Wilson, head of the British Joint Staff Mission in Washington, wrote to Admiral William Leahy on June 12, 1945. The letter is document 57 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Wilson picks up Leahy's suggestion that the two sides swap ideas on an agenda for their military chiefs.

The British Chiefs of Staff, Wilson reports, agree and go further. They want a formal meeting of the Combined Chiefs of Staff tied to the Big Three gathering, held in London beforehand, with three or four clear days for work. The British chiefs will attend the Berlin meeting with small staffs. The main topic, Wilson says, will be the war against Japan, including whether Russia joins it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d657:
A two-line secret wire from Ambassador Winant in London forms document 657 in the Potsdam papers. Dated June 25, 1945, it settles the venue fight over the Tangier talks. The French government was being told of the outcome through the British Embassy in Paris.

Winant reports that the British government had agreed to a Paris meeting on Tangier. That met France's refusal to send its team to London. Details of the message to the Soviet government were expected to be concerted in Paris at once. Washington would be promptly told when that message was sent. The brief wire closes one small contest and sets up the next. The talks could now open in Paris on July 2, with Moscow informed in parallel.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1057: Assistant Secretary James Dunn answered Nikolai Novikov's note from Berlin on July 27, 1945. The Soviet note had enclosed an aide-mémoire about German troops in Norway. Moscow claimed those troops were not being disarmed under the surrender terms. Dunn's reply is only a few lines. Norway, he points out, is an area of primary British military responsibility. He therefore assumes the British government will supply the information the Soviets seek. The letter closes without offering any American findings of its own.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1157:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson set down this memorandum on 19 July 1945, inside the Potsdam weeks. Stimson was the cabinet's elder statesman. When he put his thinking on paper, the War Department's counsel gained a fixed form the president and the team could use.

His memoranda across the summit gave Truman the military house's view in writing. This one dates from the first week, when stands were forming on Germany and the Pacific war. It is the war secretary's considered word, mid-talks. Readers get the judgment of the man who had run the army's civilian side since 1940.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1257:
Togo wrote to Sato on 27 July 1945, the day after the Potsdam Declaration reached Tokyo. The Allied terms demanded surrender and left the throne's fate unclear. Japan's leaders split over the answer, and Togo, who sought an end, kept his Moscow channel alive.

His instruction to Sato shows the foreign minister still working the Soviet door as the crisis peaked. If Moscow would mediate, Tokyo might gain terms the declaration denied it. That hope, thin as Sato's reports had shown it to be, drove this cable. It is Tokyo's hand on its last lever, pulled on the declaration's morrow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1357:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to the acting secretary of state on 23 July 1945, reporting from the Potsdam side of the Atlantic. The channel between Byrnes and Grew ran in both directions all through the conference. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Most papers in this run flow from Washington toward the summit, so a message from Byrnes homeward stands out. The secretary abroad still had to steer his own department: staff, budgets, and other talks all needed his hand. Readers get a sense of the two-way strain of summit diplomacy. The man at the table must also run the office he left behind in Washington.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-157:
State Department minutes record a meeting on August 1, 1945, the closing day of the Potsdam Conference. The leaders adopted the final protocol that day. Formal minutes from the close anchor the end of the second Potsdam volume's session records. They were kept by Department staff as the official American account.

Closing-day minutes have a summing-up quality. Readers find the last points cleared and the results stated. The record also marks the handoff: work now passed to foreign ministers and occupation staffs. These pages give the conference a documented end to match its documented start.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-57:
No record has been found of the substance of the conversation at this meeting. That single sentence is the whole of an editorial note in volume two. It is the fifty-seventh unnumbered item following document 710, in the run of conference records for July 1945.

Nothing is added about who met, or where, or what was at stake. The reader who needs the context must reconstruct it from the documents around the note. Such entries recur throughout this volume wherever the editors' searches came up empty. They serve as markers of the archive's limits. A meeting important enough to note took place, and its content is simply gone from the files the editors could search.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d757:
Document 757 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 25, 1945. Staff prepared it during the conference's second week. Working papers carried the detailed load: options, figures, and draft lines. This one stayed in the delegation's files and entered the second Potsdam volume.

The workshop papers of July 25 came after a week of contact. Drafters knew which lines the other sides resisted. Readers can look for that knowledge in the text's shape. The document shows drafting as a response, not a monologue. It forms part of the broad staff record that makes Potsdam so fully knowable.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d857:
Document 857 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 19, 1945. It comes from the conference's first weekend. Staff used the early days to turn positions into draft language. The paper remained in the delegation files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

First-week working papers show a team still exploring. Options sit side by side, not yet ranked by pain. Readers can enjoy the openness of that stage. Every later text in the volume narrows what papers like this one left wide. The document is a snapshot of possibility, taken before the bargaining began to bite.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d957:
J. Howard Marshall, general counsel to the American reparations delegation, wrote this memorandum on July 30, 1945. He states what the United States should want out of Germany. Two things rank first: German technical knowledge and know-how, and relief from the huge import burden of supporting western Europe.

Knowledge can be gathered in the western zones, Marshall notes. Food, fuel, and potash, though, can come only from the east. Russia wants capital equipment from the west. Marshall's advice is to refuse any such delivery until Russia agrees to ship food, fuel, and fertilizer east to west. Without that trade, American taxpayers pay, and rationing at home tightens.
frus-1961-63v10-d257: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the President's assistant on Cuba. The aide wrote. This entry preserves that memo. It waits for future eyes. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
gao-gaoreports-b-298757: Hamilton Sundstrand Power Systems took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Power giants get the same fair hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298957: 3SG Corporation took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Numbered names get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299457: Apptis tripled its May 2007 protest — three case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three claims. The firm challenged the awards as unfair; the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one triple-checked answer from the referee.
gao-gaoreports-b-299557: A-TEK took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Tech deals big and small get the same fair-play ruling in the end.
gao-gaoreports-b-310357: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Essan Metallix Corporation. The December 7, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-400157: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Logistics Health, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-257: Satellite TV subscribership boomed unevenly in 2005, and GAO's report says the growth varied across market types. The review maps the dish boom from city to countryside. The rural and urban viewers told different stories. The stories were measured. The boom was charted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-457: Airport screeners were sharper but not sharp enough in 2005, and GAO's report says training and performance measurement improved, with more work remaining. The report credits the gains while flagging the gaps. The checkpoints deserved the best. The work went on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-557: Container security needed flexible crews in 2005, and GAO's report says a staffing model and minimum gear would improve overseas targeting. The review writes the prescription. The cargo boxes deserved the screening. The model had to be flexible. The cargo boxes deserved the screening.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-757: Coast Guard Deepwater legacy assets were being addressed in 2005, and GAO's report says progress was made on condition issues, though more was needed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the cutters deserved sound ships. The progress had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-957: The Air Force's Berry Amendment waiver lacked full evaluation in 2005, and GAO's report says options were not fully weighed for selected aircraft. The findings demand the homework. The report warns that the buy-American rule deserved respect. The options had to be evaluated.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-57: HUD's rental assistance payments needed streamlining in 2005, and GAO's report says processes should be simplified to ensure timely payments. The findings demand the speed. The report warns that the waiting tenants deserved on-time aid. The processes had to be streamlined.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-757: Mail security at Pentagon facilities had holes in 2006, and GAO's report says incidents exposed problems requiring further action. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the war department's mail should not carry danger. The mail had to be safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-157: The FDA's device-inspection outsourcing got a GAO check in 2007, and the report reviews the program using accredited organizations. The findings grade the effort. The report asks whether the hired inspectors watched as closely as the government's own. The devices needed real eyes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-357: Tsunami rebuilding ran over budget in 2007, and GAO's report says the signature American efforts in Indonesia and Sri Lanka blew past initial costs. The findings track the overruns. The report asks whether the generosity was managed or just spent. The goodwill was real; the management was not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-457: Burma's junta was strangling the helpers in 2007 — GAO's report says aid programs there ran straight into the regime's walls. The findings document the constraints in detail. The report's quiet fury: the suffering was man-made, and so were the barriers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-557: Kids' medicines were finally being studied in 2007 — GAO's report reviews the pediatric drug research done under the children's act. The findings tally the studies one by one. The report's cause: children are not just small adults, and their drugs should prove it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-657: Breach notices needed a playbook in 2007 — GAO's report distills the hard lessons on telling people their data leaked. The findings write the notification rules in plain terms. The report's creed: the hacked deserve to hear it fast, straight, and first from you.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-857: One label for all colleges? GAO's 2007 report says lumping public, nonprofit, and for-profit schools under one definition would not fly. The findings argue the sectors differ too much for a single yardstick. The report defends nuance in the heated debate over who deserves the name ‘college.'
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-157: The Government Accountability Office dug into intellectual Property: Federal Enforcement Has Generally Increased, but Assessing Performance Could Strengthen Law Enforcement Efforts in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-57: The Government Accountability Office dug into drug-Free Communities Support Program: Stronger Internal Controls and Other Actions Needed to Better Manage the Grant-Making Process in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-657: The Government Accountability Office dug into information Technology: Agriculture Needs to Strengthen Management Practices for Stabilizing and Modernizing Its Farm Program Delivery Systems in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-757: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at border Security: Summary of Covert Tests and Security Assessments for the Senate Committee on Finance, 2003-2007. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-857: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on DCAA Audits: Allegations That Certain Audits at Three Locations Did Not Meet Professional Standards Were Substantiated. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-957: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at tax Administration: Comparison of the Reported Tax Liabilities of Foreign- and US-Controlled Corporations, 1998-2005. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gaskell-life-of-charlotte-bronte-1857:
Elizabeth Gaskell published The Life of Charlotte Brontë in 1857, two years after Brontë's death. Charlotte's father and husband asked Gaskell, her friend, to write the authorized life of her. The book fixed the Brontë myth of the lonely moorland parsonage for the next century.

Gaskell traces Haworth's graves, the sisters' childhood worlds, and their secret writing lives in detail. She tells of Brussels, the Bell books, fame, and the deaths that emptied the house. Some portraits of living people drew threats of lawsuits and forced cuts in later editions printed. Her warm, novelistic hand made the life read like one of Brontë's own tales of Yorkshire. It remains the source all later Brontë lives must start from and argue with.
gosse-omphalos-1857:
Philip Henry Gosse tries to untie the knot of Genesis and geology in Omphalos, from 1857. God, he argues, created the world with the look of age upon it. Fossils lie in the rocks as Adam bore a navel, signs of a past that never truly happened in his bold and strange solution.

Geologists and clergy alike rejected the clever argument at once. The book appeared just as Darwin's Origin loomed over the age. Ingenious yet untestable, it convinced almost no one on either side. It stands as the most famous failed peace treaty between Genesis and geology, a landmark of creationist thought in the Victorian age.
hegel-philosophy-history-sibree-1857:
G. W. F. Hegel gave his Lectures on the Philosophy of History in Berlin in the 1820s. The English text here is J. Sibree's translation of 1857. Hegel argues that world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. Each great people, from China to the German world, plays its part and passes.

He divides history into Oriental, Greek, Roman, and German worlds. Reason, he claims, governs the whole process despite war and suffering. The state is the main carrier of freedom in his account. These lectures seeded Marxism and all later philosophy of history. They remain grand, bold, and hotly debated.
hitchcock-remarks-upon-alchemy-1857:
Ethan Allen Hitchcock made the first case in the United States for a soul first read of the great art. His Remarks upon Alchemy and the Alchemists came out in 1857. Hitchcock was a chief of troops who read old adepts at night in camp. He held their gold was a code for man's soul.

He walks through the chief names and their dark signs with care. His claim was fresh in his land and day. The book set the great art down in that land's thought. Waite and his peers later hailed its worth. Hitchcock served in wars on the far shore of his land. He brought a camp man's plain sense to a theme prone to sheer fog.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowi-isaac-1015:
Isaac Löwi (1803–1873) was a German rabbi born at Adelsdorf in Bavaria. A Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer recounts his contested career. Trained in Talmud at Fürth and in philosophy at Munich, he became district rabbi of Fürth in 1830. Orthodox opponents fought his reforms for years in court.

The article follows the long suit over his sermons and services. It follows the government order telling him to show more regard for tradition, and the new election of 1842 that backed him by a strong majority. His opponents were then allowed their own Orthodox rabbi. Löwi later guided the young Nuremberg congregation as well, was knighted by King Ludwig II in 1869, and died at Fürth. The entry gives readers a detailed case study of reform and resistance inside one German community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magen-dawid-dav:
Magen Dawid, the shield of David, is traced in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The sign is a six-pointed star made by two overlapping triangles. The article calls it the symbol of Judaism, set on synagogues and sacred vessels. The Zionist Congress at Basel adopted it, as had American Jewish publishers earlier.

The entry asks where the symbol came from, and answers honestly. Neither the Bible nor the Talmud knows any such symbol. Rabbinic literature never mentions the shield of David. A Jewish tombstone at Tarentum, perhaps from the third century, may carry it. The first Jewish book to name it is a Karaite work of the twelfth century, where it appears on amulets beside angels' names. Ancient magic papyri show pentagrams but not the hexagram. The writers suspect the Cabala spread the sign. The article traces a beloved emblem without inventing its past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandl-ludwig-la:
Ludwig Lazar Mandl, a Hungarian anatomist, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Budapest in December 1812, he studied at Vienna and Budapest, taking his medical degree in 1836. He then settled in Paris to study microscopy. He died in Paris on July 5, 1881.

The article follows his place in French science. His research on the embryos of higher mammals drew the Parisian Society of Physicians. In 1845 they asked him to prepare anatomical specimens. From 1846 he lectured on microscopic anatomy at the College de France. That year he was made a knight of the Legion of Honor. After 1862 he lectured on diseases of the vocal organs. His many books include a practical treatise on the microscope and a manual of general anatomy. Two of his works won prizes from French academies. The entry preserves a Hungarian Jew at the heart of Paris medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-masada-10457:
Masada, the mountain fortress west of the Dead Sea, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss, drawing chiefly on Josephus. The name is Hebrew for a stronghold, and the article credits the high priest Jonathan with building the place. Herod later took refuge there and, once king, rebuilt it as a royal escape post, ringed by a wall with thirty-seven towers.

The second half follows Masada into the war with Rome. The Sicarii seized it and killed its Roman garrison, Menahem plundered Herod's stored weapons, and Eleazar ben Jair held the fort for about six years while raiding parties struck the country around. Only three years after Jerusalem fell did the Roman general Silva march on it, against a position the article calls nearly impossible to storm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-megillot-the-fi:
The Five Megillot are the five short scrolls of the Bible. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Blau treat them as a group in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The five are the Song of Solomon, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther. The first point of the article is that the group is late. When the canon of the Writings was formed, the five were not a unit, and the oldest arrangements do not place them together.

Only Esther was called a megillah in Talmudic times, and only Esther was read aloud in public. Lamentations was read privately in that age. Ruth and the Song entered the liturgy after the Talmud. Ecclesiastes came last of all, and the oldest prayer sources omit it pointedly. The article closes with the manuscripts and midrash collections that the festival use of the five scrolls called into being.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendel-henriett:
Henriette Mendel was a Bavarian actress. Her marriage carried her into a ducal house. Isidore Singer and A. M. Friedenberg notice her in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born on July 31, 1833. Early on, she was noted for her beauty and her talent on the stage. On May 19, 1859, she was created Baroness of Wallersee. The title was in the peerage of Bavaria. Nine days later she married Duke Ludwig Wilhelm. He was eldest son of Duke Maximilian Joseph. He had renounced his rights of primogeniture. He did so in favor of his younger brother.

The entry calls the union signally happy. Their daughter Marie Luise married Count Georg von Larisch. The baroness died at Munich on November 12, 1891. She died after a protracted illness. She was buried there with Catholic rites. The whole notice rests on the Almanach de Gotha. It rests on the obituary in the Allgemeine Zeitung too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-ludwig-10:
Ludwig Meyer, born at Bielefeld on December 27, 1827, was a German psychiatrist who helped shape the modern mental hospital. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied medicine at Bonn, Würzburg, and Berlin, taking his degree in 1852 and assisting at Berlin's Charité hospital.

After posts at Schwetz and as chief physician at Hamburg, Meyer became professor of psychiatry at Göttingen in 1866 and directed its asylum until his death in 1900. With Griesinger he founded the Archiv für Psychiatrie in 1867 and published more than a hundred essays. Hospitals at Hamburg, Göttingen, St. Urban, and Marburg were built following his plans and advice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minneapolis-108:
Minneapolis, Minnesota's chief commercial city, held about six thousand Jews in a population of 202,718 in 1900, as Cyrus Adler and S. N. Deinard report in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first settlers — Germans, Bohemians, and Russians — arrived between 1865 and 1870. Ralph Rees, who came in 1866, was for years the community's most active member.

In 1876 a dozen families rented a hall and hired a minister; in 1878 they organized the congregation that became the Reform Shaarei Tov, building a frame synagogue on leased ground downtown. Henry Iliowizi served as rabbi for eight years, and Deinard himself, the entry's co-author, took the pulpit in 1901. A new synagogue was dedicated in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montana-10957:
Montana's Jewish communities are inventoried in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Cyrus Adler, published in 1906. The territory was organized in 1864 and statehood came in 1889. Three towns carry the whole story: Helena the capital, Butte, and Anaconda, each with its congregation and benevolent society.

Helena's Jews founded a benevolent association in 1872 and the Emanu-El congregation in 1887, with Rabbi Jacob Mielziner, a social club, and a ladies' auxiliary. Butte had two congregations — the older, B'nai Israel of 1897, under Rabbi Harry Weiss, its benevolent association dating to 1881 — and Anaconda one. Mining-country Judaism, organized the way mining camps were: mutual aid first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-abrah:
Moses ben Abraham of Pontoise was a French tosafist of the twelfth century. Solomon Schechter and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was a disciple of Jacob Tam, the leading tosafist of the age, and corresponded with him on scholarly questions. He also sat in the assembly over which Tam presided.

Moses wrote tosafot on several Talmudic treatises, partly under Tam's direction, and later writers quote them often. He composed liturgical poems as well, some still extant in manuscript. His commentary on the Mishnah is mentioned by Samson of Sens, and a later cabalist claimed to own a copy. The entry shows a working scholar inside Tam's circle rather than a lone author.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-isaa:
Nathan ben Isaac ha-Kohen ha-Babli was a Babylonian historian. His entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and M. Seligsohn for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the tenth century. His subject was the exilarchate, the line of Babylonian Jewish leaders. He wrote with special care about his own time.

Nathan gave many details on the exilarch Ukba in particular. Parts of his history were printed long after his death. Samuel Shullam used them in Zacuto's Yuhasin at Constantinople in 1546. Neubauer later printed more of the extracts. The entry also clears up an old scholarly mix-up. Grätz had wrongly merged Nathan with a later namesake from Narbonne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuberg-joseph-:
Joseph Neuberg was a German-born helper of Thomas Carlyle. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Würzburg on May 21, 1806. He died in London on March 23, 1867. He first worked in business at Hamburg and Nottingham.

Neuberg cared much for the working classes' welfare. He led the People's College and a Mechanics' Institute section. Emerson presented him to Carlyle in 1848. He served Carlyle as voluntary secretary from 1849. In 1852 he guided Carlyle over Frederick's battlefields. Carlyle dedicated his Frederick the Great to Neuberg. The words praise his faithful attendant and helper. Neuberg turned Carlyle's works into German until death stopped him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissi-ben-noah-:
Nissi ben Noah was a Karaite scholar of the east. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Bassora, then at Jerusalem, in the 800s. Tradition makes his father a senior of Anan himself. His own life was marked by want and suffering.

He lost his parents while still a child. A poor, aged grandmother raised him on little. He earned a poor living by teaching as a youth. Travel took him through Irak, Persia, and Syria. He learned Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, and Latin there. He urged his fellow Karaites to study philosophy too. His book treats precepts drawn from the Ten Commandments. Hadassi copied his words later without naming him. Frankl even charged his work with borrowing in reverse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ochs-siegfried-:
Siegfried Ochs was a German band leader and song writer. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Frankfurt am Main in 1858. At first he read in drugs and the science of matter. He read those fields at Darmstadt and at Heidelberg. In time he gave his whole life to music.

Ochs trained at the royal music school in Berlin. He founded the Philharmonic Choral Society of that city. At first the group was small and little known. It grew to be the greatest choral group in Berlin. It was known for help to young writers of music. Their new works were oft sung there for the first time. Ochs wrote a comic opera in three acts. He wrote songs, duets, and male choruses too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ophites-11257:
The Ophites were a set of Gnostic sects in old times. Kaufmann Kohler and Samuel Krauss wrote their entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Gnostics sought a hid, deep knowledge of God and the world. The Ophites held the serpent in high regard. They saw it as a sign of creative wisdom.

Such groups may have lived within Judaism at first. Some Ophites cast the Christian Gospels aside in full. The sources on them are late and muddled, the piece warns. So Jewish and Christian Ophites are hard to tell apart. They taught that the serpent of Eden was wisdom itself. It brought the knowledge of good and evil to earth. They praised Cain and Seth as heroes for that gift. Other groups of like mind praised Esau and Korah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oregon-11757:
Oregon is a state in the north west of the United States. Cyrus Adler, Stephen S. Wise, and D. S. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It joined the Union in the year 1859. Its first Jewish settlers came from south Germany in the main. They came by way of Panama and California.

Most of those settlers made their homes in Portland. Their count grew fast in that young, rough town. On May 2, 1858, they formed Congregation Beth Israel. Twelve men are named as the founders of that flock. A burial group came first, though, the piece notes. It made a Jewish grave yard for the town. A year on, the same men set up an aid group. It was the first Hebrew aid group in Oregon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palache-samuel-: Samuel Palache was an envoy of the King of Morocco. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was sent to the Netherlands about the year 1591. He then worked as a consul in that land for years. He died at The Hague in the year 1616. He urged one town to take in the Maranos as a haven. He did much for their new home in Amsterdam in 1593.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pavia-angelo-11:
Angelo Pavia was an Italian lawyer who sat in parliament. He was born at Venice on February 24, 1858. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. By 1904 he was district attorney for Como. His legal work came before his seat in the chamber.

Pavia entered parliament after a by-election in 1894. He took the seat for Soresina, in the province of Cremona. Voters returned him at the general election of 1895. They elected him again in December 1904. The entry is brief and gives no more of his record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesaro-12057:
Pesaro is a town in the Marches of Italy. Richard Gottheil, Ismar Elbogen, and Joseph Jacobs wrote the entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews had lived there since the fifteenth century. A famed Hebrew printer was born there.

In 1555 the Duke of Urbino welcomed fleeing Marranos. After Rome burned Marranos at Ancona, Pesaro planned revenge. Its Jews would boycott Ancona's port and take its trade. Gracia Mendes and Joseph Nasi backed the bold plan. The harbor proved too unsafe, and the plan collapsed. The duke then exiled seven hundred Marranos by sea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pina-de-12157:
The de Pina were a Portuguese Marrano family. Four scholars shared this entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were Isidore Singer, Meyer Kayserling, and Richard Gottheil. Ismar Elbogen also took part in the work.

Some fled the Inquisition and professed Judaism at Amsterdam. Jacob de Pina, born at Lisbon in 1616, was a poet. He reached Holland about 1660 and took that name. He mourned dead martyrs in elegies there. Paul de Pina nearly became a monk instead. Montalto won him back to his fathers' faith. He reached Amsterdam in 1604 as Rohel Jeshurun.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polotsk-polotzk:
Polotsk is a district town in the government of Vitebsk, Russia. Herman Rosenthal, A. S. Waldstein, and Peter Wiernik wrote its history for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews may have lived there as early as 1490. A record of 1551 names Polotsk among towns freed from a special tax.

In 1509 a baptized Jew farmed the town's revenues and customs. His brother held the same post some years later. In 1563 Ivan the Terrible took Polotsk in war with Poland. He ordered Jews who refused the Christian faith to be killed. About three hundred died at that time, the article says. Later sections trace the community under Russian rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prideaux-humphr:
Humphrey Prideaux was an English scholar of the East, born in Cornwall in 1648. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Christ Church, Oxford. In 1679 he became a lecturer in Hebrew there. He died at Norwich in 1724.

Prideaux wrote a life of Mohammed in 1697. That book was in large part an attack on the Deists. His great work links the Old and New Testaments. It gives a history of the Jews and their neighbors. It covers the years between the two parts of the Bible. For long it stood as the standard book on that span. It was reprinted often and turned into French.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quebec-12457:
Quebec is the capital city of the province of Quebec in Canada. Joseph Jacobs and Clarence I. de Sola wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city stands on the left bank of the St. Lawrence. The first Jew known to have lived there settled in 1767. His name was Abraham Jacob Franks.

Franks's son David lived in Quebec before 1774 as well. That son later led the Jewish community of Montreal. He served as an officer in the American war too. Abraham Joseph was a leading figure in Quebec for long. The entry traces the small group from those first men. It names the families who built its public life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ramoth-gilead-1:
Ramoth-gilead was a city of refuge east of the Jordan. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lay in the tribe of Gad. Levites received it as one of their towns.

The article follows the city through wars with Syria. King Ahab died trying to take it back. His son Joram later won it and was wounded there. Jehu was proclaimed king at Ramoth-gilead in that same war. The writers then weigh where the city stood. They argue for a northern site near the frontier. Old guesses placed it too far south, they say.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reicher-kinderm:
Hedwig Reicher-Kindermann was a German prima donna born on July 15, 1853. Isidore Singer and Regina Neisser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. She was born at Munich, daughter of baritone August Kindermann. She died at Triest on June 2, 1883.

The article says her mother first taught her piano. At fifteen she entered Munich's music school for voice study. Her father trained her voice there. She debuted at Munich's court theater in small roles. She sang in chorus, danced, and acted at first. In 1875 she married actor Emanuel Reicher. They divorced in 1881. At Leipzig she won fame singing Wagner's heroines. She toured the Ring across Europe and to London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-right-and-left-:
Right and left carry strong meanings in Bible and Jewish thought. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The right side is seen as better than the left. Hebrew calls south yamin, meaning right, and north left.

The article calls the right the sunnier, brighter side. The left is bleak, dark, and unlucky in this view. Evil is said to break forth from the north. The place of honor stands at a person's right hand. Solomon seated his mother on his right side. Priests used the right ear, thumb, and toe in rites. Jacob blessed Ephraim with his right hand on purpose. Right becomes a synonym for goodness and brightness. The entry gathers custom, ritual, and story behind two sides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenroth-baron:
Christian Knorr, Baron von Rosenroth, was a Christian Hebraist born in Silesia on July 15, 1631. Gotthard Deutsch and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. After study and travel, he settled at Sulzbach and took up Hebrew.

Rosenroth became a deep student of the Cabala, the Jewish mystical tradition. He believed its teachings proved Christian doctrines, such as the Trinity. His Kabbala Denudata, printed in 1677 and 1678, opened that world to Latin readers. It gave terms, key texts, and essays by Jewish mystics. Later volumes added writings of Herrera and Isaac Luria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saalschutz-jose:
Joseph Lewin Saalschütz was a German rabbi and archaeologist born at Königsberg on March 15, 1801. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his doctorate in 1824 and taught in Berlin and Vienna.

From 1835 Saalschütz served as rabbi in his native Königsberg. In 1847 he became privat-docent in Hebrew archaeology at its university. Among Jews he was a pioneer in that field of study. His first book treats the form of Hebrew poetry and Hebrew music. His Gotteslehre, a school book on Judaism, served schools across Austria and Hungary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samarcand-13057:
Samarcand is a town of Central Asia, chief place of the Zerafshan district. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Alexander the Great conquered it in 329 B.C., when it was Maracanda.

Under Muslim rule Jews were shut out of sacred Samarcand entirely. Russia's annexation in 1868 made it a favored refuge for Bokhara's Jews. Nearly all its Jews were Orthodox, and they numbered 2,500 in 1890. One rich member, Raphael Moses Kalendarov, built the synagogue at his own expense. The community spoke Tajiki, and only a tenth knew Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuely-nathan-:
Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Nathan Samuely. He was an Austrian ghetto poet. Samuely was born at Stry, in Galicia, in 1846. At seventeen he published a story in Hebrew. Two volumes of his Hebrew poems followed. Their subjects came from old Jewish history.

The German poet Moritz Rapoport urged Samuely to write in German. His Culturbilder, pictures of Jewish life in Galicia, appeared at Leipsic in 1886. A second volume came five years later. The stories were translated into many languages. His longer tale Zwischen Licht und Finsterniss came out at Vienna in 1889. More short stories followed from Berlin publishers. In 1902 he published Alt Lemberg, a sketch of that city's past. He kept writing Hebrew books as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schenk-leopold-:
Frederick T. Haneman worked with Isidore Singer on this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Leopold Schenk. He was an Austrian embryologist. Schenk was born at Urmény, in Hungary, on August 23, 1840. He died at Schwanberg, in Styria, on August 18, 1902. He studied at the University of Vienna, taking his degree in 1865. In 1873 he became professor of embryology there.

Schenk won fame, and then trouble, from one bold claim. He held that a child's sex depends on the mother's food. His 1898 book on the subject was translated in America as The Determination of Sex. Virchow and other leading scientists attacked the theory sharply. In 1900 his own faculty forced him to resign his chair. Schenk clung to his claims to the end. He had earlier written textbooks on embryology and histology. Vienna's embryology department itself was his creation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seville-13457:
Seville, long one of Spain's greatest cities, held an old and large Jewish community. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Jews were said to have settled there soon after the Temple fell. When a Muslim conqueror took the city, he left it in Jewish hands.

Later, Jews fleeing a massacre at Granada found welcome at Seville. Their king gave some of them state posts and missions. He made Isaac ibn al-Balia court astronomer and prince over the realm's Jews. Through him Seville grew into a center of Jewish learning. The entry opens a long civic history in which Jews helped rule and enrich a famed city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemariah-b-mor:
Shemariah ben Mordecai, called Shemariah of Speyer, was a German tosafist of the early twelfth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Louis Ginzberg wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He learned from the tosafist Isaac ben Asher. Contemporaries prized him as an authority on religious rites.

Shemariah seems to have written formal legal decisions, or poskim. Jacob ben Meir Tam consulted him on a hard question. That fact alone shows his standing among scholars. His best pupils included two men named Judah ben Kalonymus. One pupil called him my aged teacher in his writings. The entry corrects a common error about Eleazar of Worms. Eleazar was not Shemariah's pupil, despite some claims.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silberman-eliez:
Eliezer Lipman Silberman was a German rabbi and Hebrew journalist born at Königsberg in 1819. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His Russian parents had settled there during the Napoleonic wars. Orphaned young, he was raised by kin in Russia.

As an adult Silberman returned to Prussia and settled at Lyck. There he served as slaughterer and rabbi for the community. In 1856 he founded Ha-Maggid, the first Hebrew weekly newspaper. That paper made him the actual founder of Hebrew journalism. He also helped organize the Mekize Nirdamim society in 1864. That group revived old Hebrew texts for print. David Gordon assisted him ably in both ventures. Leipzig gave Silberman an honorary doctorate for his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simonyi-sigmund:
Sigmund Simonyi was a Hungarian linguist born at Veszprim on January 1, 1853. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at Budapest, Leipsic, Berlin, and Paris. In 1877 he became a lecturer at Budapest. By 1889 he was a full professor there.

The Hungarian Academy chose him as a member in 1879. He shaped Hungarian philology for a whole generation of students. His works covered foreign words in Hungarian and Hungarian conjunctions. He also wrote on adverbs and on the Hungarian language itself. His historical dictionary of Hungarian ran to three volumes. He also helped compile a German-Hungarian dictionary in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-eli:
Solomon ben Eliezer ha-Levi was a Turkish Talmudist of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Wilhelm Bacher and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was brother of Abraham ben Eliezer ha-Levi. Abraham quotes him in his work Ma'amar ha-Yihud. Solomon wrote his main work while still very young.

That work is called Moreh Zedek, or Abodat ha-Lewi. It is a treatise on the 613 commandments of the Law. For each command it points to passages in the Talmud and codes. It cites Sifra, Sifre, Mekilta, and Maimonides' Yad as well. The book may have been published at Constantinople in 1516. Later writers sometimes confused its authorship with another Abraham.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spiegel-frederi:
Frederick S Spiegel was an American jurist born in Westphalia in 1858. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Hovestadt on November 20 of that year. At fourteen he emigrated with his parents to America. They settled at Gadsden, in Alabama, for a time.

He studied law at the College of Cincinnati in Ohio. In 1881 he became chief of Ohio's bureau of statistics. He revised how the state compiled its statistics then. He later practiced law and served on Cincinnati's education board. In 1890 he was elected county solicitor for the district. In 1896 he became a justice of the court of common pleas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tartan-assyrian:
Tartan was a title borne by top Assyrian generals. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Bible mentions a tartan twice in its pages. One came to Jerusalem with Sennacherib's envoys. They demanded that Hezekiah surrender the city at once.

Another tartan appears as Sargon's envoy to Ashdod. Isaiah dates a prophecy by that mission's year. Only the two generals next to the king held the title. They ranked as great tartan and second tartan. The Bible's tartans can no longer be identified by name. Three holders of the office are known from records. Their years run from 720 to 686 B.C.E. The entry defines a rank behind two famous scenes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theodor-julius-:
Julius Theodor was a German rabbi and a leading student of midrash. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Theodor was born in East Prussia in 1849. He studied at Breslau and took his doctorate at Königsberg in 1876.

He served as rabbi at Bromberg, Berent, and Bojanowo. In 1890 he toured London, Oxford, and Paris. There he examined midrash manuscripts in great libraries. His studies mapped how haggadic sermons were built. His chief work edited Bereshit Rabba with notes and apparatus. Parts of that edition appeared in 1903 and 1904. The entry traces a scholar's life spent on one great text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tosafot-additio:
Tosafot are critical glosses on the Talmud printed opposite Rashi's notes. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Their authors are called Tosafists. Scholars dispute what the name itself means. Graetz took them as additions to Rashi's commentary. Weiss read them as additions to the Talmud itself.

The work began right after Rashi finished his commentary. Rashi's sons-in-law and grandsons were the first Tosafists. Their notes mainly challenge and sharpen Rashi. Like the Gemara, the Tosafot grew across schools and centuries. Editors later gathered them into one body. Their hallmark is respect for no authority. Even Rashi could be corrected in their margins. That free criticism reshaped Talmud study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tyrol-14557:
Tyrol, an Austrian crownland, first documents its Jews in the early 1300s. Isidore Singer and Aaron Tänzer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A tale of Charlemagne fighting Jewish castle owners cannot be credited. Jews settled at Bozen, Meran, Riva, and Trent. They worked as merchants, money-lenders, and tax-farmers.

Isaac of Lienz farmed the mint at Meran in 1308. Black Death years brought bitter persecution over well-poisoning charges. No general statute governed Tyrol's Jews as a whole. Bishops and dukes granted privileges person by person. A 1403 decree from Brixen ran to twenty-seven clauses. Duke Frederick gave still broader terms in 1431. The Simon of Trent trial darkened Sigmund's reign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vegetarianism-1:
Vegetarianism means living on plants and avoiding animal food. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article asks what Jewish sources say about eating meat. It starts with Adam, who the rabbis said could not eat meat. Dominion over animals meant using them for work only.

After the Flood, the rules changed. Genesis chapter nine grants meat to Noah and his sons. One limit remained: no flesh torn from a living animal. The entry follows the theme through Exodus and Numbers. It covers the craving for Egypt's flesh pots and the gift of quails. It ends with the clean and unclean animals of Leviticus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahrmann-moritz:
Moritz Wahrmann was a Hungarian politician and merchant. He was born at Budapest on February 28, 1832. Isidore Singer, Eduard Neumann, and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the grandson of Rabbi Israel Wahrmann. He joined his father's firm in 1847 and later led it.

Wahrmann worked to free Hungarian trade from Austrian control. He built large firms in commerce and industry. In 1869 voters sent him to parliament. He was the first Jew in the Hungarian delegation. He won reelection six times. He also led Budapest's chamber of commerce. Jewish causes gained a strong advocate in him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-well-song-of-th:
The Song of the Well is a short poem in Numbers. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Numbers chapter twenty one quotes the song. It follows a list of Israel's desert camps. One camp was Beer, named for its well. God there promised Moses water for the people.

The song hails the well dug by princes. Nobles sank it with scepter and staves. Scholar Budde argues the list hides more poem lines. Words like wilderness and gift may belong to the song. Cheyne supports that reading of the text. The song is a scrap of ancient folk poetry. Few such fragments survive at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yalkut-compilat:
Yalkut, also called Yalkut Shimoni, is a large store of old tales on the Bible. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its maker drew from the old tale books at his hand. He set each tale by the verse it treats.

Long quotes are cut short in the work at times. The rest of a quote may stand at a far verse. One tale may serve two or three verses in turn. In such cases the same tale is told more than once. At times just the head of a tale is given. A note then sends the reader to its full place. The work is split in parts by book and verse. The count starts fresh at the Book of Joshua.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamosz-abraham-:
Abraham ben Isaac ha-Kohen Zamosz was a Polish rabbi of the 1700s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi of the town of Tarly. He was a stern foe of the Shabbethaian sect in Poland.

He hounded that sect where it had set roots in Podolia. On that theme he wrote to Jacob Emden in two years. Those years were 1759 and 1760 in the count. In the great feud of Emden and Eybeschutz, he took a side. His writs show that he stood with Emden in that fight. His one book holds two court replies and Talmud notes. Its name is Bet Abraham, or House of Abraham in tongue. The entry rests on a book of the great men of Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ziklag-15257:
Ziklag was a town of the tribe of Simeon that later became Judean. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible first names Ziklag when it lists the lands and borders of the tribes. In the early days of the kings, the Philistines held the town.

King Achish gave Ziklag to David, who lived there as his vassal. While David was away at war, Amalekites raided the town and burned it. After the return from exile, Judeans again settled there. The entry notes that the site was still unidentified, though some linked its ruins to remains east-southeast of Gaza found in 1877.
jonston-history-wonderful-things-nature-:
John Jonston's History of the Wonderful Things of Nature came out in English in 1657. Its Latin original bore the grand title Thaumatographia naturalis, a writing of nature's wonders. Jonston collected marvels the way other scholars collected coins or books, eagerly and at length.

Monsters, prodigies, and strange births fill the volume. Jonston draws cases from every corner of the known world and from authors old and new. A comet, a two-headed calf, and a rain of blood all count as nature speaking. The Renaissance loved a wonder, and this book fed that love. It also shows how thin the line then ran between science and sign-reading.
king-richard-iii-pg2257: The ghosts gather in this edition: on Bosworth's eve the murdered visit Richard's tent, each crying "Despair and die." He wakes to battle and his famous cry for a horse. The villain-hero's last night, terrifying and magnificent.
lycosthenes-prodigiorum-chronicon-1557:
Conrad Lycosthenes, a Swiss scholar, published his Chronicle of Prodigies in 1557. The Latin book gathers omens and wonders from Creation down to his own year. It is among the most richly pictured prodigy books of the Renaissance, a chronicle in which history itself becomes a book of signs.

Monstrous births, sea monsters, and wonders in the sky mark the turning years. Comets and strange rains appear beside the falls of kings. Lycosthenes drew on ancient historians and on fresh reports alike. His readers learned to scan the past for God's warnings. The chronicle taught Europe to read events, bodies, and skies as one long message.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Book three of the Duchesse d'Orleans's memoirs lists Henrietta of England first. The Duc and Duchesse de Berri stand next in the contents. The Regent's natural children and the Chevalier de Lorraine follow.

Henrietta, Monsieur's first wife, was too trusting of false friends. She told Turenne her secrets on the talks with England. His mistress passed each word to the Chevalier de Lorraine at night. That leak set Monsieur against his wife with fresh wrath. Prince Francois-Louis de Conti and the Abbe Dubois end the heads. Court love, faith, and money twist through each portrait in turn.
miller-testimony-rocks-1857:
The Testimony of the Rocks appeared in 1857, a year after Hugh Miller's death. It gathers lectures the Scottish geologist gave on the link between rocks and scripture. Miller was devout, yet he trusted what the stones showed him.

He argues that the fossil record tells a long, ordered history of life. That history, he holds, can sit beside the Bible's account when both are read with care. Miller speaks to church readers who feared geology would kill faith. His calm case made the book a landmark in the science-and-religion debate. The lectures were among the last works he prepared for print.
mistress-wilding-pg1457:
Rafael Sabatini's swashbuckling romance unfolds during Monmouth's rebellion in the west of England. Anthony Wilding loves Ruth Westmacott, whose nuptials fill a central chapter. Diana schemes, Sir Rowland rescues, and Mr. Trenchard plots his counterstroke. The rebels march under the words Pro Religione et Libertate.

This text runs to twenty-two chapters, three more than some printings show. The last three are The Reckoning, The Sentence, and The Execution. Between banquet and scaffold, Sabatini stages betrayal at Lyme and Wilding's return. Few historical novelists matched his pace: swordplay, court intrigue, and a love story bound to a doomed cause.
my-battle-for-life-the-autobiography-of-: David George Goyder titled his 1857 life story The Autobiography of a Phrenologist. Phrenology was the once popular study of head shape as a key to character. Catalog notes mention a song with words and music near the book's end. The hosted sample preserves only a garbled scan of the title pages, with no readable body text, so the life's events cannot be described from the sample itself.
openalex-w2121408857:
Mirko Manchia, Mazda Adli, Nirmala Akula, and colleagues published this report in PLoS ONE in 2013. They wrote for the Consortium on Lithium Genetics. Their question was how to judge lithium response in a fair, shared way. The treatment helps many people with bipolar disorder over the long term. Uneven treatment lengths and uneven pill taking make that judgment hard.

The group describes the scoring scale its study uses to rate past lithium response. Twenty-nine research sites tested the scale on written case stories in two rounds. Raters agreed well with each other. The team also studied score patterns for more than thirteen hundred patients. The work gives later genetic studies a common yardstick.
openalex-w2131618757:
Fernando Dini Andreote, Diego Jiménez, Diego Chaves, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2012. They surveyed the microbes living in mangrove sediments in Brazil using metagenomics, which reads DNA straight from the environment. Mangrove mud hosts dense microbial life that drives coastal carbon and nutrient cycles.

The team sequenced DNA from four mangrove areas and recovered a large body of sequence data. Two great bacterial groups, Deltaproteobacteria and Gammaproteobacteria, dominated the samples. Each site still held its own mix of groups in distinct shares. The genes found point to active cycling of carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur, matching the wet, oxygen-poor conditions of mangrove mud.
openalex-w2145725157:
Andréia Caverzan, Gisele Passaia, Sílvia Rosa, and colleagues published this review in Genetics and Molecular Biology in 2012. They cover ascorbate peroxidase, a plant enzyme family that guards cells against stress damage. When conditions turn harsh, plants make more reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules that can injure cells.

The enzymes sit at the heart of a detox cycle that turns hydrogen peroxide into water, using ascorbate as fuel. Different forms of the enzyme work in distinct cell parts, from chloroplasts to mitochondria. Their genes switch on in response to attack, drought, and other stresses, and during growth. Plants with broken copies grow and cope abnormally, proving these enzymes matter beyond emergencies.
openalex-w2210053857:
Magali Teurlai, Christophe Menkès, Virgil Cavarero, and colleagues published this worked example in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. They studied why dengue fever spreads unevenly across New Caledonia, a Pacific territory with repeated outbreaks. Their focus was the joint role of social and economic conditions and climate in shaping that patchy pattern.

The team combined local health records with population and housing data from the territory's statistics office. Weather observations came from the national weather service, and climate model projections extended the view forward. By working one island territory in depth, the study shows how such mixed data can be assembled anywhere. It offers a template for mapping dengue risk at fine local scales.
openalex-w2288397357:
Driss Ezzine-de-Blas, Sven Wunder, Manuel Ruíz-Pérez, and Rocío Moreno-Sánchez published this meta-study in PLoS ONE in 2016. They systematized fifty-five payments for environmental services schemes worldwide into one quantitative database. Such programs are hugely varied, which has blocked fair comparison of what their designs achieve.

Analysis confirmed familiar gaps between public and private schemes. It also split private schemes anew: commercial and non-commercial ones differ in service focus, area size, and market aims. Environmental extra benefit, called additionality, rose with three best-design features: spatial targeting, varied payment levels, and strong conditions. The authors conclude that customized design beats operational details in deciding program outcomes.
openalex-w2341640557:
Irene da Cruz, Rosana Rodríguez-Casuriaga, Federico Santiñaque, and colleagues published this study in BMC Genomics in 2016. They mapped which genes switch on and off as mouse sperm cells develop. The process runs three programs in sequence, but mixed cell types and fleeting early stages had blocked clean molecular study.

A new flow-sorting method delivered highly pure cells for each stage, including the briefest early ones. Sequencing their RNA gave the most reliable stage signatures yet. Many division genes were already active at the earliest stage, some only briefly. At the middle stage, pachytene, sperm-building genes switched on en masse. The switch from division to sperm formation thus happens surprisingly early, with much control exerted after genes are read.
openalex-w2391304757:
Hudson Golino and Sacha Epskamp published this methods paper in PLoS ONE in 2017. Counting the dimensions behind a psychological test is a long-standing headache: too few hides real structure, too many invents noise. Their new method, exploratory graph analysis, treats questionnaire items as a network and counts its communities instead.

They tested it against six classic techniques on thirty-two thousand simulated datasets. Structures varied in factors, items, sample size, and factor correlation. The graph method matched the best rivals in most situations, especially with two factors. With four strongly correlated factors it stood alone: at the largest sample size it found the right count every time. A real dataset demonstration closes the paper.
openalex-w2508274757:
Saravanan Rajendran, Mohammad Mansoob Khan, and F. Gracia, with colleagues, published this materials study in Scientific Reports in 2016. They built tiny composite particles mixing zinc oxide and cerium oxide. Such materials can break down pollutants when light shines on them, a process called photocatalysis. The team wanted a version that works under ordinary visible light, not just ultraviolet.

The researchers made the particles by heating and checked their makeup with standard lab techniques. They then tested them on methyl orange, methylene blue, phenol, and factory textile wastewater. The best mix, ninety parts zinc oxide to ten parts cerium oxide, beat either pure material. It also kept working after repeated use, showing good stability. Materials like this could help clean polluted water using sunlight.
openalex-w2808973857:
Mary Furlan Feitosa, Aldi T. Kraja, and Daniel I. Chasman lead a huge consortium hunting blood pressure genes in PLoS ONE in 2018. Heavy drinking is an established risk factor for hypertension, but its mechanism is unknown. The team reasoned that genes might interact with alcohol to shape blood pressure. Standard gene hunts ignore such interactions and could miss loci.

The two-stage study covered up to five hundred seventy thousand people across ancestries. Stage one flagged thousands of variants; stage two tested them in independent samples. Five new blood pressure loci were confirmed, along with forty-nine known ones. Extra analyses added eight more candidate loci, and African-ancestry samples suggested further novel regions. Several implicated genes were already tied to alcohol use itself. The findings illuminate how drinking and inheritance jointly build hypertension risk.
openalex-w2921342657:
René Hendriksen, Patrick Munk, Patrick Njage, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It sets out a way to monitor antimicrobial resistance worldwide by reading the DNA found in urban sewage. Resistance in bacteria is a rising global threat, shaped by travel, trade, climate change, and population shifts.

Current resistance tracking often covers only a few germs and relies on slow reports from clinical labs. That leaves delays, mismatched data, and many resistance genes uncounted, including genes carried by healthy people. Sewage offers a pooled sample from whole communities instead. The authors use metagenomics, the study of all DNA in a sample, to build a global sewage surveillance approach.
openalex-w2965771657:
G. Aad, B. Abbott, D. Abbott, and colleagues of the ATLAS collaboration published this paper in The European Physical Journal C in 2019. It measures how well ATLAS, a giant detector at the Large Hadron Collider, can spot jets of particles that contain b-hadrons. Such jets, called b-jets, are a key signature in many particle studies.

The paper presents the tagging algorithms used during the collider's second run. Their performance was checked in simulations, and their success rate was measured directly in collision data. The test sample was rich in top quark pair events, whose decays give a clean source of b-jets. Extracting the success rate and the sample makeup at the same time sharpened the measurement for future analyses.
openalex-w3013358557:
Federico Coccolini, Raul Coimbra, Carlos Ordoñez, and colleagues present the 2020 liver trauma guidelines of the World Society of Emergency Surgery in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery. Liver injuries rank among the most frequent life-threatening wounds seen in trauma patients.

The guidelines advise weighing three things before choosing care: the exact injury, the patient's circulation, and any other injuries. Treatment may avoid surgery or require it, always aiming to restore stable body function. Care should be shared by a team spanning trauma surgeons, imaging specialists who can block bleeding vessels, and emergency and intensive care doctors. The paper sets out the society's shared rules for adults and children alike.
openalex-w3038797657:
Kelly McNulty, Kirsty Elliott-Sale, Eimear Dolan, and colleagues published this systematic review and meta-analysis in Sports Medicine in 2020. It asks whether the phase of the menstrual cycle changes exercise performance in women with regular cycles. Hormone levels swing across the cycle, but study results had conflicted for years.

Following standard review rules, the team searched four databases for experiments that tested performance in at least two defined cycle phases. They pooled the results with multilevel statistical models, first comparing the early follicular phase against all others. A second, network analysis compared every phase with every other. The goal was evidence-based, practical advice for athletes and coaches, replacing guesswork with pooled data.
openalex-w3133809357: Simon Pittman, Kim Yates, Phil Bouchet, and dozens of colleagues authored this paper in Marine Ecology Progress Series in 2021. Its title, 'Seascape ecology: identifying research priorities for an emerging ocean sustainability science,' frames seascape ecology as a young field serving ocean sustainability, with agenda-setting as the paper's aim. The hosted sample, however, is only a reprint cover sheet and citation record. It preserves no abstract or body text, so no methods or findings can be reported from it.
openalex-w3192962357:
Javier Brazo-Sayavera, Salomé Aubert, Joel Barnes, and colleagues compared activity levels of boys and girls across Latin America. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2021, using data on more than two hundred thousand children and teenagers. Worldwide, girls are less active than boys, and the gap is wide in this region. Data on young people there had been scarce.

The authors describe how gender gaps appear in physical activity and in recreational sitting time, such as screen use. Knowing where the gaps are largest helps target programmes at the groups that move least. The study gives health planners a regional baseline for a problem tied to obesity and later disease.
openalex-w4408308157:
Dai Ishikawa, Xiaochen Zhang, and Akihito Nagahara review the current uses and future prospects of faecal microbiota transplantation. Their review appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2025. The treatment moves gut microbes from a healthy donor into a patient. It aims to fix an unbalanced gut mix, called dysbiosis.

The therapy proved highly effective against Clostridioides difficile infections, which often follow long antibiotic use. It is also linked to bowel diseases, diabetes, autoimmune conditions, and mental disorders. The review weighs where the treatment already helps and where evidence is still thin. It also sets out what must improve before this therapy becomes routine care.
openalex-w7211888757: The Assembly of God is one of Brazil's largest evangelical churches, and in the state of Amazonas its churches run an active program of Christian teaching. This article studies the ideas behind that work: how the church aims to shape the whole person in faith and daily life. It treats church education as a planned, purposeful effort and maps the thinking behind it.
openalex-w7212000857:
Eufrazio dos Santos, a historian at the University of Luanda, writes on Angola under Portuguese rule in the first decades of the twentieth century. His article covers the years from 1900 to 1922. The focus is the shift from military conquest to settled colonial rule. He works from books and past studies of the period, in a reading that is both historic and interpretive.

Colonial rule, he shows, rested on far more than holding land. The state built offices, tax rules, and labor rules to pull Angola into a colonial economy. Under Governor Norton de Matos, new roads and reforms came with tighter control of African life and work. Yet Africans in Luanda also formed their own groups and associations. The colonized, in his account, were never passive.
openalex-w7212012957:
Vinicius Arantes Campos and Allan Gomes Doriguetto pool trial data on berberine, a plant compound, and insulin resistance in adults who do not have diabetes. Past reviews looked at blood sugar or parts of the metabolic syndrome. None had focused on insulin resistance itself, scored by a standard home-based index. The pair searched for trials that tested berberine, in any form or dose, against a control group.

Nine trials qualified, and six gave usable data from close to five hundred people. On average, berberine lowered insulin resistance scores against control. The gain looked strongest in women with polycystic ovary syndrome. But the result rests on small trials with more risk of bias. The single large, low-risk trial found no effect. The authors ask for bigger, stricter trials before any firm advice.
openalex-w7213305157:
Fabio Pirelli Junior leads a team that charts self-killing in Caceres, a town in Mato Grosso, Brazil, from 2017 to 2023. The team read the files of the town's morgue law post.
