Fifty-one deaths by own hand fill the span. They charted who died, at what age, by what means, and where. They also set the years of the plague next to the years before it.

Four in five of the dead were men. The thick of them were in their teens and twenties. Most had not wed, and most had left school early. The deaths came most at home, and most by the rope. And the count jumped from 2020, the plague's first year. A chart of this kind is no mere list. It tells a town where its pain sits: in young men, at home, in years of strain. That is where help must go first.
openalex-w7213870757:
Michelly Chrystina da Silva Cavalcanti studies extra budget credits in Brazilian state governments. Her single-author 2026 article uses official data for all twenty-six states and the Federal District, from 2015 to 2019. Panel regression tests whether political cycles shape the opening of additional credits.

The pre-election year showed a significant positive influence on credit openings, she finds. Election year itself, party alignment with the president, and a governor seeking re-election showed no significant effect. That pattern suggests additional credits are used in electoral management. Spending flexibility rises before voters go to the polls, the author argues, even when the election year itself looks unremarkable in the data.
openalex-w7214068457:
Caio César da Costa Santos writes on proportionality as a binding test for unusual enforcement measures in Brazilian civil cases. His single-author 2026 article uses Robert Alexy's three-part rule: adequacy, necessity, and proportionality in the strict sense. Two binding precedents from Brazil's superior courts anchor the analysis.

Courts often invoke proportionality rhetorically without unpacking its structure, Santos argues. That habit empties the rule and returns discretion to the judge it meant to bind. Read together, the precedents demand qualified reasoning built step by step through the three sub-rules, he holds. Skipping that structure flaws the decision's reasoning. The triad is offered as the best method for granting atypical enforcement measures.
openalex-w7221025957:
Maria Eduarda Pereira Rios and Marco Antônio Alves Bezerra examined how well Brazilian law works against cybercrime as digital technology expands, in a 2026 legal study. They focus on two statutes: a 2021 law that stiffened penalties for electronic crimes, and the 2018 general data protection law.

Brazilian law, they find, has advanced through new offenses, data protection rules, and procedures shaped to digital evidence, with courts adapting older norms to new crimes. Hard problems remain: naming the author of an attack, preserving digital proof, crimes that cross borders, and officials who lack training. They conclude that effectiveness needs steady legal updates, forensic investment, professional training, cooperation, and prevention.
pages-from-an-old-volume-of-life-a-colle: Oliver Wendell Holmes's pages from an old volume of life: essays from 1857 to 1881. The Autocrat's wisdom gathered, mellow and bright. A lifetime's table talk. Holmes's old volume is wisdom mellowed with age, a lifetime's bright talk.
plos-pbio-0020057:
David Serre, André Langaney, Mario Chech, and a large team tested ancient DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. They pulled mitochondrial DNA, the small genome passed down by mothers, from Neandertal fossils and from early modern human fossils. The question was whether Neandertals left genes in people alive today.

Mitochondrial DNA from the early modern humans matched living people, while the Neandertal type stayed apart. The authors found no sign that Neandertal maternal lines survived into our species. That result shaped debate on how modern humans spread out of Africa. It suggested replacement more than mixing, at least along the maternal line that this kind of DNA can trace.
plos-pbio-0020257:
Marina Kniazeva, Quinn T. Crawford, Matt Seibel, and their team found a fat the worm C. elegans cannot live without, reported in PLOS Biology in 2004. The fat is a branched-chain fatty acid with a single branch. This tiny worm is a standard lab animal for studying growth.

Without this fat, worm embryos fail to develop properly. A fat acting as an essential building signal is more than fuel; it is part of the growth program itself. The study gives the worm field a new required nutrient to track. It also hints that branched fats, long ignored next to common fats, may hold key roles in other animals too.
plos-pone-0000057:
Sebastian Graefe, Thomas Streichert, Birgit Budde, and co-authors hunted genes behind resistance to Chagas disease in a 2006 paper. Trypanosoma cruzi, a parasite spread by insects, causes Chagas, which can damage the heart for life. Some mouse strains resist the parasite; others fall ill. The difference lies in susceptibility loci, regions of the genome.

The team found genes from those loci that are switched on differently in resistant mice. Those genes are candidates accounting for the resistant mice's impaired immunity, the odd cost that can come with resisting this parasite. Candidates like these are where drug and vaccine work starts: named genes, in named places, doing measurable things.
plos-pone-0000157:
Angèle Viola, Véronique Saywell, Laurent Villard, and colleagues published this brain chemistry study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It uses a mouse model of Rett syndrome, a disorder that disrupts brain development, mostly in girls. The authors built metabolic fingerprints of the model, profiling chemical changes tied to brain growth, water balance, and neurotransmission.

A fingerprint of small-molecule changes can reveal what a gene defect does to the brain in practice. The authors map those shifts across the systems named in the title. Such profiles help researchers judge disease severity and test whether a treatment moves the brain's chemistry back toward normal.
plos-pone-0000257:
Antoinette C. van der Kuyl, Remco van den Burg, Fokla Zorgdrager, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Sialoadhesin, also called CD169, is a protein on the surface of certain immune cells, the CD14+ cells tracked here. The authors report that its expression rises early after HIV-1 infection and keeps increasing as the disease progresses.

A protein that climbs steadily from early infection onward is a candidate marker of disease stage. The authors measure that climb in patients over time. The work also raises questions about what this adhesion protein does for, or against, the virus as infection advances.
plos-pone-0000357:
Caroline Costedoat, Nicolas Pech, Rémi Chappaz, and colleagues published this evolutionary biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hybrid zones are places where two species or populations meet and interbreed. The authors present novelties in hybrid zones, framing them as a crossroads between population genomic and ecological approaches to the same natural laboratories.

Hybrid zones reveal what keeps species apart and what lets genes cross. Combining genomic scans with field ecology gives a fuller account than either alone. The paper argues for that combined approach and illustrates what it can find.
plos-pone-0000457:
Ekaterina Dadachova and colleagues reported that radiation feeds certain fungi instead of only harming them, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Melanin, the dark pigment in these fungi, changes its electronic properties when hit by ionizing radiation. The team found that this change enhances the growth of melanized fungi.

Melanized fungi are famously found in extreme places, including the walls of the damaged Chernobyl reactor. A pigment that converts radiation into usable energy would explain that success, making melanin act a little like chlorophyll does for light. The work suggests radiation is not a universal poison but, for the right chemistry, a resource.
plos-pone-0000557:
Simone S. Santos-Lopes, Rinaldo W. Pereira, and Ian J. Wilson traced the human X chromosome's history across the world, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. A phylogeography reconstructs where lineages lived and how they spread. Their worldwide phylogeography for the human X chromosome used its inheritance pattern, two copies in women and one in men, to read population history.

The X chromosome records male and female histories differently, so it can reveal sex-biased migrations that other markers miss. Comparing its tree with those from the Y chromosome and mitochondria gives a fuller account of how peoples moved. Such studies underlie much of what genetics says about human origins.
plos-pone-0000657:
Cornelia Thedieck, Hubert Kalbacher, Markus Kuczyk and co-authors announced a new surface marker for kidney fibroblasts in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fibroblasts in the kidney's interstitial tissue are a minor share of its cells but a very important one. They secrete and remodel the matrix around cells and produce active compounds such as erythropoietin, the hormone that drives red blood cell production.

Studying human renal fibroblasts had been hampered by a lack of suitable markers to identify them. The title names cadherin-9 as that marker for this mixed cell pool. A reliable tag lets researchers pull these cells out of tissue and study kidney scarring directly.
plos-pone-0000757:
Pieter W. Uys, Robin M. Warren and Paul D. van Helden put a number on how long tuberculosis can wait before diagnosis becomes dangerous. In communities where TB is common, transmission is the major force driving the epidemic. The typically long delay from onset of infectious disease to diagnosis and treatment is plausibly the major factor behind continued spread.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study seeks a threshold value for that delay. Below the threshold, each case infects few enough others that control can hold. Above it, the epidemic feeds itself. A concrete threshold tells clinics how fast is fast enough, turning a vague call for earlier diagnosis into a measurable target.
plos-pone-0000857:
Sittiporn Pattaradilokrat, Sandra J. Cheesman and Richard Carter hunted the genes that make malaria immunity strain-specific. Protection against blood-stage malaria works in part only against the strain a person has met before. The targets of that strain-specific protection should therefore differ between parasite lines, in both their genes and the immune response they raise.

Their method is called linkage group selection. Parasite strains are crossed, and the young that survive strain-specific immunity are checked for which genome chunks they kept. Chunks kept under pressure point to the target genes. Such targets are prime vaccine leads, since natural immunity already proves they can be hit. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.
plos-pone-0000957:
Marielle Gold, Tammie Robinson, Matthew Cook and colleagues showed that newborn dendritic cells can handle a key immune task, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Newborns fall harder to many infections than adults do. The usual explanation is an immature immune system, but several parts of newborn immunity simply differ from the adult form.

Dendritic cells start immune responses by processing antigens and presenting them. The team report that human neonatal dendritic cells are competent at the class I form of that job. A strength in newborns, where weakness was assumed, changes the picture. It may also matter for designing vaccines that work in the first weeks of life.
plos-pone-0001057:
Ian Cowell, Nicola Sunter, Prim Singh and colleagues mapped where a DNA damage mark forms in the genome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. H2A.X is a histone variant making up to a quarter of its family in mammal cells. Within minutes of a DNA double strand break, nearby H2A.X molecules gain a phosphate tag, forming foci that flag the damage.

The team report those foci form preferentially in euchromatin, the open, active parts of the genome. Where damage flags rise fastest may shape how repair proceeds. Open regions hold the genes a cell is using, so fast marking there has clear logic. The map guides repair research.
plos-pone-0001157:
In hybrids, one parent's set of ribosomal RNA genes often falls silent while the other's keeps working, a phenomenon called nucleolar dominance. Olga Pontes and co-authors studied when that silencing is set up, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The silenced region can stretch over megabases of DNA.

The authors describe the postembryonic establishment of this large-scale silencing, meaning it takes shape after the embryo stage rather than being fixed from the start. Ribosomal RNA genes sit in tandem arrays, and choosing between parental copies is an epigenetic decision. Their timing findings clarify how such a sweeping choice gets locked in during development.
plos-pone-0001257:
Epstein-Barr virus persists in its host for life as episomes, small circles of viral DNA kept in the cell nucleus. Jayaraju Dheekollu and colleagues studied how those episomes copy and stay stable, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The virus's origin of plasmid replication, OriP, gives this episomal upkeep.

The authors report roles for the DNA repair proteins MRE11 and NBS1, and for recombination junctions, in copying and keeping the episomes. Structures formed at replication origins may support fidelity and chromosome stability in general. Their findings link how the virus persists to the host's own repair tools.
plos-pone-0001357:
Respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, is a major cause of infant lung infections, and fast diagnosis guides care. Ramona Tillmann and colleagues evaluated a commercial NASBA assay for detecting RSV in clinical specimens, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They compared three diagnostic procedures, including an FDA-cleared ELISA kit and an in-house RT-PCR protocol.

The aim was to judge how usable the three methods are, side by side. NASBA amplifies RNA directly and can be faster than culture-based methods. Hospital labs need a sensitive commercial assay that works well on real samples. This study tested exactly that.
plos-pone-0001457:
Suha Naffar-Abu-Amara and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on genes that help cancer cells move. Cell movement is a complex act steered by many genes and signals. To find genes or drugs that change it, labs need screens that watch movement in fine detail. The team built a screen based on fast, counted microscopy.

With that screen they found new genes that push cancer cells to migrate. Cell spread is what makes many cancers lethal, so each new driver matters. Hits from the screen give drug teams fresh targets to test. The method itself can be reused for other movement based hunts.
plos-pone-0001557:
Yuan-Chang Chao and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on dengue fever and a common enzyme lack. The lack, called G6PD deficiency, is rife in Asia, where dengue is also rife. The team asked whether the lack changes how dengue infects blood cells. They used cells drawn from donors with and without the lack.

Cells from donors with the lack took up more of one dengue type. That hints the lack may raise risk or weight of dengue in those who bear it. In lands where both are common, the link has real public health weight. It urges joint screening where funds allow.
plos-pone-0001657:
Jeri D. Barak and Anita S. Liang traced how Salmonella bacteria reach tomato plants in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tomatoes had become the food most often blamed for produce-linked salmonellosis in the United States, with 12 outbreaks since 1998. Trace-back work pointed to contamination before harvest, in the field, but the routes were unproven.

The authors tested three suspects: the soil, crop debris left in fields, and a plant pathogen that infects tomatoes. The full text gives the greenhouse and field tests and where the bacteria turned up on the plants. Knowing which route matters most tells growers where to act, whether in soil care, debris cleanup, or disease control, to keep a common food safer.
plos-pone-0001757:
Shizhong Han, Joel M. Guthridge, Isaac T. W. Harley, and their co-authors tested a bone protein's gene for links to lupus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Osteopontin, made by the SPP1 gene, is a bone matrix mediator with key roles in inflammation and immunity. Earlier small studies had tied SPP1 variants and high osteopontin levels to systemic lupus erythematosus.

The team evaluated the association in a larger study and report a probable gene-gender interaction: the effect differs between men and women. The full text gives the patient groups and the variant statistics. Sex-dependent gene effects fit lupus, a disease far commoner in women, and they warn that genetic studies pooling sexes can miss real signals.
plos-pone-0001857:
Michael T. Bethune, Erin Ribka, Chaitan Khosla, and their co-authors studied gluten handling in gluten-sensitive macaques in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In previous work the group characterized gluten sensitivity in juvenile rhesus macaques similar in many respects to human celiac disease. The animal model may therefore be useful for studying both how gluten crosses the gut lining and how it can be detoxified.

The team examined transepithelial transport and enzymatic detoxification of gluten in these macaques. The full text gives the transport measurements and the enzyme treatments. Enzyme pills that digest gluten in the stomach are a leading celiac therapy idea. This primate model tests them in a gut much like ours.
plos-pone-0001957:
Christer Bronmark and co-authors asked why fish in lakes migrate with the seasons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Migration is common in land and water animals alike, and much work has gone into why it evolved and what it does to populations. In lakes, fish often move between deep and shallow zones across the year.

As the title states, the team frames the move as a trade-off: shallow water offers faster growth, but also more predators. Fish shift zones as the balance of food and risk changes with the season. Framing migration as a bargain helps predict how lake life will shift when climates or predator numbers change.
plos-pone-0002057:
Olivier Delmas and co-authors read the full genomes of the rabies virus family, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Lyssaviruses are RNA viruses that cause rabies-like diseases in mammals. Past genome and evolution studies had mostly used partial sequences, above all two genes, with little from the rest of the genome.

The team compared complete genomes across the family to chart its genomic diversity and evolution. A fuller tree can show where new rabies-like viruses come from and how they adapt to bats and other hosts. That matters for vaccines, which must cover a moving family.
plos-pone-0002157:
Markus Pfenninger and Carsten Nowak asked how two near-twin midge species manage to live side by side, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The non-biting midges Chironomus riparius and Chironomus piger look almost the same and can breed with each other in the lab. Yet in nature they often share the same waters without merging into one species.

The authors studied the larvae to see how the two split their living space and food, a pattern called niche partition. They also weighed the barriers that keep the species apart. The case offers a clean look at how new species can form while still living in the same place.
plos-pone-0002257:
Langzhou Song, Valerian Nakaar, Uma Kavita, and co-authors made influenza vaccine proteins in bacteria at high yield, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Linking a vaccine antigen to a molecule that alarms the immune system is known to make the vaccine stronger. The team applied that trick to the flu's protective surface protein, hemagglutinin.

They fused the head of hemagglutinin to a bacterial alarm signal and produced the vaccine in bacteria, a fast and cheap factory. High yields from a simple system could ease the chronic shortage of flu vaccine in pandemics and bad seasons alike. Recombinant vaccines like these can be redesigned quickly when the virus changes.
plos-pone-0002357:
Grant Challen and Margaret Goodell examined a fluorescent labeling trick for finding quiet stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Studying adult stem cells depends on isolating them with complex mixes of markers. A recent method used a switchable H2B-GFP mouse: cells that divide rarely keep the glowing tag longest, mimicking classic pulse-chase labeling.

The team reports that the H2B-GFP transgene is expressed promiscuously in hematopoietic stem cells, switched on in cells it should not mark. That leakiness can mislead studies that trust the label. A caution from inside the field helps every lab using the model read its results more carefully.
plos-pone-0002457: Jakob Schnetzer and co-authors published the article in PLOS ONE in 2008. It looks at the early ANTP gene set through the genome of a placozoan, a very simple sea animal. ANTP genes help guide how an animal body takes shape as it grows. Placozoans sit near the base of animal life, so their genes offer clues about first body plans.
plos-pone-0002557:
Wang and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Xiaohong Wang, Shuang Tang, Shu-Yun Le, among others. Its subject is aberrant Expression of Oncogenic and Tumor-Suppressive MicroRNAs in Cervical Cancer Is Required for Cancer Cell Growth. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play important roles in cancer development.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002657:
Sallouha Aidoudi and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of the CXC-Chemokine CXCL4 interacts with integrins implicated in angiogenesis. Authorship is credited in the record to Sallouha Aidoudi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The human CXC-chemokine CXCL4 is a potent inhibitor of tumor-induced angiogenesis. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002757:
In 2008, E. Alejandro Herrada and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about universal scaling in the branching of the tree of life. The full author list in the catalog record begins with E. Alejandro Herrada, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Understanding the patterns and processes of diversification of life in the planet is a key challenge of science. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002857:
Shaun E. Grosskurth and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of emergence of xin demarcates a key innovation in heart evolution. The catalog record names Shaun E. Grosskurth first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The mouse Xin repeat-containing proteins (mXinα and mXinβ) localize to the intercalated disc in the heart. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002957:
Cesar Bonilla, Aldo Crossa, Hector Jave and co-authors reported outcomes for extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis in Peru in 2008. XDR-TB resists most of the drugs used against tuberculosis, and many assumed cure was out of reach. Peru kept a national registry for multidrug-resistant cases over more than ten years.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team describes how often XDR-TB appeared in that registry and gives treatment outcomes for a cohort of patients. Their title states the core message: cure is possible. That evidence matters for programs deciding whether to fund full treatment for the hardest cases.
plos-pone-0003057:
R. Alexander Bentley charted academic keywords over time as an evolution problem in 2008. Keyword frequencies were recorded in the ISI Web of Science citation database. Across four case studies, change in keyword frequency through time was compared with a model of random copying.

The question contrasts random drift with selection in academic vocabulary. If copying alone explains the patterns, fashionable terms need no quality advantage to spread. Published in PLOS ONE, the analysis treats science's own language with the tools of evolution, a check on how fields convince themselves. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003157:
Nelson J. R. Fagundes, Ricardo Kanitz and Sandro L. Bonatto revisit the first peopling of the Americas in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The Americas were the last continents humans settled, and many details of that process remain disputed or unknown. One hard topic is how the early settlement of Beringia, the land bridge region, actually unfolded.

The authors re-evaluate diversity in Native American mitochondrial genomes and what it implies for models of early colonization. Readers get a fresh check on a long debated history using genetic evidence. The study shows how DNA from living peoples can still test stories about ancient migration.
plos-pone-0003257:
Philippe A. Parone, Sandrine Da Cruz, Daniel Tondera and colleagues block mitochondrial division in cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondria form a highly dynamic tubular network, whose morphology is regulated by frequent fission and fusion events. However, the role of mitochondrial fission in homeostasis of the organelle was still unknown. The team report the effects of preventing fission.

The title gives the outcome: preventing mitochondrial fission impairs mitochondrial function and leads to loss of mitochondrial DNA. Readers learn that constant division is not waste but upkeep. That insight bears on diseases where mitochondrial dynamics fail, from nerve to muscle disorders.
plos-pone-0003357:
Guohui Ding, Zhonghao Yu, Jing Zhao and colleagues build a tree of life from genome context in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Efforts in phylogenomics have greatly improved understanding of the backbone tree of life. However, due to systematic error in sequence data, a sequence-based phylogenomic approach leads to well-resolved but statistically significant incongruence. An independent test was therefore needed.

The authors propose a tree of life based on genome context networks. Readers get a phylogeny drawn from gene neighbourhood and context, not raw sequence alone. Agreement between two different data types would strengthen confidence in the deepest branches of life.
plos-pone-0003457:
Christopher Vollmers, Satchidananda Panda, and Luciano DiTacchio built a screening tool for body clocks in 2008. Gene silencing screens had sped up many fields of biology. Mammalian circadian rhythms, the daily body clock, had lagged behind. The team set up a faster screen in human U2OS cells.

Their assay uses small RNAs to knock down genes one by one. Cells with broken clocks then stand out for study. The method runs at medium to high throughput. It should speed the hunt for genes that keep daily time. Clock genes affect sleep, mood, and metabolism across the whole body.
plos-pone-0003557:
Arlene E. Dent and co-authors measured malaria protection across ages in Kenya in this 2008 study. Antibodies can slow the growth of Plasmodium falciparum, the main malaria parasite. Children and adults in Kenya face repeated infection from early life. The team linked antibody strength to age and to parasite loads.

They tested how well each person's antibodies inhibited parasite growth. Older subjects generally carried stronger growth-inhibiting activity. Protection from high parasite levels rose with that activity. The age pattern shows vaccine designers the immunity nature builds slowly. Malaria kills most often in young children, before this slow shield can build up over years of bites. Knowing how fast the shield grows helps set the age targets for any new vaccine drive.
plos-pone-0003657:
Francisco M. Camas and Juan F. Poyatos published this systems biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Gene control networks in the bacterium E. coli reuse small wiring patterns called motifs. Why those patterns appear is debated. Some say use shaped them; others favor chance.

The authors offer a new picture of how motifs assemble in these networks. Their account weighs adaptive and neutral routes side by side. The work helps explain why the control system of a well-studied bacterium is built from the parts it has. That is a basic question in how cells evolve.
plos-pone-0003757:
P. J. Nico de Bruyn, Armanda D. S. Bastos, Candice Eadie, and colleagues published this wildlife study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Die-offs of marine mammals from infection are reported more and more often. Most strike males and females, young and old, alike. This event on land broke that pattern.

Adult male subantarctic fur seals died in large numbers while others were spared. The team asked whether alien mice on the island, possible carriers of disease, were the culprits. Their detective work tests a surprising chain from tiny invaders to very large victims.
plos-pone-0003857:
Thierry Poynard, Patrick Ingiliz, Laure Elkrief, and colleagues published this liver study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Liver fibrosis is traditionally staged by biopsy, an imperfect gold standard that cuts tissue. Non-invasive options include stiffness measurement and blood marker panels such as FibroTest. The team compared their accuracy without a perfect reference.

Their methodology judges concordance between markers in a world without a gold standard. It identifies factors linked to disagreement between the tests. The aim is more accurate staging of liver scarring without the needle, for patients who need repeated checks.
plos-pone-0003957:
Laura J. Marinelli, Mariana Piuri, Zuzana Swigoňová, and co-authors presented a phage engineering method in 2008. Sequencing had revealed hundreds of genomes for bacteria and their viruses, called phages. Some bacteria had easy genetic systems, but phages lagged behind. Building mutant phages stayed slow and hard for many labs.

Their PLOS ONE article describes BRED, a method to rebuild phage genomes. It lets users make mutants and mixed recombinant phages directly. Simpler phage engineering speeds studies of what each phage gene does. Those studies support phage therapy work against resistant bacteria. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004057:
David W. Dowdy, Maria C. Lourenço, Solange C. Cavalcante, and co-authors weighed TB testing costs in Brazil in 2008. Growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis in culture is the closest test to a gold standard. Data on its impact in HIV-infected patients were scarce. Resource-limited settings must judge whether culture is worth its cost.

Their PLOS ONE article assessed culture diagnosis for HIV-infected Brazilian adults. It counted both health impact and cost-effectiveness. HIV and TB together strain clinics across Brazil. Evidence for culture helps labs spend limited budgets wisely. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004157:
Ayumi Kishioka and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fear is a strong emotion that helps animals answer real threats. Too much fear, or fear in the wrong place, sits behind many common psychiatric problems. The amygdala, a small brain region, is thought to be central to learning fear.

The team studied auditory fear conditioning, where an animal learns to fear a tone paired with an unpleasant event. Using only a weak version of that event, they describe a novel form of memory for the learned fear. Their work refines what scientists know about how gentle threats can still leave lasting marks.
plos-pone-0004257:
Tal Yarkoni and colleagues published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reaction time is one of the most widely used measures in experimental psychology. Yet few fMRI studies had used trial-by-trial differences in reaction time as a predictor in their analyses.

Combining several studies, the team asked which brain regions track how fast a person responds on each trial. They report BOLD signal correlates of reaction time variability in both gray and white matter. The white matter result is striking, since that tissue is usually treated as background in brain scans.
plos-pone-0004357:
Marina Marcet-Houben and Toni Gabaldón published this phylogenomics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Combining many sequence alignments to reconstruct a single tree of evolutionary relationships is a recurrent topic in phylogenomics. Critics argue that such an approach cannot properly represent the diversity of histories found across a genome.

The authors frame the problem as the tree versus the forest. They use the fungal tree of life and the topological diversity within the yeast phylome. The phylome is the set of all gene trees for a species. Their study measures how much one species tree hides the forest of differing gene trees.
plos-pone-0004457:
Male fruit flies court females with a set dance of moves. Dimitrije Krstic, Werner Boll, and Markus Noll studied how the senses steer that dance in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fruit fly courtship is a classic model for how brains produce complex inborn behavior. Knowing the wiring alone, though, does not explain the behavior.

The team focused on sensory integration, the merging of sight, smell, sound, and touch into one flow of action. A male must track the female's signals moment by moment and adjust his moves. By tracing how those senses feed the courtship network, the study shows how a small brain runs a flexible routine. The lessons reach toward general rules for how nervous systems turn sense data into behavior.
plos-pone-0004557:
Doing good for others might carry a mental health risk, a possibility examined by Takeo Fujiwara in PLOS ONE in 2009. A previous cross-sectional study, a snapshot at one time, had suggested altruistic behaviors were harmful for major depression. Snapshots cannot show which came first, so a prospective look was needed.

Fujiwara followed the question forward in time, asking whether altruistic behavior is associated with the onset of major depression. The data came from the National Survey of Midlife Development in the United States. The study also separated altruistic acts by their content, since helping a stranger and heavy caregiving are different burdens. A careful answer matters for advice given to volunteers and caregivers alike.
plos-pone-0004657:
A ring of smell detectors in the mouse nose draws input from many sources. Renee Cockerham, Adam Puche, and Steven Munger map its wide links inside the smell brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The nose uses more than one smell system to pick up chemical cues. These systems sit in different places, send signals to different targets, and work in different ways.

One system forms the necklace glomeruli, a ring of round processing units at the back of the olfactory bulb. The team describes their mixed sensory input and their wide links within the bulb. Mixed input plus rich links suggest the ring blends several kinds of smell signals rather than passing on a single channel. That may be how social scent cues are joined with other smells.
plos-pone-0004757:
Elad Maor, Antoni Ivorra, and Boris Rubinsky tested a non heat electric method to remove artery wall muscle cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The method uses strong electric pulses that damage only the cell membrane. All other tissue parts are spared, which sets it apart from heat based removal used in surgery today.

Past work in rodents showed it can reduce excess wall growth after artery injury. The team focused on vessel wall muscle cells, the cells that drive that regrowth. Selective removal could keep treated arteries open longer. It offers a new tool for vascular care.
plos-pone-0004857:
Barkha Srivastava and colleagues showed host genetic background strongly influences response to influenza A infections, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genetic makeup of the host has major influence on combating pathogens. For influenza A, several single gene mutations contribute to survival, immune response, and clearance. The team compared genetically distinct mouse lines challenged with virus to quantify background effects on disease.

Some backgrounds resist while others succumb quickly. Mouse choice therefore shapes experimental conclusions. Human diversity likely mirrors that range. Personalized risk prediction may follow genetic mapping. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004957:
People often seek expert financial advice under uncertainty. Jan Engelmann and colleagues asked what that advice does inside the brain. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They scanned volunteers making risky financial decisions. Some decisions came with an expert's recommendation.

Advice effectively offloaded the decision work. Brain activity for weighing risk quieted when a recommendation was available. Neuroeconomics had mapped risky choice in depth before this. The neural effect of external advice was largely unknown. The study gives a brain-level account of advice. It helps explain why following an advisor can feel like relief.
plos-pone-0005057:
Prions are deadly proteins that spread between cells. Their route from infection sites to the brain was not clear. Vincenzo Mattei and colleagues found a possible vehicle in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells shed tiny bubbles from their membranes. These microvesicles carry cargo to neighboring cells.

The bubbles carried the normal prion protein, PrPC. They also propagated prion infectivity to other cells. The microvesicles act like taxis for the disease. That reveals a new vehicle for prion spread. Blocking the bubbles might slow the disease. The finding also matters beyond prions. Membrane bubbles move many kinds of cargo, and this study shows their dark side.
plos-pone-0005157:
A simple blood draw could reveal disease biomarkers. Reading gene activity from whole blood is the route. Technical noise has plagued that route, though. Ze Tian and colleagues built a practical platform in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used global gene expression profiling of peripheral whole blood. Their aim was a platform ready for biomarker studies.

The platform tames the technical factors that distort results. Standardized steps make profiles comparable across experiments. Blood biomarkers could serve many diseases at once. Reliability is what the field lacked. This work turns a messy method into a usable tool. Later biomarker claims stand on such groundwork. Without it, promising markers fail to replicate.
plos-pone-0005257:
When insulin calls, fat cells move a sugar transporter called GLUT4 to their surface to take in glucose. Small switch proteins of the Rab family help run that traffic. Kaddai and colleagues identified one more switch, Rab4b, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Rab4a was already known to help control GLUT4 in fat cells. The team found fat cells also make Rab4b and that it shares control of GLUT4 placement. Each added gear in this traffic system is a possible factor in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Each new switch in this chain is one more place where a drug might help fat cells take in sugar when insulin alone can no longer do it.
plos-pone-0005357:
Cystic fibrosis is caused by faults in the cftr gene and brings airway inflammation with stubborn Pseudomonas infections. Tracheal glands, small glands in the windpipe, may play a specific part in that process. Bastonero and colleagues compared those glands in normal and CF cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study found new microbicidal functions for tracheal glands, ways they kill microbes directly. In cystic fibrosis, that anti-infectious response to Pseudomonas aeruginosa is defective. A broken gland defense helps explain why CF airways cannot clear this germ. Thick mucus gets the blame in this disease, but glands that fail to kill germs are a fault of a kind. And one that may be open to a drug in its own right.
plos-pone-0005457:
Eric Sijbrands, Erik Tornij, and Sietske Homsma followed a huge group of men for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Insurance firms use medical checks to judge how long an applicant is likely to live. People now debate whether gene tests should be added to those checks.

The authors compared what one firm predicted for tens of thousands of men with what really happened over time. Knowing how well the old method works sets a fair bar for any new gene-based method. The long follow-up gives rare hard evidence in a debate often run on guesses.
plos-pone-0005557:
Abdelali Agouni and co-authors tested red wine compounds in obese rats for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Obesity raises the risk of heart and blood vessel disease. Population studies link plant compounds called flavonoids, found in foods such as grapes, with lower death rates from heart disease.

The team fed compounds from red wine to a strain of rats bred to become fat. They checked the rats' metabolism and blood vessel health for signs of protection. Early animal results like these guide, but cannot prove, dietary advice for people. Fatty rats are a standard first test, but human trials would be needed before any claim could be made for people.
plos-pone-0005657:
Daniel Correia and co-authors studied signals in anti-tumour T cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A special group of T cells reacts to small phosphate compounds from microbes. That reaction is the basis of efforts to use these cells against cancer.

A highly active microbial compound switched the cells on fast and kept two signalling paths running for a long time. Strong, lasting signals may explain the cells' strong anti-tumour action. Knowing the paths helps design treatments that wake these cells up in patients. Cancer use of these cells is still early, and mapping their signals is basic groundwork for any trial.
plos-pone-0005757:
Lichuan Yang and co-authors tested in 2009 whether a synthetic compound can shield nerve cells by switching on their defense genes. The switch, Nrf2, turns on a battery of detox and antioxidant enzymes. The compound, CDDO methyl amide, is a potent activator of that switch.

In their tests, the compound showed neuroprotective effects worth pursuing for brain diseases. Many such diseases involve oxidative stress that Nrf2 defenses counter. A drug that safely raises those defenses could help across several conditions. The study adds evidence for the approach and details the compound's action in nerve tissue.
plos-pone-0005857:
W. Shawn Carbonell and co-authors challenged in 2009 the standard picture of how cancer spreads to the brain. The classic seed-and-soil idea holds that tumor cells seek out brain tissue itself, drawn by its special chemistry. Direct evidence for that neurotropic growth in living animals was thin.

Instead, the team found metastases growing along the vascular basement membrane, the sleeve around brain blood vessels. The vessel wall, not the neurons, may be the true soil. That shift in view changes where researchers look for the signals that feed brain metastases. It may suggest blocking the vessel niche to starve them.
plos-pone-0005957:
Sarin is a nerve gas that jams a vital enzyme and can kill within minutes. Fredrik Ekström, Andreas Hörnberg, Elisabet Artursson and colleagues studied an antidote called HI-6 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The jammed enzyme is acetylcholinesterase, which the body needs to end nerve signals, and HI-6 is built to free it.

Using X-ray methods and computer models, the team solved the shape of HI-6 bound to the poisoned enzyme. That shape shows how the rescue works at the level of single atoms. A clear view of the rescue step guides the design of better antidotes, work that serves both medicine and defense against chemical weapons.
plos-pone-0006057:
A tumor sample is never pure tumor, and that mix can skew every measurement made from it. Hanna Göransson, Karolina Edlund, Maria Rydåker and colleagues built a correction in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses SNP array data from clinical lung cancer samples to estimate the normal cell fraction. It also spots regions where one gene copy is lost yet the total count stays two.

That second pattern, copy-neutral loss, hides from cruder tests. Measuring both lets labs read a tumor's true genome through the normal cells mixed in. The method sharpens cancer genomics where it matters most: in real patient samples, not in pure cell lines grown in a dish.
plos-pone-0006157:
Donor marrow cells can help a patient rebuild blood without taking over the marrow themselves. Stephan Fricke, Manuela Ackermann, Alexandra Stolzing and colleagues tested that helping role in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies non-adherent bone marrow derived cells, a population that can give rise to several mesenchymal cell types and aids tissue regeneration.

The donor cells facilitated hematopoietic recovery but did not lead to donor engraftment, the title reports. Help without takeover is an attractive profile for transplant support, since lasting foreign engraftment carries its own risks. The mouse results guide strategies that borrow donor cells' support while keeping the patient's own blood system in charge.
plos-pone-0006257:
Imatinib transformed treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia, but resistance and late-stage disease remain problems. Zheng Hu and colleagues tested whether proteasome inhibitors, drugs that block the cell's protein shredder, boost imatinib, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Low-dose imatinib combined with such blockers was the combination on trial.

The two drug types worked in synergy against leukemia cells, the authors report. Combining them may help patients whose disease no longer answers imatinib alone. Heart side effects linked to imatinib also motivate lower-dose strategies. The study supports trials of the pairing in harder phases of the disease.
plos-pone-0006357:
People who have never seen numbers still handle them with familiar quirks. Elena Salillas and colleagues studied numerical tasks in blind participants in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Blind people perform similarly to sighted people on number comparison and parity judgments, especially with sounds instead of sights.

Surprisingly, the blind show the same spatial effects in their number judgments. Numbers seem to be laid out along a mental line even without vision. That result suggests the number sense does not depend on visual experience. It informs how maths should be taught to blind students.
plos-pone-0006457:
Maria Morales and Robert Gereau checked a routine lab practice in PLOS ONE in 2009. To genotype mice, staff often snip a small piece of tail at weaning and take DNA from it. That is how genetically modified mice are identified. But when such mice are used in pain research, the snip itself could alter how the animals respond to painful stimuli.

The authors tested whether tail biopsy changes behavioral responses to noxious stimuli. A practice meant only to label animals might quietly bias pain data. Their study warns pain researchers to account for the procedure. It also speaks to animal welfare, since a common step may carry lasting effects.
plos-pone-0006557:
Elodie Fino, Jean-Michel Deniau, and Laurent Venance showed small signals can drive lasting brain change in PLOS ONE in 2009. Action potentials are thought to be determinant for inducing long-term synaptic plasticity. That plasticity is the cellular basis of learning and memory. However, neuronal activity does not always reach full spikes.

The authors show brief subthreshold events can act as Hebbian signals for long-term plasticity. Hebbian learning strengthens connections when cells are active together. If small, below-threshold events count, learning rules are more forgiving than thought. The finding reshapes models of how synapses decide to change.
plos-pone-0006657:
Reto Baertschiger and co-authors tested stromal cells in injured liver in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multipotent mesenchymal stromal cells are currently investigated clinically as cellular therapy for a variety of diseases. Differentiation of these cells toward endodermal lineages raised hope they could rebuild liver. The team examined the fibrogenic potential of human cells in injured liver.

Fibrogenic means scar-forming, the opposite of what therapy wants. Their title flags that potential directly. Testing for harm is as important as testing for benefit in cell therapy. The study tempers enthusiasm with a concrete safety question.
plos-pone-0006757:
Marie-Cécile Caillaud and colleagues watched checkpoint proteins at work in dividing plant cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The spindle assembly checkpoint guards chromosome division. It blocks segregation until chromosomes attach properly to the spindle. That surveillance prevents cells gaining or losing chromosomes. Most checkpoint knowledge came from animals and yeast, not plants.

The team characterized checkpoint protein dynamics in plants. Some roles matched those known in other organisms. Others were conserved in form but unsuspected in function. Plants divide differently, with no centrioles and open cell walls forming. Their checkpoint adaptations reflect those differences. The work widens the checkpoint story across the tree of life.
plos-pone-0006857:
Oliver J. Sabot and colleagues piloted a global malaria drug subsidy in rural Tanzania in PLOS ONE in 2009. Only a small share of fever patients used recommended combination therapies. High retail prices were a major reason. Many patients buy treatment from private drug shops. A global subsidy for artemisinin-based combinations was proposed to cut prices.

The pilot distributed subsidized therapies through private drug shops. The team measured the impact on availability, price, and use. Subsidies that work in shops can reach patients clinics miss. The results inform whether a worldwide subsidy deserves launch. Malaria policy depends on evidence like this from real markets.
plos-pone-0006957:
Maritza Jaramillo, Marie-Josée Bellemare, Caroline Martel, and others studied malaria pigment in PLOS ONE in 2009. As malaria parasites digest blood, they leave a dark pigment called hemozoin. More and more work tied this pigment to immune harm in malaria. One point was still in dispute. Could pure pigment alone stir the immune system, with no other parasite parts mixed in?

The team made hemozoin-like crystals in the lab. They matched the crystals' shape and effects against the real pigment. The lab-made crystals did switch on immune responses. That answer matters, since the pigment may be a target for easing the worst harms of malaria.
plos-pone-0007057:
Adrián Granada and Hanspeter Herzel asked how rhythms lock on quickly in PLOS ONE in 2009. Entrainment is the process where oscillators sync to an outside signal. It appears everywhere in nature, from fireflies to brain waves. The time taken to sync up matters in many living processes.

The pair studied a generic oscillator model. They searched its dynamics for what makes entrainment fast. Slow settling can mean missed signals in real biological clocks. Their results give design rules for rhythms that must lock on swiftly, from circadian clocks to neural circuits.
plos-pone-0007157: Wei Song, Avima Ruder, Liangyuan Hu, and colleagues examined the genetic epidemiology of glioblastoma in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study covered human leukocyte antigen alleles and motifs, the immune identity markers people inherit. It reported findings that confirm earlier results and added new ones. Work of this kind tests whether immune system genes shape the risk of this aggressive brain tumor.
plos-pone-0007257:
Zahirul Islam, Alex van Belkum, Jaap A. Wagenaar, and colleagues compared bacterial strains from paralysis patients in Bangladesh in 2009. Campylobacter jejuni commonly causes acute gastroenteritis, or gut infection. It is also linked to later nerve disorders such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and Miller Fisher syndrome, which can paralyze patients.

The authors genotype dozens of C. jejuni strains from Bangladeshi patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome. Comparative genotyping shows which strain features cluster with the syndrome. Their work may reveal why only some gut infections trigger severe nerve damage afterward. It also builds regional data where such studies are scarce.
plos-pone-0007357:
Colin K. Franz, Eric T. Quach, Christina A. Krudy, and colleagues tested nerve injury effects in a rat model of ALS in 2009. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis causes muscle weakness and wasting through progressive motoneuron loss. Before motoneurons die, their junctions with muscle fail and axons retract, cutting muscles off from nerve control early in disease.

Effective treatment will need to protect those junctions. The authors apply a conditioning lesion, a prior nerve injury, in the rat model. They report selective protection from that lesion. Their PLOS ONE result suggests injury signals can activate defenses in vulnerable motoneurons.
plos-pone-0007457:
Mariane Schleimann and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on human herpesvirus 6B, a widespread virus that infects most people in childhood. A related virus carries a gene whose protein has been linked to tumor formation in lab tests. The counterpart gene in the 6B virus, called dr6, was less understood. The team characterized the protein it encodes.

They found the DR6 protein gathers in the nucleus of infected cells. There it forms a complex with p41, the viral factor that helps copy viral DNA. That partnership ties DR6 to the virus's replication machinery. Each mapped interaction exposes a possible point of attack for antiviral drugs. The study adds one more piece to the picture of how this common virus copies itself.
plos-pone-0007557:
Pietro Mazzoni and Nancy Wexler published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how people control reaching movements. A reach can be guided attentively, with conscious correction, or automatically, without thought. Explicit control tends to engage when a movement is new. Implicit control allows several actions to run at once. The two systems are usually assessed indirectly, and this study examined them side by side.

The authors show that explicit and implicit control operate in parallel during reaching. Both steer the arm at the same time, rather than taking turns. That two-pilot picture changes how motor learning should be modeled. It matters for rehabilitation, where retraining one system may not fix the other. The study gives movement science a cleaner account of how a simple reach is governed.
plos-pone-0007657:
Xiao Li Shi and colleagues published a survey in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the smallest photosynthetic life in the southeast Pacific. Photosynthetic picoeukaryotes, cells under three micrometers wide, drive much of the ocean's primary production. Molecular methods had begun to reveal their communities. The open ocean there is oligotrophic, poor in nutrients, and vast. The team censused the tiny eukaryotes in those waters by their DNA.

Most of the community belonged to groups with no cultured representatives. The ocean's primary production in that region rests on organisms science has never grown. That fact humbles laboratory-based oceanography. DNA surveys reveal a workforce that experiments cannot yet touch. Knowing who is there is the first step toward knowing what they do. The study charts the unknown majority of a marine desert.
plos-pone-0007757:
Christopher Brower and Alexander Varshavsky published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines mice missing a protein-tagging step called arginylation. Cells mark some proteins for destruction through the N-end rule pathway. That marking needs an arginine tag, added by the enzyme Ate1.

Mice lacking this step lost fat and burned energy at a higher rate. Their sperm production was damaged. Their brains also showed disturbances. One small chemical tag thus touches body weight, fertility and brain function. The study maps how far a single protein-editing step reaches into whole-animal biology.
plos-pone-0007857:
Hiroaki Kimura and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It traces the origin of odd thyroid cells called oncocytes, or Hurthle cells. These cells appear in thyroid tumors and autoimmune disease. They look swollen, with heaps of granular cytoplasm and a dark nucleus.

Why they form had remained unknown. Using transgenic mice and human samples, the team points to overactive immunoproteasomes. These are protein-shredding machines tuned for immune defense. Their excess underlies both the oncocyte pattern and primary hypothyroidism in the study. The finding connects an immune machine to a classic thyroid puzzle.
plos-pone-0007957:
Kevin Parsons and colleagues stress-tested a common math tool for comparing species, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tool, principal components analysis, shrinks many traits into a few axes for easy plotting. Biologists use it to ask whether groups evolved in like or unlike ways.

The team showed the tool has real limits when used to build a shared trait space. Plots can look neat while hiding what truly sets groups apart, which can mislead claims about chance and selection. Their warning helps researchers pick better ways to compare how lineages diverged.
plos-pone-0008057:
Matthias Dehmer and colleagues graded dozens of scores that claim to measure how complex a molecule is, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Such scores boil a chemical's tangle down to one number, which drug designers use to sort candidates. Many scores exist, but their true worth was murky.

Tested on large sets of real structures, some scores split molecules into clear, useful kinds while others mostly echoed each other or added noise. The grading lets designers drop the weak scores and keep a short, trusted set. Cleaner sorting early can save costly lab work later.
plos-pone-0008157:
Philip Leopold and colleagues measured the airway's cleaning hairs in smokers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cilia are tiny moving hairs that sweep mucus, dust, and germs out of the airways. Smokers clear that mucus poorly, and past work blamed damaged or slow-beating hairs.

Smokers' cilia proved shorter than those of non-smokers. Short hairs sweep weakly, however well they beat. Length thus joins the list of what smoking takes from the lung. Whether length returns after quitting is an open question for lung clinics. Shorter hairs also clear less of the tar and germ load each breath brings in.
plos-pone-0008257:
Helena del Corral and colleagues studied tuberculosis risk in Colombia in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. People living with a tuberculosis patient face high risk of infection. They also face risk of developing disease early. Finding who is most at risk is a goal for tuberculosis control. Blood tests based on interferon-gamma help detect infection.

The team measured interferon-gamma responses to the tuberculosis bacterium in household contacts. They related those responses to later infection and disease. A test that flags high-risk contacts could focus preventive treatment. The study supports smarter follow-up in homes of patients.
plos-pone-0008357:
Toshinori Hinoue and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a mark found in some bowel cancers. A set of bowel tumors shows a trait in which many gene sites gain a small chem tag, known as methylation. The set of sites hit is more or less the same in each such tumor. A changed gene named BRAF, in a form called V600E, shows up most times in the same tumors. The tie between the trait and that gene form called for a close look.

They mapped the tags at a large set of gene sites in the tumors. Wide maps show how firm and how tight the tie is. Tag forms may help sort bowel cancers for the right care. The work adds fine points to the chart of this cancer's types.
plos-pone-0008457:
Michael Wallner and co-authors study birch pollen allergy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Allergy to the main birch pollen protein, Bet v 1, is a top cause of spring hay fever. It affects many people in mild zones of the north. Natural Bet v 1 is a mix of many close forms. Those forms may not act the same on the immune system.

The team make forms in the lab and compare them with natural ones. They test how each form triggers immune cells and antibodies. The work shows that lab-made forms can behave unlike natural mixes. That matters for allergy tests and for shots that retrain the immune system.
plos-pone-0008557:
Anna Cogen and co-authors study a toxin from a skin germ in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Peptides that kill germs are a key part of host defense. A common skin germ, Staphylococcus epidermidis, makes such peptides. One is called delta-toxin. These peptides act on germ membranes and can kill other germs. The team test delta-toxin against Group A Streptococcus. That germ causes strep throat and more severe disease.

They find delta-toxin works with host peptides to kill the germ. The pair works better than either one alone. A friendly skin germ thus helps the host fight a harmful one. Skin germs act as active guards, not just passive guests.
plos-pone-0008657:
Peter Mumby and co-authors test marine reserves in the Caribbean in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The fisheries and biodiversity benefits of marine reserves are widely recognised. There is mounting interest in using herbivorous fishes to help ecosystems recover from climate impacts. Grazing fish keep algae from smothering corals after bleaching. Reserves that ban fishing should boost those grazers. The team compare coral recovery inside and outside Caribbean reserves.

They find marine reserves enhance the recovery of corals on those reefs. Protected reefs regain coral cover faster after disturbance. Herbivorous fish are a key link in that recovery. Reserves thus serve as a climate adaptation tool, not just a fisheries one.
plos-pone-0008757:
Rui Guo and Jun Ren examined how fast alcohol breakdown can harm the heart. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heavy drinking weakens heart muscle in many people. A breakdown product, acetaldehyde, is a prime suspect for that damage. An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase speeds the making of that product. Mice engineered around this enzyme let the team test cause and effect.

Faster breakdown deepened heart dysfunction after alcohol exposure. Damage inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants, grew worse as well. A cell-death pathway in mitochondria carried part of the injury. Slowing that pathway might shield drinkers' hearts.
plos-pone-0008857:
Eriko Kage-Nakadai, Hiroyuki Kobuna, Masako Kimura, and colleagues guarded the worm's outer skin with two fat-handling genes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Every multi-celled animal needs a surface barrier to hold its inner world together. In mammals that barrier is the outer skin layer. A protein called FATP4 is key to building it. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans uses a cuticle instead, with similar fat chemistry.

Two genes, acs-20 and acs-22, proved necessary for the cuticle barrier. Worms lacking them leaked and struggled to keep their inner balance. The worm genes mirror the mammal system closely. Barrier biology can thus be studied cheaply in worms.
plos-pone-0008957:
Olivier Roux and co-authors reported a recruiting signal that ant watchers had missed, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The African weaver ant Oecophylla longinoda rules the treetops where it lives. Workers call nestmates to food or battle with scents and body marks. Known signals included anal spots and trails laid by dragging the abdomen.

Close watching revealed workers also rub their jaws against the ground while recruiting. The jaw-rubbing deposits a signal that helps guide nestmates to the goal. It had been overlooked because the motion is small and quick. Finding it fills a gap in how this well-studied ant organises its workforce.
plos-pone-0009057:
Malgorzata Miller and co-authors introduced a staph enzyme as a first of its kind, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proline-directed kinases run many processes in human and other eukaryotic cells. MAP kinases are the best known members of that family. Such signalling enzymes were long thought to belong to eukaryotes alone.

The Staphylococcus enzyme PknB proved to be a proline-directed kinase. It is the first clear bacterial example of this class. Bacteria apparently run versions of signalling once thought uniquely complex. The find could matter medically, since staph kinases may offer drug targets.
plos-pone-0009157:
Anne-Laure Daniau and co-authors tested whether early humans burned land on purpose, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mastering fire is cast as a key innovation of early modern humans. That control may have helped them spread across the world. Some proposed our ancestors, and Neanderthals too, used fire to manage ecosystems.

The team read the charcoal record left in ancient sediments. Fire use for landscape management should leave a distinctive signal there. Comparing Neanderthal and modern human periods tested the claim. The verdict shapes how deliberate we picture Stone Age burning.
plos-pone-0009257:
Yrsa Bergmann Sverrisdóttir and co-authors published this physiology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The sympathetic nervous system, which readies the body for action, also talks to blood vessel linings. Animal work shows the two systems interact to control circulation. In humans, that interaction was largely unexplored.

The team measured muscle sympathetic nerve activity in healthy people. They compared it with a stand-in marker of endothelial function, how well vessel linings work. The two measures were related. That link in healthy volunteers sets a baseline for studying diseases where both nerves and vessels misbehave, such as hypertension.
plos-pone-0009357:
Laura Perin and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Acute tubular necrosis kills the lining cells of the kidney's tubules. The damage often leaves patients with severe kidney failure. Stem cell therapies might offer a new way to repair it.

The team tested stem cells taken from human amniotic fluid. They used mice lacking immune defenses, so the human cells could survive. The transplanted cells protected the kidneys against acute tubular necrosis. That protection in a mouse model supports the idea that these easy-to-collect cells could one day treat sudden kidney injury.
plos-pone-0009457:
Jie Zhu and colleagues traced the history of a hormone part in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inhibin is a hormone that puts a brake on signals tied to reproduction. It belongs to the large TGF beta family of signal proteins. Its alpha part is found in no close cousin, which makes it stand out. The team searched genomes across animal groups.

By comparing those genomes, they worked out when the alpha part first arose. Their tree shows how a new piece could join an old family and gain a fresh role. The study explains the birth of a one of a kind brake in animal reproduction. It also shows how gene families grow by invention.
plos-pone-0009557:
Wei-Guo Du, Bo Zhao, and Richard Shine tracked turtle heart rates around hatching in PLOS ONE in 2010. Turtles are cold blooded, so heat speeds their hearts. Embryos gain from fast growth, since a shorter stay in the egg means less risk. Speed costs energy, though. The team measured heart rates of embryos and hatchlings at high temperatures.

Embryos kept high heart rates when warm. After hatching, the same high temperatures no longer drove the heart as fast. So the animal retunes its heart for its new life stage. The change balances the need for speed in the egg against safety outside it.
plos-pone-0009657:
Yosef Buganim and co-authors found a chromosome break tied to early cancer change in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sometimes two chromosomes swap pieces, and the break point lands inside a gene. Here the break falls inside BPTF, a gene that helps control how DNA is packaged and read. Cells carrying the break showed a pre malignant character. The team characterized the break and those cell traits.

A pre malignant state is a step on the road to cancer, not cancer itself. Catching such steps clarifies how malignancy begins. The break in BPTF may disturb gene control enough to prime cells for later change. Studies of this kind help map the earliest events that screening might one day detect.
plos-pone-0009757:
Bhushan Lokesh and co-authors published a virology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study examines a protein called NSs from groundnut bud necrosis virus, a plant virus that harms many legume and nightshade crops in India. The team made the protein in bacteria and purified it for tests.

The purified protein showed two distinct enzyme jobs, the team reports. It could split energy molecules such as ATP when RNA was present, a task blocked by an ATP-like drug. It could also strip a phosphate from the end of DNA and RNA strands without ATP. Changes at two key spots cut one or both of the jobs.
plos-pone-0009857:
Myotonic dystrophy weakens muscles and can dull motivation. Anna Matynia and colleagues used mouse models to find which gene defect drives which part of the disease. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease is one of the most common adult muscular dystrophies.

Three suspects were tested: Muscleblind1, Dmpk, and Six5. Only Muscleblind1 contributed to the complex phenotype of muscular and motivational deficits. A phenotype is the full set of traits a gene change produces. Pinning symptoms on one gene focuses the search for treatments. Motivation loss is often missed in this disease.
plos-pone-0009957:
Giant clams that live at deep-sea vents and seeps form a family of their own. Elena Krylova and Heiko Sahling reviewed that family's naming and global spread. Their review appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bivalves are mollusks with two hinged shells.

The family is Vesicomyidae, bivalves that host bacteria to feed on chemicals. Current taxonomy means the up-to-date naming and grouping of its species. The authors also mapped distribution, where each species lives worldwide. A single review steadies a fast-changing field. Some members rank among the world's largest clams. They cluster where chemicals leak from the seabed.
plos-pone-0010057:
The authors were Anna Phillips, Renzo Arauco-Brown, Alejandro Oceguera-Figueroa, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper named a striking new leech, Tyrannobdella rex. Most leeches feed on blood from outside the body. A few enter body openings instead, most often the nose and throat, and feed from inside.

The team described the new genus and species and traced where such mucosal leeches came from in evolution. Cases also include leeches found in eyes and other openings. Naming this lineage helps doctors and biologists link odd clinical cases to a real family history.
plos-pone-0010157:
Shuhua Zhan and Lewis Lukens studied small RNAs in a model plant in 2010. Their PLOS ONE paper covered Arabidopsis thaliana, the standard lab plant. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs, twenty or so letters long, cut from longer folded precursors. In plants they mainly work by slicing target messages, and many guide development.

The pair identified new microRNAs not cataloged before. They also tracked how gene activity shifts during development under microRNA control. A fuller catalog helps plant scientists link specific small RNAs to growth traits in crops as well as models.
plos-pone-0010257:
The authors were Clémence Lesimple, Carole Fureix, Hervé Menguy, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined how human handling affects horse welfare. Back pain is a known welfare problem in people and in animals. Vertebral problems are often reported in riding horses, yet they are not always spotted, and affected horses keep being worked.

The team studied nineteen horses from two riding centers. They linked direct human actions to signs of poor welfare in the horses. Better awareness of handlers' impact could spare working horses preventable pain. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010357:
Raffaella Melzi and a large team tested neural stem cells as helpers for islet transplants in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early data suggested these precursor cells can calm immune attacks. That raised a plan: graft them together with insulin-making islets to stop rejection. The team tried the pairing in mice. They wanted both protection and safety data before any human talk.

The joint graft did help the islets avoid rejection, the authors report. Worryingly, the stem cells also formed tumors in the mice. That double result is the heart of the study. A therapy that shields grafts but seeds tumors is not ready for patients. The work shows why long safety watching matters as much as early success.
plos-pone-0010457:
Andrea Petróczi and colleagues questioned whether athletes who deny doping can be believed, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research on doping leans heavily on athletes' own reports. Studies of drug use show people under-report stigmatized behavior. Doping is both banned and shamed, so under-reporting is likely worse. The authors looked behind clean self-reports for signs of pretense.

They explored indirect ways to detect hidden doping attitudes and use. Better measurement matters because policy built on false low numbers will fail. The study treats honesty itself as the variable to test. That is a brave move in a field built on questionnaires. Its lessons apply to any survey of forbidden behavior.
plos-pone-0010557:
Manuel Forero and colleagues released an automatic counter for dividing cells and glial cells in fly tissues in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell counts change in growth, degeneration, and cancer. Genetic studies therefore often need counts after a gene is lost or boosted. Counting cells by eye in images is slow and error-prone. Their tool, DeadEasy Mito-Glia, counts the two cell types in fruit fly images automatically.

Automation makes large genetic screens with cell counts practical. Consistent machine counts also remove human drift between scorers. The fly is a workhorse for gene function studies, so the audience is large. Tools like this quietly change what experiments are feasible. The paper documents accuracy as well as speed.
plos-pone-0010657:
Hridayesh Prakash and colleagues studied a fat-based signal that helps immune cells fight germs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cells are called macrophages, and they swallow germs that enter the body. An enzyme inside them, sphingosine kinase-1, makes the signal when a fight starts.

The team exposed mouse macrophages to Mycobacterium smegmatis, a kin of the TB germ. When the enzyme was blocked, the cells held far fewer germs in check. When it worked as usual, the cells kept the germs down. Boosting a host defense like this might aid TB drugs one day, with less risk of drug failure.
plos-pone-0010757:
Camila Figueiredo Pinzan and colleagues asked why one fungal disease strikes men far more than women, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Paracoccidioidomycosis is a whole-body fungal infection found across Latin America. At least ten men fall ill for every woman, a gap too large for exposure alone to explain.

Male and female mice were infected under matched conditions. Their immune responses diverged clearly, with females mounting the stronger defense. Hormones and immune wiring both seemed to play a part. Sex gaps this wide hint that treatments and vaccine plans may need to account for sex, not treat it as noise.
plos-pone-0010857:
Sean Carlin, Nahida Khan, Thomas Ku and co-authors published this imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many tumors contain low-oxygen zones that resist treatment, and a protein called CAIX helps those zones manage acid. The authors tested whether an antibody aimed at CAIX could find such zones in living tumors.

They compared a full antibody and two smaller fragments, each tagged so its path could be tracked, in mice carrying human colon tumors. The tumors showed strong CAIX in poorly supplied, low-oxygen areas, and the agents gathered there in different patterns. The full antibody first lit up the rim of those zones. Carlin and colleagues weigh which form best reports tumor hypoxia. A reliable hypoxia tracer could help doctors pick patients for oxygen-targeted therapy.
plos-pone-0010957:
Matthew Becker and Reid Harris published this salamander study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The chytrid fungus devastating amphibians worldwide grows on skin, and earlier lab work showed that bacteria living on redback salamander skin can inhibit it. The authors tested whether that skin community actually protects living salamanders from the disease.

They reduced the skin bacteria of some salamanders before exposing them to the fungus, and compared them with infected salamanders keeping a normal community. The reduced-bacteria animals lost significantly more body mass, a disease symptom, and more of them showed limb loss. Becker and Harris demonstrate that a salamander's resident microbes act as a living shield. That finding supports probiotic-style treatments being explored to save threatened frog populations.
plos-pone-0011057:
Teiichiro Shiino, Nobuhiko Okabe, Yoshinori Yasui and co-authors published this flu evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus reached Japan in May of that year, sparking outbreaks in Osaka and Hyogo before spreading across prefectures. The authors reconstructed the virus's family tree from full genomes to trace how it entered and moved through the country.

Comparing dozens of Japanese isolates with worldwide sequences, using both distance and Bayesian statistical methods, they found the global viruses fell into four distinct clusters. One cluster arose earlier, while another spread most widely around the world. Shiino and colleagues show the Japanese epidemic drew from that global structure rather than a single introduction. Such profiles help public health officials distinguish imported cases from homegrown transmission chains.
plos-pone-0011157:
Dusa, Mouton, Pecquet and colleagues pinpointed a blood cancer target in PLOS ONE in 2010. A mutant form of a signaling protein stays switched on and drives some blood cancers. The mutant needs help from a second region of the same protein to stay active, and the team located a key spot in that region.

That spot, a single building block in a helper domain, proved required for constant activity. A drug aimed there could block the mutant while sparing normal signaling proteins. Such precise blockers promise fewer side effects than broad drugs. The finding turns a structural detail into a concrete drug design goal.
plos-pone-0011257:
Klassen compared pigment genes across microbes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many bacteria make carotenoids, the bright pigments that color carrots and autumn leaves. By comparing pigment making genes across many genomes, the author traced how this pathway evolved and spread among microbes.

The patterns show the recipe was inherited, borrowed and reshaped over long time spans. Knowing its history helps industry find microbes that make useful pigments. Those pigments serve as vitamins, food colors and health products. Evolution thus becomes a prospecting guide for biotechnology, pointing to lineages most likely to yield new products.
plos-pone-0011357:
Yurong Xin and colleagues compared DNA marks across two major brain regions in a 2010 study.
