Cells add chemical tags to DNA that help set which genes stay active, and the pattern differs from tissue to tissue. The team mapped those tags genome-wide in the cerebrum, the seat of thought, and the cerebellum, which fine-tunes movement.

The two regions carried clearly divergent tag patterns, far more distinct than a simple tissue label would predict. Many differences fell near genes with brain roles, hinting that tagging helps lock in each region's identity. The maps give neuroscientists a baseline for spotting tag changes in brain disease. They also show that studies pooling the whole brain can hide strong regional contrasts that matter for how the brain works.
plos-pone-0011457:
Syed Meeran, Shweta Patel, and Trygve Tollefsbol reported in 2010 that a broccoli compound can silence a cancer gene without changing its code. Sulforaphane, the sharp-tasting chemical in broccoli and related vegetables, has long interested cancer researchers. The team tested its effect on hTERT, the telomerase gene that lets cancer cells divide without limit, in human breast cancer cell lines.

Sulforaphane lowered hTERT activity through epigenetic repression, chemical marks that switch a gene off while leaving its letters intact. Switching off an immortality gene with a food-derived compound is a striking lead. The authors' result comes from cells in dishes, not from diets, and that gap remains wide. Still, the work shows a concrete mechanism by which a plant chemical can reach a central cancer switch.
plos-pone-0011557:
Morio Ueyama and co-authors modeled a severe human disease in fruit flies in 2010 and found muscle precursors dying in excess. Walker-Warburg syndrome is a congenital muscular dystrophy with grave brain and eye defects, and children with it rarely survive long. A fly model lets researchers watch the disease's cell biology quickly and test its genes one by one.

In the fly model, myoblasts, the precursor cells that build muscle, died by apoptosis at increased rates. Dying precursors explain a muscle that never builds properly, linking the syndrome's genetics to a concrete cellular failure. A fast model with a clear readout, precursor death, is exactly what screening for suppressor genes and candidate drugs requires. The study gives a cruel human disease a workable laboratory handle.
plos-pone-0011657:
Cathal Seoighe and Chris Gehring asked whether people inherit differences in RNA quality control, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells destroy faulty RNA messages through a pathway called nonsense-mediated decay. Messages that keep an intron by mistake usually gain an early stop signal and are shredded by this system.

The authors measured how efficiently this decay works across individuals and tested whether the variation runs in families. They found a heritable component to decay efficiency in humans. Inherited differences in basic message clean-up could help explain why the same RNA faults affect people unevenly.
plos-pone-0011757:
Sara Branco and Richard Ree surveyed fungi living on plant roots in harsh serpentine soils, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stressful environments usually host few and highly specialised species. Serpentine soils, rich in heavy metals, impose well-known hardships on plants, but their effect on other organisms was poorly understood.

Using combined field and genetic methods, the authors measured diversity of mycorrhizal fungi, the root partners that trade nutrients with plants. Diversity was not reduced by the harsh soil. The thriving partnerships show that this underground teamwork survives even ground that is toxic to many plants.
plos-pone-0011857:
Xin-He Lai and colleagues studied in 2010 how a dangerous bacterium gets taken in by mouse immune cells. They worked with Francisella novicida, a close relative of the germ that causes tularemia, a serious fever disease. Macrophages normally swallow and kill such bacteria, yet Francisella can survive the encounter.

By testing bacterial mutants, the team found changes that alter the way macrophages carry out the swallowing process. A different route in can mean a different fate for the germ once inside. Pinpointing which bacterial genes change that route helps explain how Francisella slips past a key immune defense, and it marks steps that future treatments might try to block.
plos-pone-0011957:
Wilbert Vermeij and Claude Backendorf reported in 2010 that proteins of hardened skin do double duty during wound healing. Healing follows a set sequence from a small scratch to major injury, and reactive oxygen species, aggressive oxygen-based molecules, play roles at several stages. Too much of them damages tissue; too little stalls repair.

The team found that skin cornification proteins, the building material of the skin's tough outer layer, link oxygen detoxification with the cell migration that closes wounds. One protein system serving both cleanup and movement ties two healing steps together. That connection suggests wound treatments could target the shared machinery rather than each step separately.
plos-pone-0012057:
Yasushi Noguchi and co-workers fed mice in 2010 a diet rich in ketogenic essential amino acids and watched their livers stay lean. Fatty liver, or hepatic steatosis, builds when fat synthesis outruns fat burning. The molecular conversation between these amino acids and lipid metabolism was not fully mapped.

Their diet, with a high ratio of essential to non-essential amino acids, modulated lipid synthetic pathways and prevented fat accumulation in the liver. A dietary pattern that switches off the liver's fat-making program is a candidate strategy against a very common condition. The study also shows amino acid balance, not just calories, talking to metabolism.
plos-pone-0012157:
Ryan Edwards and Jennifer Roff re-examined claims that older fathers harm children's thinking skills, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recent studies had linked advanced father age to weaker scores in children, a worrying pattern as parents everywhere delay having kids. But older fathers differ from younger ones in other ways too, including who they partner with and how many children they already have.

Once the mother's education and the number of siblings were taken into account, the apparent harm from father's age could be explained away. The paper is a caution against reading a simple pattern as a cause. It also steadies a debate where alarming headlines can outrun what the data really show.
plos-pone-0012257:
Hélène Foussard, Pierre Ferrer, Philippe Valenti, and co-authors introduced a new family of cell-skeleton regulators in PLOS ONE in 2010. Comparing genomes across animals reveals thousands of conserved proteins whose jobs nobody has tested. The LRCH proteins were one such blank spot: present across species, built with parts that hint at scaffolding, but functionally unknown.

The team's experiments place this family among the regulators of the cytoskeleton, the cell's inner frame of rods and ropes. Naming a family's trade is the first step toward finding which diseases involve it. Biology's catalog still holds many such untested proteins, and each characterized family shrinks that unknown map.
plos-pone-0012357:
Janine Kimpel, Stephen Braun, Gang Qiu and fellow researchers tested gene-based ways to shield T cells from HIV in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Many lab-made blockers can slow HIV in a dish, but few studies had compared them head to head. The team also asked whether protected cells gain an edge and outlive unprotected ones once HIV attacks.

They placed a membrane-bound fusion blocker into CD4 T cells, the very cells HIV targets, and infected the mix. Cells carrying the blocker survived while others died off, so the protected group took over. That survival edge is exactly what a gene therapy needs: a small dose of guarded cells could grow into lasting defense.
plos-pone-0012457:
Sarah Bush and Johannes Schul tracked mating songs in katydids, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Male songs bring the sexes together, and new song traits are usually credited to female taste. In the katydid genus Neoconocephalus, some males evolved novel call features even though females showed no preference for them.

The study argues that other forces, such as predator pressure or habitat acoustics, can drive song change without female choice. That widens the standard story of sexual selection. It reminds biologists that mating signals answer to survival needs too, not only to the preferences of the listening sex.
plos-pone-0012557:
Susanna Dunachie, Tamara Berthoud, Sheila Keating and colleagues searched for immune signs that track malaria vaccine success, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Malaria still kills huge numbers, and a vaccine is urgently needed, yet no proven correlate of protection exists — no blood sign that certifies a vaccine worked. Trial teams must wait for infections to judge success.

The chemokine MIG and the calming cytokines IL-10 and TGF beta correlated with both immunogenicity and efficacy in their vaccine trials. Candidate correlates like these, if confirmed, would let developers compare vaccine versions in weeks rather than seasons. That speed is crucial in a field with many designs and few resources.
plos-pone-0012657:
Dozmorov, Guthridge, Hurst and co-authors built a yardstick for the many ways of reading gene activity data. New lab and maths methods for expression data appear constantly, and choosing among them is hard. Their 2010 paper offers a single, broad method for scoring how well each analysis performs.

A shared yardstick lets labs compare old and new methods on equal terms. That matters because the method chosen can change which genes a study calls important. Fair scoring brings order to a crowded field and raises trust in published gene lists.
plos-pone-0012757:
Bentley, Asselbergs, Coffey and co-authors tested how gene variants from three blood systems combine to shape heart risk. The systems govern clot breakdown, blood vessel tightening and related pressure control. Earlier work had linked single genes in these systems to heart disease, with mixed results across studies.

Their 2010 study looked at the interplay among the variants rather than each one alone. Risk that only appears when several variants coincide would explain why single-gene studies disagreed. The approach reflects how the body actually works, with systems acting together rather than in isolation.
plos-pone-0327957: Black garden ants — their foraging trajectories hide search strategies. This paper discovered those behaviors in ant movement data. The findings reveal the algorithms of tiny brains — with lessons for robotics and optimization.
plos-pone-0331157:
Maxwell Ateni Assibi and co-authors reviewed studies in 2026 on how medical students experience learning alongside other health professions. Working across professions is now a stated goal of training, yet student experience of it is patchy.

Eight studies from a decade of literature met the criteria. Students generally welcomed collaborative learning and valued contact with other professions, but grasp of each other's roles stayed shaky. Role confusion, professional hierarchy, and timetabling blocked progress, while real practice placements, curriculum integration, and staff support helped. The review gives course designers a short, evidence based list of what to fix first.
plos-pone-0332357:
McCurtin and colleagues, in a 2026 study, count how often doctors in England dispense thickeners for people who swallow unsafely. Thickened drinks flow more slowly, which can stop liquid entering the airway. The products are widely used, especially for older people, yet basic facts about their dispensing were missing. The team mined a national prescribing database for 2019 to 2024.

Nearly three million thickener items were dispensed in primary care over the five years, costing the health service nearly ninety million pounds. Use fell steadily among adults, who are the main users, while dispensing to babies under one rose. Costs still climbed in the last year, despite falling use in most age groups. Gum-based products made up the vast majority of items. The authors say this first map of practice raises sharp questions about when thickeners help, what they cost, and why use is shifting by age.
plos-pone-0336457:
N. V. Satyanarayana and his team built a thin sheet that soaks up radar waves. It is printed on denim, so it bends. Most such sheets catch waves at one pitch. This one catches them at three. The sheet's face is a patch of copper shapes in mixed sizes. It was shaped in four rounds of work.

At each of its three pitches, the sheet drank in near all the waves that hit it. It did so at all wave twists. Bend tests showed it keeps its skill when curved. The team sees use in stealth, space links, and shield work for next-wave gear.
plos-pone-0337157: Lashley and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study testing whether rats can model Gulf War illness. Male Sprague-Dawley rats from Charles River faced several chemical and stress setups drawn from war exposures. The title reports the result with care: signs like those of the illness showed up only in limited ways. A weak animal model warns researchers to rethink how they test causes and cures.
plos-pone-0340557:
Poramad Trivalairat and colleagues assessed drinking water risks in six mountain villages above Bhumibol Dam in Thailand. Indigenous families there rely on natural sources whose dangers they may not know. Water from thirty eight sources, plus soil and edible crop parts, were tested for acidity, nitrate, and pesticide traces over six months, alongside a village filter trial.

Sources villagers liked best for drinking proved riskiest, with high nitrate, strong alkalinity, and pesticide traces likely washed from farms. Every soil sample and the underground parts of food crops carried residues, so diet adds exposure. The village filter did not improve water quality across the trial. Still puddle water, prized for taste, needs urgent safer handling.
plos-pone-0343457: Zhang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that sorts brain tumor scans. Their system aims to name tumor types with high accuracy. A design feature called complementary downsampling blocks helps the system keep fine detail while shrinking images for speed. Fast, accurate scan sorting could help doctors in busy hospitals decide sooner which patients need urgent care.
plos-pone-0343757:
Gabriel Bafunyembaka and colleagues study children in French Guiana who live with both sickle cell disease and asthma, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The pairing is common and dangerous, since asthma raises the odds of painful crises and acute chest syndrome, the condition's deadliest complication.

Among one hundred thirty-eight children with confirmed asthma, nearly three-quarters had a severe course, defined by repeated hospitalizations for crises or chest syndrome in the previous year. Yet when the team tested many candidate factors together, none independently predicted severity. That negative result is itself useful: it warns clinicians in tropical settings not to rely on a simple checklist to guess which child will suffer most.
plos-pone-0343857:
Sarah Alkhatib and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about research funding. Grant abstracts submitted to the NIH, the United States National Institutes of Health, are often coded by hand, meaning readers sort them into categories. The authors compare that human coding with coding done by artificial intelligence.

A head-to-head comparison shows where machine coding matches trained readers and where it drifts. Coding thousands of abstracts is slow, costly work, so a reliable automated option would change how agencies track their research portfolios. Science administrators and research evaluators are the natural audience for this test of AI against human judgment.
plos-pone-0344857:
Jing Wu and four colleagues published this 2026 algorithms paper on nonnegative matrix factorization, a workhorse method that breaks big data tables into simpler parts for tasks like image and text analysis. Their hybrid method alternates between two solvers, guided by a relaxed line search with a tunable looseness setting and room for larger steps.

Under mild assumptions the authors prove the method settles at a solution. On artificial and real data sets it ran more efficiently than leading rivals. Wu aims the improvement at anyone factoring large data on a deadline.
plos-pone-0344957:
Yekai Feng led a team of eight authors building a prognostic tool for head and neck cancer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These cancers need better ways to predict outcomes and choose treatment. The team built an index based on PANoptosis, a combined form of cell death, and applied it to squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck.

Feng's index sorts patients by risk, and the work also revealed a gene, DSCAM, as a possible treatment target. A tool that both predicts and points to a target is doubly useful. Clinicians gain a risk score for planning, and drug researchers gain a named lead. Head and neck cancers often return after treatment, so sharper prognosis can guide how closely each patient is watched.
plos-pone-0345157:
Mahdieh Maazalahi and Soodeh Hosseini model how botnets, networks of hijacked computers, spread through complex computer networks. Spread is treated like a disease, with machines moving from open to exposed to infected to recovered states. Alongside the spread model, the pair built a detection system that blends learning methods with search tricks to pick telling features.

Simulations showed their spread model lowered the share of infected machines and halted spread sooner than rival models. The detector, tried on three public attack data sets, spotted attacks with accuracy in the low ninety percent range and fewer missed or false alarms. Early maths on spread helps defenders judge whether an outbreak will grow or die out.
plos-pone-0347557:
Dwita Rian Desandri and colleagues gathered the trials that test if gym-based heart rehab can shrink the fatty build-up in heart arteries, not just boost fitness. Drugs that lower blood fats are known to shrink this build-up, but the proof for exercise was spread thin. The team searched in 2025 and kept the trials that took scans of the arteries before and after rehab.

Five trials with two hundred seventeen patients fit, with plans built on hard interval work, steady aerobic work, and weights, all next to standard drug care. The plans cut the size of the build-up by a clear margin. If exercise truly shrinks artery build-up, rehab moves from a support act to a direct way to treat the disease.
plos-pone-0347657:
Hasti Garjani, Joel S Brown, and co-authors asked which math model best matches how lung cancer cells grow and resist drugs in the lab. They used published data on non-small cell lung cancer, tracking drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cells grown alone and together, with and without the drug alectinib and helper cells called fibroblasts. Their 2026 study compared several growth curves and drug-effect formulas against the data.

A classic logistic growth model with a ratio-based drug effect fit the single-type cultures best. Carrying those settings into mixed cultures showed that fibroblasts helped both cell types live together, while the drug pushed one type out. The authors stress that a model must fit the data and also make biological sense before doctors lean on it for treatment planning.
plos-pone-0347757:
Steffen Herbold and three colleagues published a 2026 study testing whether large language models can convincingly imitate real people in political debate. They drew on Question Time, a BBC television programme where panellists answer audience questions. Then they asked language models to write replies in the panellists' place.

A cross-section of the British public then judged both versions without knowing which was which. The machine-written answers were rated more authentic, more relevant, and more coherent than the originals, and writing style did not explain the gap. The authors warn that such convincing fakes could mislead voters, so the public urgently needs warning about the risk.
plos-pone-0347957:
Xiaowei Luo and co-workers design a safer way to pick out gene-edited plants without leaving antibiotic resistance genes behind. Standard selection uses such markers, which raise safety worries. Their 2026 study gives tobacco a microbial gene that lets it break down biuret, a plant-harming by-product found in common fertilizer, and turns the poison into food.

On biuret feed, nearly four in five shoots carried the new gene, beating the standard method, and plants grew ready weeks sooner. Edited plants also shrugged off biuret at sprouting, even when nitrogen was scarce. In mixed pots, biuret cut weeds back hard while edited plants thrived. One chemical could thus select crops and suppress weeds at once.
plos-pone-0348357:
Daniel Oliveira dos Santos and his team probed a germ in wild opossums of Brazil. The germ, a strep type, was known from kin of these beasts in the north. Ten dead beasts were cut open for checks. Thirty-four live ones, caught in the wild, had their noses swabbed. Germ samples from the dead were grown and read gene by gene.

The germ showed in skin sores on the dead beasts. It also showed in the heart, the spleen, and the kidneys, a sign it can spread through the body. All live beasts tested clean. The germs bore no drug-shield genes and fell to most drugs. This is the first full sketch of the ill in these beasts.
plos-pone-0348957:
Anina van Leeuwen and colleagues lay out the plan for StepuP, a trial testing treadmill training for people with Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's stiffens walking and raises fall risk, and walking on a treadmill at varied speeds already helps in clinics. What remains unclear is how the training changes the body and brain, which this trial is built to measure.

About a hundred twenty-six patients at four sites will be assigned by chance to standard speed-based treadmill training or to an enriched version with virtual reality or sudden nudges. Brain waves, muscle signals, and three-dimensional movement will be recorded before training, after it, and three months later. Healthy older adults serve as a comparison group. No results are reported here.
plos-pone-0349257:
Fábia Fernandes, Ricardo Bezerra, and Isabelle Barbosa assess in 2026 how well people with diabetes in Brazil receive proper care, and how gender, race, and income combine to shape that care. They used a national health survey covering several thousand adults who reported a diabetes diagnosis. Adequate care was judged against expected checks and referrals.

Gaps centred on foot checks and referral to specialists. Low income Black men and women had the highest rates of poor care. Oddly, people without complications or hospital stays also got less complete care. The authors name poverty and structural racism as core drivers needing policy action.
plos-pone-0349357:
Karin van der Burg and six colleagues compare two laboratory strains of the eastern spruce budworm, a major forest pest, in this 2026 genomics study. Most budworm caterpillars pause development as tiny larvae to survive winter, a state called diapause, but a selectable minority skip it and keep growing. The team assembled a chromosome-level genome for the non-diapausing strain and compared it with the published genome and gene activity of the diapausing one.

Despite the dramatic life-history difference, the genomes showed no major rearrangements, suggesting the trait rests on small genetic differences. Gene activity, by contrast, diverged sharply: the diapausing strain ramped up genes for sugar burning and for processing environmental signals. The split in expression appeared midway through the first larval stage, before the paths visibly separate. The work narrows where researchers should hunt for diapause's genetic switches.
plos-pone-0349757:
Sanjida Sultana Santa and colleagues measured heavy metals in soils beside an open landfill in Jashore, Bangladesh, where household and industrial waste are dumped together. They tested for eleven metals and converted the readings into standard risk indexes. Arsenic, mercury, cadmium, lead, zinc, copper, and manganese all stood out at levels of concern.

Open dumping is the usual practice in Bangladesh, so this one site stands for many. Comparing the metals' patterns helps separate what the landfill adds from what was already in the ground. Families farming and living near such dumps face the exposure directly. An index-based assessment like this turns raw chemistry into a ranked warning that local officials can act on.
plos-pone-0349857:
John Hart and seven colleagues formally describe a new species of monkey from the forests of the Democratic Republic of Congo, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The animal, known locally as Likweli, lives between the Lomami and Congo rivers in high, closed-canopy forest. Over four years the team logged more than a hundred observations across its small estimated range, where it travels in groups of about six, often alongside other monkey species.

Genetic and anatomical evidence places it in the black colobus group, as the closest relative of a species found over a thousand kilometres away, and its calls match that kinship too. Rare, shy, and barely known even locally, the new species begins its scientific life already in need of protection.
plos-pone-0350157:
Correction notice: Zhibin Yuan, Yuqi Gao, and co-authors issued this 2026 correction to their rat study of a gene regulator called MKL1 in lung hypertension caused by low oxygen. One panel in a main figure duplicated another by mistake, the chart beside it lacked axis labels, and some values in that chart were wrong. The notice supplies a corrected figure with the proper image from the original experiments and a fixed chart, plus fuller details of animal monitoring and humane endpoints.

The authors state the changes do not affect the results or conclusions. The original study reported that silencing the regulator calmed lung inflammation in this rat model of hypoxia-driven pulmonary hypertension. Underlying image and chart data for the corrected figure are shared with the notice.
plos-pone-0350457:
Beyhan Başkan, Hatice Kübra Başkan, and Nevzat Koç tested eight leading language models on past exam questions for dentistry specialisation in Turkey in 2026. The questions covered endodontics, the root canal specialty, across a decade of national exams.

One hundred twenty-seven questions, split between knowledge and clinical cases, were put to each model and scored against official keys. Scores differed widely. The top model cleared ninety percent and beat rivals clearly on clinical cases, while the weakest sat near sixty percent. Such spread warns students and teachers that model choice, not just model use, decides study value.
plos-pone-0350557:
Ya-Qin You, Han-Han Song, and Yu-Liang Feng surveyed streaming video users to learn which parts of the viewing experience turn casual watchers into loyal ones. With fast networks everywhere, over-the-top platforms compete on experience as much as content. Their 2026 study asked two hundred thirty users about convenience, interaction, emotional engagement, and service quality, then modeled how those shaped perceived value, satisfaction, and intention to keep using a service.

Smooth, easy use lifted value, satisfaction, and intention alike. Emotional experience helped on all three fronts too, partly by raising satisfaction. Service quality and functional value, though, did not directly drive intention; they worked only through satisfaction. Interactive features pushed intention directly. The practical lesson: platforms win loyalty when smooth performance and engaging content leave users satisfied, not merely impressed.
plos-pone-0350657:
Root canal treatment sometimes fails because a hardy bacterium, Enterococcus faecalis, survives deep in the tooth. Daniel K Arens and co-authors collected viruses that infect this bacterium, called phages, from wastewater, and tested them as a possible treatment aid in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Fourteen phages were isolated and checked against many strains of the bacterium, including two taken from mouths. Several attacked a wide range of strains, slowed growth even at low doses, and stripped away up to ninety-seven percent of tough bacterial films. The team offers the set as fresh candidates for fighting stubborn dental infections.
plos-pone-0350857:
Sidartawan Soegondo and colleagues reported the Indonesian part of a large Asia Pacific survey on obesity care in 2026. A thousand adults living with obesity and two hundred health workers answered questions online about beliefs, talks, and barriers.

Views clashed. Most health workers called obesity a chronic disease, but only about half of patients did, and most patients blamed themselves while few workers did. Two thirds of patients saw themselves as merely overweight, and few had discussed weight with a clinician in five years. Money worries also blocked care. The gaps point to kinder, clearer first conversations as the place to start.
plos-pone-0351057:
Wenze Yu and colleagues used single cell gene reading to study cells other than heart muscle in diabetic heart disease, where the heart stiffens and weakens without blocked arteries. Public cell data from diabetes and heart muscle disease were sorted into cell types, with metabolism scores, life path tracking, and cell to cell signal maps. One marker gene was then tested in vessel cells in dishes.

Eight cell types appeared, with natural killer and smooth muscle cells shared across both diseases. Immune, vessel lining, and nerve cells ranked most metabolically active. Dish tests probed how one immune marker gene affects vessel cell growth and movement. Non muscle cells, long treated as background, may drive much of diabetic heart damage.
plos-pone-0351157:
Xin Fang and Xingyue Peng asked how United States tightening of money policy since 2022 spilled onto share prices in China. Higher United States rates and a shrinking central bank balance sheet can shake foreign markets. The pair tracked short term price moves for listed Chinese firms around tightening news, sorting each firms overseas links into trade, investment, and finance.

Trade links helped, with exposed firms gaining stronger extra returns after shocks. Investment and finance links hurt, dragging returns down. Firms with heavy foreign ownership or overseas deals fared worst. Manager skill and venture backing softened or sharpened effects in distinct ways, and tech level mattered too. Where a firm reaches abroad, not just how much, shapes its risk.
plos-pone-0351557:
Baduanjin, a gentle traditional Chinese exercise of eight movements, draws loyal older practitioners. Haixu Ji and colleagues interviewed twenty-five community-dwelling older adults living with chronic diseases to learn why they keep practicing, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Five reasons held people to the routine. The movements felt safe and easy to learn. Bodies felt better with practice. Mood and mental calm improved. Group sessions widened social life. And many valued the exercise as a piece of their own traditional culture. The authors suggest community programs lean on all five draws, not health claims alone, to keep attendance high.
plos-pone-0351657:
Borianne and colleagues, in a 2026 study, race six artificial intelligence models at spotting cocoa pods in photos of farms in Côte d'Ivoire. Counting pods early helps farmers forecast harvests and bargain with buyers. Photos were low-resolution, as farm pictures often are. Models ranged from tiny versions to ones with many times more internal parts, all trained on thousands of hand-labeled pods.

The small, fast models won. Tiny versions of two YOLO designs beat the bigger transformer and classic models, scoring especially well on trees in the foreground. That upset the usual expectation that bigger is better. Reviewing why, the authors found fault in the training data itself: labels were inconsistent, and there were too few images to feed the giant models properly. The honest conclusion is two-sided: small models already work well for pod counting, and cleaner, larger teaching sets are needed before crowning any champion.
plos-pone-0351757:
Juan Du and seven colleagues teach a neural network to read brain tumour scans in this 2026 study. Two traits guide glioma treatment: whether the tumour carries an IDH mutation, and how fast its cells divide, marked by Ki-67. Both normally need tissue from surgery. The team built one model that predicts both at once. It feeds on four kinds of MRI, taken within a month before surgery at two hospitals. One hospital trained the model, the other tested it independently.

Hand-crafted image measurements and clinical details were fused with the network's features. Rival models served as comparisons. Accuracy was judged with standard curves, calibration checks, and decision analysis. Explanation tools highlighted which image regions drove each prediction. Non-invasive prediction matters because some patients cannot be biopsied. A validated scan-based estimate could shape treatment planning days earlier, while sparing patients an operation whose only purpose is information.
plos-pone-0352157:
Jaehoon Yeom, Minji Kim, and Sang Don Kim tackled a missing number in river science. Nobody knows what most freshwater invertebrates weigh when dried. Yet weight feeds food-web models and pollution risk work. The team mined field guides and papers for length and weight records. The records covered invertebrates from Korean rivers. From them they built formulas that predict weight from length alone.

Formulas tuned at the genus level matched real weighed specimens best. Broader family and order formulas did worse. More source studies also made the formulas sharper. The team then produced reference dry weights for over five hundred kinds of invertebrates. A quick length measure can now give the living mass of a whole river sample.
plos-pone-0352257:
Jaime Barranco and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One imaging paper on the eye. It teaches a computer to outline the eye and its socket in MRI scans. Drawing these parts by hand is slow. That has kept eye-imaging studies small. The team used scans from more than twelve hundred adults. They trained a leading deep learning system to trace five parts: the lens, the eyeball, the optic nerve, the eye muscles, and the orbital fat.

The system traced all five parts well. It could also estimate eye length and tissue volumes on its own. That let the team check how eye parts relate to body mass at scale. As a headline product, they release the first large eye atlases made without bias. There are atlases for women, for men, and for both combined. They are meant to standardize future eye MRI research.
plos-pone-0352357:
Shumani Makhadi and three colleagues pool the evidence on emergency trauma surgery in poorer countries. Their 2026 systematic review covers damage control laparotomy. The technique opens the abdomen, stops the bleeding fast, and postpones full repair. It serves patients caught in the lethal triad of cold, acidity, and failed clotting. Ten retrospective studies, covering nine hundred fourteen patients in five countries, met the criteria. South African hospitals supplied over three-quarters of the cases.

The pooled death rate landed near thirty-eight percent. Study results varied widely, with substantial statistical heterogeneity. Fragmented evidence is itself the finding. Wealthy countries document this operation thoroughly; the places carrying the heaviest trauma loads report it patchily. A pooled mortality figure gives surgeons and ministries a first benchmark for their own units. It also argues for trauma registries in low-income settings, so the next review can compare like with like.
plos-pone-0352457:
Aaron Kolb and six colleagues infect mice with herpes simplex virus to test whether a protein called thrombospondin-1 shapes eye disease, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The protein normally helps control inflammation and blood-vessel growth in the cornea, and herpes infection there can cloud vision. Mice bred to lack the protein were compared with normal mice after their corneas were infected with two virus strains.

Disease severity, corneal clouding, vessel growth, and nerve loss were the same in both groups. Antibody and T-cell responses also matched. A severe whole-eye inflammation appeared with one strain in both kinds of mice. The negative result suggests other family proteins cover for the missing one.
plos-pone-0352757:
Sama Koliaei and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One chemistry study of four hawthorn species. Hawthorn is valued for medicine and food. The team tested leaves and fruits of each species. They measured phenolic compounds, the plant chemicals behind hawthorn's antioxidant fame. They also measured total antioxidant strength. The question was how much species and growing site shape that chemistry.

Phenolic levels varied hugely between species. Some compounds differed several-fold. Fruit phenols and flavonoids rose together closely. Grouping placed two species near each other. A third stood clearly apart, with the richest store of key compounds. Tests linked antioxidant strength to certain phenolic families. The authors say these profiles can guide which species to develop for health products. Local growing conditions should be factored in too.
plos-pone-0352857:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, sort younger Chinese patients with high blood pressure by how well they understand their medicines. Taking daily pills for decades only works if patients grasp doses, timing, and risks. More than five hundred patients at two large hospitals answered scales on medication knowledge, social support, confidence, and how they view their illness.

A profiling method found three groups: about a third with low medication literacy, half in the middle, and a small top group. Education and household income sorted people strongly: less of each meant the low group. Rich social support, confidence in managing health, and a more hopeful view of the illness marked the top group. The authors propose tiered help: plain teaching for the lowest group, habit-building support for the middle, and lighter touch for the strongest.
plos-pone-0353157:
Mols and colleagues ran a one-day check of emergency care across hospitals in the Netherlands in a 2026 study. For twenty-four hours, twenty-eight hospitals recorded adults who came to emergency rooms for internal medicine care. The aim was to see how many visits grew out of long-term illness and how many could be handled elsewhere.

Nearly half of the visits involved a sudden flare of a long-term condition. About a quarter of all visits were judged avoidable, and about two in five patients could have used a clinic or direct admission unit instead. Most hospitals had such options, but poor organization blocked their use, which points to fixes in planning rather than new buildings.
plos-pone-0353257:
Hongyang Chen and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One systematic review of radiomics, a technique that mines medical images for patterns predicting whether lung cancer carries a particular resistance mutation. The mutation, called T790M, blunts the effect of a major class of targeted drugs, so knowing its status guides treatment. The reviewers pooled thirteen studies covering more than twenty-six hundred patients.

Models tested on their own data performed strongly, but accuracy dropped when applied to outside patients, a common warning sign in this field. Performance also shifted with imaging type, the body site imaged, and study quality. The authors conclude that image-based prediction is promising for avoiding repeat biopsies, though better-standardized studies are needed before clinical use.
plos-pone-0353357:
Ryan A Denu led a team of eight authors on this 2026 claims study of a cancer drug used in the United States. Regorafenib is approved as a later option for advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors, a rare gut cancer, after earlier targeted drugs fail. The team mined insurance records spanning 2015 to 2023 for patients who filled the drug.

Patients starting on a lower dose stayed on treatment about as long as those on the standard dose, and waited similar times before switching therapy. People who had taken only one earlier drug fared longer than those who had taken two. Denu calls for outcome studies next.
plos-pone-0353457:
Murungweni and colleagues interviewed fishing stakeholders about plastic pollution at a South African reservoir in a 2026 study. Thirty people took part: commercial fishers, recreational fishers, and fish sellers around Nandoni Dam. Nearly all knew plastic pollution was a problem, yet most had only a thin grasp of microplastics.

Groups differed in who they blamed, most often pointing to visitors, with some naming local residents. Willingness to join cleanup action was also explored. Managers who understand how each group sees the problem can design campaigns that fishers support rather than ignore, since daily users witness the waste first.
plos-pone-0353757:
Michihiro Tateyama and Yoshihiro Kubo examine how the female hormone estradiol interacts with an ion channel found in immune cells of the brain, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The channel, THIK-1, lets potassium ions flow and helps control inflammation in microglia. The team applied steroids to the mouse channel in the laboratory and measured the currents that passed.

Estradiol turned the channel down by roughly forty percent. Computer docking and targeted mutations pinpointed where the hormone likely sits: a cavity above the channel's gate. Some mutations made the channel exquisitely sensitive instead, responding to far weaker hormone levels. The work hints that hormone differences could tune brain inflammation between people.
plos-pone-0354157:
Suxiang Qin and Songwen Wei build in 2026 a combined vision and language system for studying marketing images. Their system must find brand logos in busy scenes, link pictures with their text, and judge how much viewers will like the look of an advert. Three linked parts handle detection, alignment, and a tuning method that keeps training costs low.

On public logo and beauty rating sets, their system beat well known earlier methods on detection and on predicting taste scores. It also sorted marketing success well in their tests. Brands could use such tools to check creative work before spending on a full campaign.
plos-pone-0354257:
Siam and colleagues, in a 2026 study, trace the family tree of the small white butterfly, a cabbage pest found on nearly every continent. The butterfly spread worldwide through both natural flight and human trade. The team read one gene from more than a thousand samples across five continents to see how populations connect.

They found well over a hundred distinct versions of the gene. Europe held the richest mix, which fits an old home range. North America held few versions but with deep differences between them, a sign the continent was colonized more than once from different sources. Most variation sat within populations rather than between them, and distance alone did not explain the pattern. A web-like family tree, with a few very common versions at its center, points to recent rapid spread. The authors say trade routes, not just wind, wrote this pest's travel history.
plos-pone-0354357:
Pons-Gomila and colleagues, in 2026, measured how hard different training tasks are for women who play basketball. Fourteen players wore tracking and heart rate gear across twenty-two weeks of practice. The team sorted drills into three kinds: drills with no opponent, small-sided games, and full competitive formats.

Small-sided games produced higher values than competitive play on almost every measure, from distance run to jumps and hard changes of speed. Drills with no opponent also beat full games on distance, bursts of speed, and jumps, though full games kept heart rates high for longer. Bigger court space raised the load for most measures as well. For coaches, the message is practical: the shape of a drill and the size of the space can tune how much strain a session puts on players.
plos-pone-0354457:
Majima and colleagues, in a 2026 field study, measure radiation in parts of Okuma Town, Fukushima, where residents are being allowed to return. The town sat next to the damaged nuclear plant, and some zones are set aside for returnees before homes are cleaned up or torn down. Knowing actual dose levels is basic to honest return policy.

Surveys drove radiation meters along roads across the return zones, and teams also measured at house entrances before cleanup. Road readings fell clearly between late 2024 and late 2025. At homes, yearly dose estimates for most areas sat under the government's reference level for lifting evacuation orders. They did not, however, reach the long-term target set after the accident, which is far lower. The authors offer the gap between those two benchmarks as the real policy question: safe enough to return by rule, yet above the level promised for the long run.
plos-pone-0354757:
Can Çelebi and Stefan Penczynski test in 2026 how well human codebooks work as prompts when large language models classify text from experiments. Three codebooks from experimental economics were used, covering promise keeping and strategic thinking. Prompt detail, format, framing, and wording were varied across two commercial and two open models, and results were compared with human annotators.

Codebooks as prompts agreed with humans at a high rate across tasks. On a recognition heavy task, model choice drove accuracy most, while on learning heavy tasks, instruction detail mattered as much. Extra content helped larger models but could hurt smaller ones. Write prompts like good human instructions, the authors urge.
plos-pone-0354857:
Lijing Yang, Wanju Wang, and Yajuan Chen apply in 2026 an explainable learning method to find what shapes how long mothers breastfeed. Records followed a modest group of mothers after birth, covering birth details, body factors, and social background. The model was built to handle tangled, non straight line links and to show which factor mixes mattered most.

The model sorted long and short feeding well, above all catching most long term cases. Risk rose when a surgical birth combined with long milk blockage, and when highly educated mothers moved to mixed feeding. The authors argue for support aimed at such specific profiles rather than general lessons for everyone.
plos-pone-0354957:
Haoran Wang and colleagues study in 2026 what helps visitors feel restored at Mount Emei, a sacred heritage site in China. Hundreds of visitors at ten spots answered surveys, and crews also measured real sound levels on site. The team tested whether liking the site's sounds worked in part by making the place feel culturally true.

Liking the sounds linked both directly to feeling restored and to a stronger sense of cultural truth, which itself linked to restoration. Sound thus helped in two ways, through the senses and through meaning. Site managers may treat bells, chants, and natural sounds as part of care for visitors, not mere background.
plos-pone-0355057:
Martin Aman and seven colleagues compare surgical strategies for preventing painful neuromas after nerve cuts, in this 2026 rat study. When a nerve is severed, its stump can sprout a disorganized, tender ball of fibers. Forty rats received either a sham operation, heat coagulation of the stump, or one of two commercial nerve caps, made of chitosan or a biodegradable plastic, over the cut sciatic nerve. Twelve weeks later the team examined the tissue directly, by MRI, and through blinded surgeon ratings.

Capped stumps formed denser, more contained neuromas with far more nerve fibers and thicker insulation than untreated stumps. Coagulation, however, matched the caps on those microscopic measures despite lumpier outward shapes, and surgeons' ratings echoed the macroscopic pattern. The authors conclude caps genuinely organize regeneration, while the simpler coagulation remains a credible option, supporting more personalized surgical choices.
plos-pone-0355457:
Olusiji Adebola Lasekan and co-authors dissected how African leaders built sustainability arguments in their 2025 United Nations speeches, then turned the patterns into a teaching model. The corpus held twenty-one English speeches totalling about fifty thousand words. Their 2026 analysis worked across word choice, grammar, sentence shape, persuasive strategy, and whole-speech structure.

Meaning rode mainly on vocabulary and on how speeches were organised. Urgency and collective agency dominated the persuasive moves. Tools like obligation verbs, conditionals, and problem-then-solution sequencing mapped onto named sustainability skills. Strategic and people skills dominated the speeches. Lasekan and colleagues package the mapping as a grammar-to-sustainability classroom model for education programmes.
plos-pone-0355557:
Camilla Mapstone, Julia Handl, and David Talavera stress-test the hope that machine learning on whole genomes can find disease-causing gene combinations. Dosage effects across many genes are thought to drive disease, but the search space is enormous. The team built benchmarks two ways. Real data came with known answers. Synthetic data came with dials for size and noise. Standard models were then trained to classify patients and to name the guilty genes.

A plain regression model proved most reliable at fingering the true genes across synthetic worlds, even when its raw classification score lagged flashier rivals. Attempts on a major biobank dataset failed outright, and digging in showed why: models stumbled unless the activity of working genes was taken into account. Mapstone and colleagues say genome-wide learners must respect which genes are actually switched on.
plos-pone-0355957:
Khai Truong and co-authors re-tuned a DNA test for a gut parasite increasingly found on American-grown produce. Cyclospora spreads through contaminated food and water, and tracing outbreaks needs reliable environmental testing. The original assay was validated on a discontinued machine. Their 2026 study optimised it for a current laboratory platform.

Only three settings needed change: a slightly lower binding temperature, more cycles, and a later cutoff for calling a result positive. With those tweaks, the test matched the original platform's performance on spiked farm water. Checks against near-neighbour organisms guarded against false alarms. Truong and colleagues deliver a ready protocol for labs that must run the official method on modern equipment.
plos-pone-0356257:
Olivia Smith and seven colleagues check whether a lab test for filoviruses, the family that includes Ebola, gives the same answers in very different laboratories, reporting in 2026. Their bead-based test can detect antibodies against several filoviruses at once, which is valuable for tracking past infections and vaccine responses. Samples were tested both at a university lab in Hawaii and at the national research institute in Kinshasa, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Results from the two sites matched closely, with variation staying below preset limits for every target. Samples from Ebola survivors and close contacts, plus hundreds taken before and after vaccination in Congo, showed the expected patterns. Vaccine-related antibody signals rose after vaccination, while signals for other filoviruses stayed flat. The authors say the test is reproducible enough for surveillance and vaccine studies across settings.
plos-pone-0356757:
Thomas U Grund, writing in PLOS ONE in 2026, asks whether a well known quirk of the mind also shapes whole crowds. People tend to dwell on bad news more than good news, a pattern called negativity bias. Grund tests whether fan communities focus their dislike on a few targets while spreading their affection much more widely.

He studies reports from more than thirty-six thousand German football fans about the clubs they love and hate. Dislike turned out to be far more tightly focused than affection, both in what fans sent out and in what clubs received. Love and hate also moved mostly independently of each other. The result suggests that the structure of rivalry, and of conflict more broadly, is built into how groups divide their attention.
plos-pone-0357057:
Donghuan Bai, Xiaodong Cao, and Shuolei Feng studied a common running injury in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Marathon runners often develop pain around the kneecap, called patellofemoral pain syndrome. Weak hips are one suspect, since hip control affects how the knee tracks during each stride.

Bai and his colleagues compared records of runners given hip stability training with runners given standard care. They tracked pain and the Q-angle, a measure of knee alignment. The comparison tests whether stronger hips truly ease this pain. For coaches and physios, evidence of that kind guides whether hip work should be a routine part of treating runner's knee.
plos-pone-0357457:
Guillaume P Fernandez, Eric D Widmer, and Robin Dodsworth ask whether the company around a conversation changes how speakers talk, in PLOS ONE in 2026. People unconsciously match a partner's way of speaking to signal closeness, a habit called linguistic accommodation. Most research treats that matching as a private affair between two people. This team suspected the speaker's wider personal network shapes it too.

Twenty-one young adults recorded themselves across seventy-one conversations and mapped their personal networks. The researchers measured matching through the use of intensifier words, those small boosters like really and so. Speakers matched more when their partner sat at the center of a dense, uniform cluster inside the speaker's network, a tight subgroup drawn from one social world. Accommodation, it turns out, answers not just to the person in front of you, but to the audience standing behind them.
plos-pone-0357957:
Kuan-Ting Chen and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE from a humanitarian medical mission that a Taiwanese hospital ran at three sites in Ukraine in April 2026. War disrupts the steady care high blood pressure needs, yet screening data from active conflict zones are rare. The team measured blood pressure in adults attending the mission and traced the care cascade: who knew their condition, who was treated, who had it controlled.

About two-thirds of adults screened had raised blood pressure on the raw count, and even after age adjustment more than half did. Rates climbed with age and were higher in men and in people with obesity. About three-quarters of those affected knew it, but fewer than six in ten were treated and only about one in six had pressure controlled. The mission model, they say, can find and reconnect patients whose care the war has broken.
plos-pone-0358257:
Eirette Santiago and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on plant defense. Plants can react to a warning cue that an attack is coming, before any insect actually feeds. The authors study responses that are specific to the herbivore involved, rather than one general alarm.

A pre-attack risk cue lets a plant prepare defenses early, but preparing the wrong defense wastes resources. Testing whether responses match the coming herbivore shows how finely plants can read these signals. Ecologists and crop scientists share an interest here, since pest warning systems in farming rest on the same idea of early, targeted defense.
plos-pone-0358357:
Koray Samet Altınçekiç leads a team of eight testing whether a minute of foam rolling sharpens young basketball players' reactions, in PLOS ONE in 2026. One hundred two male players aged sixteen to eighteen were assigned to roll for thirty seconds per body region, sixty seconds, or simply rest. Hand reaction time to a visual signal was measured before and after, with the best single trial as the headline score.

The shorter rolling dose beat the longer one clearly across best, average, and median scoring. Against rest, the advantage reached significance only on the best trial analysis, not on average or median performance, and one standard statistical model broke its own assumptions, forcing a bootstrap recheck. The authors' honest summary is mixed: brief foam rolling may sharpen a player's single fastest response, but claims of a broad reaction boost outrun this evidence.
plos-pone-0358457:
Juliana Ofosua Addo leads a team of eight measuring fear of childbirth among pregnant women in Kumasi, Ghana, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two hundred eighty-two women attending antenatal care at a primary facility completed a standard fear questionnaire. The authors deliberately split their analysis by parity, whether a woman had given birth before, arguing that first time mothers and experienced mothers fear different things and need different support.

About twenty-two percent of the women scored in the high to severe fear range. First time mothers reported clearly higher fear than those who had delivered before. When the team modeled what drives fear inside each group separately, the determinants differed by parity, matching their opening argument. A first time mother's fear grows from the unknown; a returning mother's often grows from memory. Antenatal programs that treat the two as one audience, the authors imply, will comfort neither well.
plos-pone-0358557: Munna and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on artificial intelligence in women's reproductive health. As a scoping review, it maps global trends in diagnosis tools. It also names gaps in methods and sets an agenda for putting tools to work where resources are scarce. AI tests that only work in rich hospitals leave most of the world out.
plos-pone-0358657:
Fukai Zhao leads a team of seven refining how scans predict who will benefit from bypass surgery, in PLOS ONE in 2026. In ischemic cardiomyopathy, parts of the heart muscle are starved but still alive, hibernating rather than dead. Surgery helps those patients most, and PET scans can map living tissue. The standard mismatch reading is contested, so the team compared it with a simpler ratio drawn from the same scans in fifty-three patients who went on to bypass operations.

About sixty percent of patients regained meaningful pumping strength after surgery. The uptake ratio between damaged and healthy zones predicted that recovery well, clearly beating the conventional mismatch index for the more common recovery threshold. It did not predict later major cardiac events. The authors call the ratio a useful quantitative companion to the standard reading, while asking for larger multi center validation before it guides who gets an operation.
plos-pone-0359657:
Alison McAfee and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It examines honey bee queens imported into Canada from around the globe. The authors record pheromone features, the chemical signals a queen produces, alongside morphometric features, precise measurements of her body.

Queen quality decides how well a colony thrives, and Canadian beekeepers import many queens each year. Comparing chemical and physical traits across source countries tells buyers and regulators what differs between suppliers. Beekeepers choosing stock, and scientists studying queen health, both gain from a profile of what imported queens actually look like.
plos-pone-0359957:
Sudarshawn Damodharan and James Tonsgard wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a systematic review, combined with a meta-analysis, of MEK inhibitors, a class of targeted drugs. The patients are people with NF1, a genetic condition, who have symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, tumors growing along nerves that surgery cannot safely remove.

The review weighs efficacy and safety together across the available studies. Families facing these disfiguring and painful tumors have few options, so a careful pooling of drug evidence guides real treatment choices. Neurologists and oncologists who manage NF1 are the readers who need this balanced summary.
plos-pone-0360057:
Qian Zhu and co-authors applied and evaluated in 2026 a system of quality indicators for pharmaceutical care in pain management around orthopedic surgery. Patients recovering from bone and joint operations need pain relief that is effective yet safe, and pharmacists play a central part in getting doses and drug choices right. A quality indicator system sets measurable standards for that care, so hospitals can see where practice falls short.

The authors describe building the indicator set for the perioperative period, the span before, during, and after surgery, and testing how it performs in use. Systems like this turn good intentions into checkable routines. They also give hospitals a fair way to compare units and track improvement over time.
pmc-13224757:
The 17th EUNOS Congress collects the abstracts of the European Neuro-Ophthalmology Society meeting, held in Milan, Italy, in June 2026. The journal Neuro-Ophthalmology, the society's official journal, publishes the set as a supplement. Neuro-ophthalmology covers vision problems rooted in the brain and nerves, a field where eye doctors and neurologists work side by side.

More than one hundred and fifty abstracts span the field's range. Talks cover age-related change in the optic nerve sheath, European stroke vision guidelines, and a severe case of Tolosa-Hunt syndrome. Others report pupillography catching a torn carotid artery behind acute Horner syndrome, and a nose-delivered nerve growth factor in mice. Readers get the whole meeting in brief, talk by talk.
pmc-13237057:
Wang and colleagues review the gut and bone axis, the two-way link between digestion and the skeleton. Osteoporosis thins bone and raises fracture risk worldwide. New research ties it to the microbes living in the gut, whose mix shifts with diet and which send signals that can build bone up or wear it down.

The review gathers evidence on how eating patterns and nutrients reshape gut microbes, and how those shifts reach bone. Fermented foods, fibre, and certain nutrients recur as levers worth testing. The authors argue that future care for weak bones may treat the gut as part of the skeleton's support system, not a separate organ.
pmc-13241457:
Kebke's team in Glasgow set the fats of whale skin against blubber in Northeast Atlantic pilot whales. Diet studies sample blubber almost exclusively, leaving the epidermis uncharacterized. Gas chromatography mapped epidermis plus outer and inner blubber layers separately. Twenty-nine of 34 fatty acids split sharply between layers.

Skin lipids proved rich in wax esters and saturated fats, suiting barrier and insulation roles. Diet-tied polyunsaturated fats concentrated instead in the inner blubber. Skin make-up therefore cannot substitute for blubber in dietary analysis. Kebke puts forward epidermal sampling as a health-monitoring tool for elusive whale species.
pmc-13241557:
Kim's team in South Korea screened oxide coatings computationally to protect mid-nickel cathode plates in all-solid-state batteries. Such plates promise stability and capacity, but their faces degrade against solid electrolytes. The team scored candidate coatings on voltage stability, interface strength, and lithium-ion movement. Eight materials passed the strict first pass.

A lithium scandium phosphate coating stood out among the finalists. Simulations showed it stays stable above four volts and conducts lithium ions well for an oxide. Large-scale dynamics runs showed it shields the cathode surface from breakdown. It also stopped the neighboring sulfide electrolyte from decomposing, marking it as a strong protective layer.
pmc-13241957:
Zhou's team in Chengdu ask whether smoking leaves a measurable mark on facial attractiveness. Twelve years of China Family Panel data supplied over one hundred nineteen thousand observations. Interviewers rated each respondent's looks on a seven-point scale. Fixed-effects models stripped out personal and yearly constants.

Current smokers scored slightly but significantly lower than non-smokers. Heavier daily consumption made the penalty worse in dose-response fashion. The association concentrated among men, married respondents, and those over 35. It faded among women, the unmarried, and the young. Zhou suggests testing appearance-based appeals in tobacco control.
pmc-13242357:
Goel and Mahadule at AIIMS Rishikesh defend physiology against reports of its decline. Their piece looks back over five hundred years from Fernel and Bernard onward. The field backs blood-flow science, heart tracing, nitric oxide biology, and oxygen sensing. It also guides daily bedside tests from lung checks to renal clearance.

Gene-era reductionism, they argue, pushed broad thinking aside without solving complex disease. Beta-blockers in heart failure show body logic beating first guesses. Wearables, organ chips, digital twins, and AI tools now offer the field new tools. Public health know-how campaigns could help restore the field's standing.
pmc-13242457:
Martin Bichler, writing in Electronic Markets in 2026, examines what happens when AI agents start doing the shopping. Generative agents can now search, compare, and buy across online marketplaces on a person's behalf. Classic search theory says cheaper searching should sharpen competition and improve matches between buyers and sellers. Bichler argues that this happy outcome is not automatic.

Studies show today's agents stray from optimal search behavior, and those quirks act like hidden search costs even when technical costs fall to near zero. Floods of AI-generated listings also blur the signals buyers rely on, making offers harder to tell apart. Cheap entry invites waves of low-value sellers, and the mix can lock a market into a poor equilibrium. pmc-13244257:
Pieter Juanarta and colleagues compared life quality after two laser eye operations that both promise freedom from glasses. Their prospective study appeared in the Journal of Ophthalmology in 2026. At an Indonesian eye hospital, fifty-seven patients completed vision quality questionnaires and dry-eye testing after surgery. Thirty-three had FS-LASIK, which cuts a flap. Twenty-four had SMILE, which removes a lens-shaped sliver through a small cut.

Both groups saw well, but their day-to-day experience diverged. SMILE patients reported the stronger improvement in quality of life. The pattern fits the wider literature the authors cite, where SMILE leaves fewer dry-eye complaints and fewer postoperative symptoms than flap surgery. Eyesight charts alone, they argue, understate what patients gain. A procedure can win on the letter chart and still lose on comfort. Their conclusion supports counseling patients on symptoms and daily feel, not just the prescription.
pmc-13245057:
Akhtar Ali and colleagues pin down how a stress-hormone protein times flowering in Arabidopsis, the model plant. Their study appeared in Plant Signaling and Behavior in 2026. Abscisic acid, the drought hormone, also delays the switch to flowering, but the wiring was murky. The team focused on ABI2, a core signaling protein earlier reported to promote flowering, and compared normal plants with an abi2 mutant across the flowering gene network.

In the mutant, the floral repressors FLC and CDF1 were strongly switched on. The promoters of flowering were turned down, the mark of delayed bloom. The mutant also carried more of the ABI5 protein, in a more active state. Genetic tests placed ABI2 upstream, acting as a brake on ABI5. The authors cast ABI2 as a fine-tuning switch where drought signaling meets the flowering clock. Such switches interest breeders weighing yield against climate stress.
pmc-13245757:
Islam, Shompa, and Hasnat mined an infamous weed for medicines in this 2026 PLOS One study. Water hyacinth chokes lakes and rivers worldwide, yet its flowers carry pharmacologically interesting compounds. The team separated the flower extract's petroleum-ether-soluble fraction and isolated five molecules, including the flavonoids kaempferol and luteolin and the plant sterol stigmasterol, identifying them by nuclear magnetic resonance.

The fraction fought microbes moderately, with its strongest effect against Bacillus subtilis, and dissolved blood clots modestly in a dish. In mice with castor-oil diarrhea, it cut episode counts in a dose-dependent way approaching the standard drug loperamide. Docking simulations suggested the isolated compounds engage relevant protein targets plausibly. The authors frame the invader as a low-cost raw material for multi-action natural products, pending deeper study.
pmc-13246557:
Vaia, Kim, Jeyasingh, and co-authors report an infant's case that widens the picture of a rare brain disorder, in this 2026 Neurological Sciences brief report. DEGS1-related leukodystrophy comes from a faulty gene for making fatty molecules the brain's insulation, myelin, depends on. Their patient showed abnormal eye movements and halted development early, with weak muscle tone, severe feeding trouble, and stubborn epilepsy.

Brain scans showed poor myelination, a thin corpus callosum, and cerebellar involvement, as expected. Unexpectedly, scans also revealed calcium deposits inside the cerebellum and scattered spots elsewhere, a feature not previously tied to this disease. The authors propose that such calcifications may serve as a diagnostic clue in infants with similar presentations.
pmc-13247557:
Jonsson and co-authors measured wood rotting in rivers across a continent, in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Decomposing plant litter feeds river food webs, but climate, landscape, and human pressure all tug at the rate. The team placed standardized wood sticks in seventy-two river locations across seven catchments in Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden, pairing the rot measurements with remote-sensing and field data on each site.

Decomposition sped up as mean annual temperature rose and slowed where human population density was higher, with smaller dampening effects from rainfall and wider channels. Surprisingly, land-use intensity and riparian vegetation showed no clear effect. The authors project that warming will steadily accelerate river wood decay, shortening how long this carbon source persists in streams, even as crowded catchments work in the opposite direction.
pmc-13248357:
Amaefuna, Morgan, and Bekibele ran a crossover trial on mask-related dry eye in Abuja, Nigeria, published in 2026. Exhaled air leaking upward from a facemask can dry the eyes during long shifts. The trial asked whether taping the mask's top edge to the nose bridge prevents that irritation among hospital staff.

Seventy-seven health workers each wore a mask for six hours on two days, taped once and untaped once. Symptoms, tear volume, and tear stability worsened after untaped wear and improved with taping. The authors conclude that a short stretch of mask wear can trigger dry eye, and that simple taping reduces the effect.
pmc-13248457:
Freese and colleagues surveyed German family doctors about climate duty, in a 2026 BMC Medical Ethics paper. Heat and pollution increasingly shape patient health, and professional codes cast doctors as public role models. The team asked five hundred general practitioners how far that responsibility reaches into daily practice.

About two thirds called climate and environment topics relevant to their role, and most accepted doctors as societal examples. Far fewer felt personally responsible inside the clinic, placing duty instead with institutions and policymakers. Women reported stronger concern than men. The authors recommend clearer guidance in standards, guidelines, and training so doctors know what their role asks of them.
pmc-13250257:
Ziyaei and co-authors describe a woman whose fear of a fatal brain disease produced movements that mimicked it. Their 2026 Clinical Case Reports paper covers illness anxiety disorder, where worry about serious illness persists despite normal test results. The patient became convinced that she had Huntington's disease, a rare inherited condition.

The thirty-eight-year-old woman reported rhythmic, involuntary movements of her head and body. Her history included chronic stress, repeated major losses, and a highly emotional family upbringing. Brain examinations and laboratory tests found nothing abnormal, yet her conviction about Huntington's disease held firm. The authors note that earlier reports tied such anxiety to other degenerative diseases, making this Huntington's-focused case unusual.
pmc-13250457:
Murshadul Alam Murad and colleagues surveyed stroke risk in Bangladesh for this 2026 study. Stroke is rising there, yet no local work had compared five-year and ten-year risk or pinned down which factors matter most.

The team collected data from 158 adults in the Rajshahi region using a phone-based risk tool. Average risk came out at about five percent over five years and 18 percent over ten. Age, blood sugar, and an uneven heartbeat rhythm drove the five-year risk. For ten years, age, high blood pressure, smoking, and the rhythm problem stood out. The authors call for mass awareness to cut these changeable risks.
pmc-13251057:
Takahashi surveys city dental patients who had also received care in rural areas, hunting for discontent that satisfaction scores miss. The 2026 Patient Preference and Adherence pilot ran an anonymous paper questionnaire at one Tokyo dental clinic. Ninety patients compared their urban and rural medical experiences, emotions, and unspoken complaints.

Just over two in five felt a real difference between city and countryside care, while about half felt little or none. Among those who noticed differences, nearly half reported feelings like inconvenience, discomfort, or quiet endurance. Of patients with concerns they could have raised, about two thirds never told the facility. Takahashi warns that high satisfaction and few complaints do not prove contentment, and calls for larger multi-site studies.
pmc-13251757:
Hao and Jiang review a nose-based nerve block as a gentler option for headaches after spinal anesthesia in new mothers. Their 2026 Journal of Pain Research paper covers postdural puncture headache, a common setback that slows recovery after childbirth procedures. The standard fix, an epidural blood patch, works but carries its own risks.

The sphenopalatine ganglion block numbs a nerve bundle reached through the nose, needs no opioids, and is generally well tolerated. The review explains the anatomy, proposed mechanisms, and practical techniques behind the block. Evidence so far comes mostly from case reports and small series in obstetric patients. The authors close with the controversies and open questions that larger trials still need to settle.
pmc-13253757:
Junhan Zhou and co-authors examine death risk in a 2026 study of 9,598 United States adults aged 20 and older. Data came from national health surveys in 2003 to 2006 and 2009 to 2014, with deaths tracked to 2019. The team weighed CKM syndrome, a linked heart, kidney, and metabolic state, plus psoriasis, a skin disease.

Over a median 9.3 years, 860 deaths occurred. Advanced CKM alone raised all-cause death risk, with a hazard ratio of 3.67, and psoriasis alone raised it to 2.06. Adults with both had the highest risk, at 7.09, and heart or brain death risk reached 16.47. The authors say adults with both states form a high-risk group that needs close, long-term heart and metabolic care.
pmc-13256057:
Cai, Shang, and Lu measured personal mastery, the sense of control over one's life, in two hundred thirty-four gout patients attending a Shandong gout center in late 2023. Participants completed scales for mastery, mindfulness, and confidence in managing pain, alongside general information. The team then modeled which factors predicted a stronger sense of control.

Mastery scores sat at a moderate level overall. Higher education, higher income, greater mindfulness, and stronger pain self-efficacy all predicted better mastery, while visible tophi and multiple other illnesses predicted worse. The authors advise clinicians to watch patients with fewer resources and more disease burden, and to build mindfulness and pain confidence.
pmc-13258557:

Capsaicin silenced several genes the virus needs to copy itself and cut production of new virus particles. Protein and metabolite profiling showed the treated cells rewiring metabolism, chromatin, and skeleton pathways. Several host switches that normally trigger viral reactivation were turned down. The authors frame capsaicin as a multi-target candidate worth developing against these cancers.
pmc-13264957:
